OLD rIOLLEIII. RCM shall we tell an angel From another guest? How from the common worldly herd One of the Blest? Hint of suppressed halo, hustle of hidden wings, Wafture of Heavenly frankincense— Which of these things? The old Sphynx smiles so subtly: "I give no golden rule— Yet would I bid thee, World, treat well Whom thou calFst fool." —East and West.

- - - - The following brief but pathetic sentence was in- scribed in the note-book kept at an hotel on a Welsh mountain. "Viewed the mist and missed the view P' The grand, and, indeed, the only character of truth, is its capability of enduring the test of universal experience, and coming unchanged out of every possible form of fair
discussion. "Oh, mamma, won't you please give me a piece of that cake?" "No, my dear; it will make you sick." "I don't want to eat it; I only want to make some sinkers
_ for my fish-line." Stanley claims to have discovered vast forests of indiarubber trees in the interior of Africa. Whether he has gutta perchasable claim to the territory or not re-
mains to be seen. Ella: "What makes you buy such expensive soap? I shouldn't think you could afford it." Bella: "Oh, it doesn't cost so very much in the course of the year. I

use so little, you know." : Visitor (in court room) : "What dastardly crime was committed by the prisoner who was just convicted ?" •" Fle stole a ride on a railroad." "And the man who got free?" "He stole the railroad." The motto marked upon our foreheads, written upon our door-posts. channelled in the earth, and wafted upon the waves, is and must be, "Labour is honourable, and idleness is dishonourable." By labour the earth has been subdued, and man redeemed from barbarism; nor has a single step in civilisation been made without it. Labour is not only a necessity and a duty, but a blessing. A PERPLEXING ANSWEE.—Poet (meeting editor on his way to his' sanctum) : "Does it make any difference to you if I write on both sides of the paper?" Editor (the sequence of his reflections interrupted) : "Was it not you who sent me a poem recently entitled ' Gentle Spring?'" Poet (flattered) : "Yes, sir." Editor (with emphasis) : "Then it loesn't make a particle of differ- anee. Good day, sir."‘" "We are goin to have pie for dianer,a said Bobby to the minister. "Indeed," laughed the dombaie, amused at the little bog's artlessness; "and what kind of pie, Bobby ?" "It's a new kind. Ma was talking this morn- ing about pa bringin' vOll to dinner so often, and pa Bain he didn't care what she thought; and ma said she'd make him eat humble DiA before the day was over, and I s'pose we're goin' to havedt for dinner." WALT WHTEMAN AND THE QUEEN.—WaIt Whitman has written the following lines:— " FOR QUEEN VICTORIA'S BIRTHDAY." An American arbutns bunch, to be put in a little vase, on the Royal breakfast table. Lady, accept a birthday thought—haply an idle gift and token, Right from the scented soil's May-utterance here, (Smelling of countless blessings, prayers, and old-time

s thanks). A bunch of white and pink arbutus, silent, spicy, shy, From nucleon's, Delaware's. or Potomac's woody banks. ONE WAY TO LAY A GHOST.—" Bill Skimmins buried his father in a most unhandsome way very near his barn," saidethe man at the other end of the table. "The neighbours thought it was a shame, and made a good deal of talk about it. One of them thought he would . . .

punish Bill by scaring him, and lay in wait for him near his father's grave on a dark night. As Bill went by on his way from the barn the man rose up as if from the tomb, and exclaimed in a ghostly voice: 'l'm your father, Bill.' 'Who said you wain't?' Bill answered. • Git down thar inter yer hole war yer belong?' and, with a bridle he was carrying, he struck him across the face such a rap that the would-be alarmist carried the scars for months." _2 _

The exact position of a woman's pocket is often a mystery even to herself. At a female missionary meet- , ing. the conductor had finished her address, and there was a solemn nause of expectant attention uotil some sister should feel moved to speak. Presently a white- haired old lady—a mother in Isreal—rose slowly and feebly to her feet. All eyes were turned upon her, and we waited to see whether she wished to make a few re- marks or lead in prayer. One hand, encased in its wrinkled black kid glove, went fumbling and groping among the folds of her skirt. After a long pause, she drew out n clean handkerchief, still in its folds, and then, with an air of relief, slowly sat down again. She had only risen to find her pocket. WOMEN'S RIGHTS IN SWEDEN.—In that wild time of struggle, war, and rapine, in which the foundations of our modern civilisation were laid, free Scandinavia was the home of more than common turmoil and more than common progress. The laws laid down in Sweden in the thirteenth century would shame those in many a modern statute-book, and kings and nobles, however fiercely they fought with each other for the supreme Power—the proud restless Viking blood that owns no lordship vet pulsing in their veins—were unanimous in promoting the welfare of the common people. In Scan- dinavia, first of, all European countries, was woman allowed to share authority with man, not gaining her power by subtlety nor using her influence by stealth, as in the Latin countries, but frankly accepted, in the measure of her competence, as friend fellow-worker, even as captain. Witness the fact that, when the Swedes wished to get rid of Albert of Mecklenburg, a German prince, who, on the strength of some inter- marriage, claimed the Swedish crown, they invited Margaret, Queen of Denmark and Norway. to undertake their cause. Albert, German to the core, mocked at the
idea of this Woman ice, and in his scorn Sent hers whet:

stone, bidding her use it to sharpen her needles and scissors, and leave warlike weapons to men. But Mar- garet gathered an army, took Albert prisoner, and when she had him safe in one of her fortresses sent him a skirt with a train, as if to say. "Who is the woman now ?" These laws, by reason of which, and their in- fluence on the life of the people, the women of Scan- dinavia enjoy the most enviable position in Europe, or perhaps the world, laws which justified a Swedish lady recently in saying, apropos of some English champion of woman's rights: "in our country we have no heroines, :sor our men are all heroes, and grant us our liberties as soon as we ask them"—began in the enactments of a king who never wore the crown, Eirger the Jarl,--2he Sun, • - -

THE pESY-15RESStD MAN IN EnnOPH.—The Prince co. Wales, Says the Outfitter, is undeniably the best-dressed man in :Europe, if not in the world. His wardrobe is lareer and more varied than that of any other man of ,7fas-itlon, it s recorded that upon a recent taking of in- ventory at ma.rlborougn House, it was found that the heir- apparent to ,the throne possessed as many as three hundred pairs of h'ousers. How many waistcoats, morn- ing coats, afternOon "ts, jackets, hunting. suits, dress , 4: -ners it was never learned, but coats, overcoats, and ux..' the stock was sufficiently. arge to set up a first-class .clothing establishment. the Pr...nce does not confine his. trade to any one tailor. All the btu tailors of London,' t and several of the little ones, are at differe times corn- -2 mis:ioned to make clothing for him. .The prices of these garments vary, but it may be set down as almost tam n that the PrinCB does not pay very much for them. In fact, once upon a time, when there was some discus- sion about Parliament paying off his debts, it was learned that he had not paid his tailors' bills for some years. That, however, Is neither here nor there; he pos. Sesses the clothing, and has unlimited credit to get as much more as he wishes. Usually the Prince dresses in very good taste • he has numerous valets, and one of these attends solely to his wardrobe. The Prince clothes him- self in such garments as that worthy may select for him. He is very fond of black clothing, and the Prince Albert. coat, named in his honour, or, more properly speaking, the frock coat, is one of his favourites. He is also very fond of varnished boots and white over-gaiters, and he delights in a silk hat. He had such an extensive ward- robe that it is seldom he wears the same suit twice in the same month. He sets the fashion for the town, but is now closoly pursued by his two sons, Prince Eddie, vulgarly known as "collars and cuffs," and Prince George of Wales. When the heir to the throne yes to the Scottish moors for a shooting trip or for fishing, he , arrays himself in Highland costume. If he is to attend a military gathering, he always wears his regimental uniform. If he goes to Oxford or Cambridge for a vlait, he apparels himself like one of the students, wear- ing the ordinary cap and gown. His sons follow his .gxatopfo in the matter of dressing well. They are both partial to tilt; frock coat, varnished boots, and silk hat 'satsi delight tr father. They make an interesting trio :41 Hyde Park, 01. in any of the numerous clubs in which tiirT are membent Yrince.Ediie sets the style in collars and cuffs, and he hag tin; most elaborate and varied assortment of neckwear that can be found any- where in the Queen's dominions. div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
Lord Rosebery has presented to Prince Bismarck the original drawing of the famous _Punch cartoon "Dropping the Pilot," which he purchased from Mr. Tenniel.
To celebrate the engagement of her daughter to Mr. H. M. Stanley, Mrs. Tennant, of Richmond- terrace, Whitehall, will very shortly give a ball, at which the Prince of Wales is expected to be present.

Moussa Bey, we learn from an Armenian corres- pondent, is to be put on his trial again. The Sultan has refused to decorate the " procureur Bey, who had demanded the acquittal of Moussa, and had been recommended to the honour by the recently dismissed Minister of Justice, Djeved Pacha.

Queen Margaret's stay at Naples, writes a corres- pondent, is favoured with magnificent spring weather, and the Corso every evening is crowded. Marvellously beautiful sunsets, a wealth of blossoms and flowers everywhere, and the cool and fragrant moonlight nights, render Naples at this season a scene of enchantment.

The Shah's wife, after being one month in Vienna, and undergoing operations on her left eye by Prof. Fuchs, left on Sunday night to return to Teheran. As was foreseen, adds a Vienna correspondent, her eyesight has been but partly restored, and that only for a time, as the disease, which had already des- troyed the sight of her right eye, was too far ad- vanced to admit of a cure.

A gentleman in a Midland town, dying recently, left the bulk of his fortune to the pastor of the Metropolitan Tabernacle. But the deceased had several relatives ill-provided for, and the trustees resolved to put their case before the preacher. They saw him at his house at Norwood, with the result that Mr,Spurgeon placed the property in their hands for distribution among the needy relatives of the testator.

A private letter received from Mrs. Parnell announces the completion of the negotiations for the grant to her of a pension from the Treasury of the United States. It was proposed that the sum should be fixed at £240 a year, but a Committee of the House of Representatives, to which the matter was referred, recommended an award of half that sum. It is specifically stated that the pension is accorded in consideration of the services of Mrs. Parnell's father, Admiral Stewart, who was 71 years in the active service, and was for a period of 17 years senior officer of the United States Navy.

A memorial is about to be forwarded to the Post- master-General, asking for the establishment in this country of a "Letter Express." The memorial has been signed by the Lord Mayor, Lord Randolph Churchill, Cardinal Manning, the Bishop of London, Lord Wolseley, and Sir John Lubbock. It is urged upon the Post-Master General that among the great mass of letters hourly as 'lug through the depart- ment there must be mai y ,f such importance to the senders that they would gladly pay a small extra fee for immediate delivery. It is suggested that the charge for express delivery should be threepence.

The Queen of Denmark, it is said—and all honour to her if it be correctly said—has forwarded to the Czar all the accounts of the cruel treatment of political prisoners in Siberia. According to a Berlin Correspondent the Czar has answered in a long letter that he would order a strict investigation into the cases mentioned, and punish severely all excesses committed by officials. lle would also have proposals laid before him by his Ministers, in order, as far as possible, to make the condition of the prisoners more endurable. In this connection particular mention was made of the impending Prisons' Congress.

Returned from his trip to Oberammergau, Arch- deacon Farrar sums up his impressions of the Pa.,- sion Play. No unbiassed judgment will, in his opinion, question that its influence up to the present has been good. It has deepened the religious character of" these now prosperous peasants," and been to them the very poetry of their lives. But Archdeacon Farrar also tells us that the gravest and the wisest of the dwellers in this little .village in the Bavarian Alps feel anxious misgivings about the effect of the great periodical influx of alien ele- ments, and not a few have half resolved that this decade shall witness the last Passion Play.

The project of having no pairs is making way among the Radicals. Indeed, as one Scotch Radical somewhat cynically observed, the project is now regarded as so good that already there are:rival claimants for the honour of having originated it. Mr. Labouchere may or may not be the patentee ; but it is certain there is nobody who is readier to an upon it. With all his laborious affectation of idleness and persiflage, Mr. Labouchere is really one of the most hard-working, as he is also one of the most serious, politicians in the House of Commons. As to his hard work, Mr. Horace Voules, his assist- ant in the editorship of "Truth," is sometimes driven to distraction by the amount of copy he receives from his respected chief.

The visit of Surgeon Parke to his home in Ireland has presented some pleasing incidents illustrative of the commonality of feeling between the two countries. Mr. Stanley's gallant colleague belongs to a Protestant family, settled in a purely Catholic district of Ireland, where the Protestants do not number one per cent, of the population. His father is not only a landlord but an agent, and a staunch Conservative to boot. Nevertheless Mr. Parke was met on his arrival by the local branch of the National League, which did him all the honours of its band, and accompanied him in torchlight procession to his father's:house, amid evidences of enthusiasm which could scarcely have been exceeded in the case of Mr. O'Brien or Mr. Dillon.

Huddled away in a hack room in the ancient town of Rye, unfamiliar to the inhabitants, and unknown to the visitor, lie two interesting, almost unique, illustrations ot social life in England of the last century. One is a pillory, the other the iron con- trivance in which murderers were" hung in chains." The last time this instrument (which bears no re- semblance whatever to chains) was used on the 17th of March, 1742, the convict being .a butcher who had chanced to kill the mayor of the town in mis- take for another man. The pillory, which bears evidence of constant usage, was removed to this obscure storehouse at a much later date. It seems a pity that these relics of Merry England should not be in a place where they would be more accessible to the public of to-day. - American gossir

Not very long ago, says an American go, ip, a party of distinguished English visitors were being entertained at a dinner party by Mr. George W. Childs, the millionaire proprietor of the Philadelphia "Ledger." Noticing that one of the guests was looking somewhat intently at a peculiar-shaped dish- holder at one end of the table, the host genially remarke I, "Isn't that a curious bit of plate? Do you know what it is? Well, it is the silver baron's coronet which the poet Lord Byron wore at the coronation of George IV. I have had the velvet cap removed, and by turning it upside down, have con- verted it into a dishholder !" The feelings of the
English guests present may be more easily imagined than described at seeing mashed potatoes steaming in the silver headgear of England's greatest poet.

The Indian' taxpayer has several grievances against the India Office, in that a Mr. Wollaston, with an official income of £9OO or £l,OOO a ' year, and a Mr. Burls, with an official income of £750 per annum, or thereabouts, are both directors of the Civil Service Co-operative Stores in the Hay- market ; that they, in fact, receive salaries as trad- ers, although it is contrary to the rules of the Civil Service that any members of the Service should be actively engaged in trade. What makes it worse is that these highly-salaried officials and tradesmen are men of large private means. Such abuses should be corrected. Messrs. Wollaston and Burls should be called Avon by the chief of their department, Lord Cross, either to resign their directorships at the stores, or their highly-paid posts at the India Office.

A "Gladstone phonographic cabinet" is being prepared in America for presentation to Mr. Glad- stone at an early day. It will include "voice records" of goodwill from all Cabinet Ministers. A "voice letter" from Mr. Wanamaker, Postmaster- General of the United States, one of those Ministers who has spoken to Mr. Gladstone by phonograph, has been communicated to Sir James Whitehead, as Chairman of the Penny Postage Jubilee Committee. It is one of the Jubilee greetings from the Post- masters-General of all of the civilized countries of the world, which Colonel Gouraud has undertaken to collect as a souvenir of the recent interesting , celebration, and which, when completed, will be presented to the Corporation of the City of London by Mr. Edison and Colonel Gouraud, together with a phonograph for their future interpretation.

It was a very interesting picture of Heligoland which the "Pall Mall " published on Tuesday night, but we rather fancy that Mr. Frank Gould has been misled by Sir George Campbell in furnishing the island with two cows. When the "Star", man was at Heligorand, there was only one cow. It was the great feature in the show. " Mayo you seen the cow ?" was the first question aske I of the traveller on landing, and it was asked over and over again by every Heligolander, until at last the traveller went upstairs in despair (Heligoland is built in two flats) and saw the cow. After that there was nothing in Heligoland to live for. It has been suggested that perhaps the cow has increased and multiplied since his time. But he says No; any One who knows the Heligoland cow. would scout the notion. Besides, it is an open question whether there is feed for two cows, or even a cow and a half, on the top floor of the island.

There is now no doubt that to-day's (Saturday) Anti-Compensation Demonstration in Hyde Park will be one of the most representative that has ever, taken place in London. Nearly forty members of Parliament have joined the General Council organi- sing the movement. So also have many Parliamen- tary candidates, and about twenty members of the London County Council. Aniang bodies supporting the demonstration are the National Liberal Club, the London Liberal and Radical Union, the Munici- pal Reform League, the many Liberal and Radical clubs of the metropolis, and such labour organise- lions as the Dockers' Union, The manner in which the religious denominations are entering into the movement is remarkable. The Roman Catholics will be strongly represented, and so will the rank and file of the Church of England Temperance Society, in spite of the action of some of their leaders. The Wesleyans and other Methodists will be so numer- ous as to require platforms all to themselves.

Lord Sherbrooke's biography has been written. Rather let us say the life of Robert Lowe, for since his acceptance of the peerage Lord Sherbrooke has practically withdrawn from public affairs, and it is probably with his career as a public man _that the new book will principally deal. Mr. Lowe had the misfortune to take the wrong side in Reform debates, and to introduce an unpopular Budget, but he was a good fighting man, and probably enjoyed the controversies into which he was thrown in con- sequence. It is uncomplimentary to a man to pre- sent him with his epitaph in his lifetime, especially if it is an unkind one, but when Mr. Lowe saw the following epitaph he amused himself by turning it into Latin. The original was :
Here lie the—bones of Robert Lowe, Where he's gone to, I don't know; If to the realms of peace and love, Farewell to happiness above; If haply to some lower level, We can't congratulate the Devil.

BIRDS OF A. FEATHER.
BY GEORGB HULL.
"Han yo heeard o'er owd Tommy Parker ?" in- quired Roger, taking advantage of a pause in the conversation of his guests. _ _ . .
" Nowe," replied bock Robin, up wi' th' owd boy ? " Re's gooan deead," replied Roger. "The deuce he bee !" exclaimed George Walton. " Yigh," said Roger, "he's 'typed o'er at last, for sure."
"I hev'nd ; what's
"Ten year' afoor his time an' o'," remarked Spin- ner Dick ; "poor owd Tommy 1 he wer one 'at med his-eel' owd afoear his time wi' botherin' his brains too' mich."
" He waur," said Roger, "that's true." " Wod waur he, an' wheer did he live?" inspired Rovin' Rondle ; "aw_dornd think aw knew him." . . .

"He owned 'booath a weyvin' shaid (shed) an' a bit ov a feawndry up at th' other end o'th teawn, yon," replied Roger. " Hed he a brother coed Jonathan." inquired Cap- tain Lol, "'at bed a little factory at Bowton ? " "lie just hed," replied Roger; " tha's hit o"th reet mon."

" Ther wer booath funny owd codgers were Tommy an' Jonathan," remarked Cock Robin—" terribly eccentric i' their ways. But they wer gradely business men when they med up their minds to do business: they wasted nayther time nor talk. They use' to trade together a good deeal, dud 0' two brothers, an' aw once hed th' luck to be at Manches- ter one Friday, 'when they wer booath theer. Id wer aside o' th' Exchange as aw coom across 'em, an' they wer booath marchin' away at express speed across th' flags, one comin' fro' th' left hand o me, an' th' other fro' th' reet. They booath looked as busy as possible; but they dudn'd seem to hey owt agate between their two sere, for as they passed one another just at th' front o' me they managed o their compliments an' inquiries, an' bade one another good-bye wi' threo words a-piece. This wer heaw id wawr ; Tommy spoke to Jonathan, an' Jonathan answered just i' this fashion : " Mornin'!" " Mornin' " " Owt ?" "Nowt." " Mornin' 1" _ .
name?"
- " Mornin' !" an' off they booath went, just like shot, leeavin' me starin' after 'ern." _

"0, they wer smart chaps," said Roger. Well, thad bit wer smart," said Bill o' mi Granny's; "iv everybody wer as sharp 'as thad business matters, things would run a deeal easier for everybody." " Just sooa," said Cock Robin, "they'd just geci as mich done, an' hey a deeal more time for gradely rest. . . . Let's see, Roger, yo use' to work for owd Tommy a little bit, dudn'd yo ?" " Yigh," replied Roger," aw hed several months wi' him after aw coom back hooam th' second time. . . Eh ! he were a rum owd stick as ever lived. But he met wi' fooak as quare as hissel' sometimes. Aw worked i' th' feawndry, yo know—storekeepin' an' Bich like ; an one time whol aw wer theer Tommy engaged a new fitter as torned eawt a terble ' good workman. But he wer a careless-lookin' chap, an' when Tommy wer talkia' to him at th' fost aw dudn'd think they'd come to terms. This chap gave Tommy some quare answers to his quare questions, an' aw begun to see that he wer one 'at could read fooak middlin' weel. Ile read owd Tommy at a glance, an' findin' th' owd chap to be eccentric, th' chap evidently thowt th' best way to ged on wer to be as eccentric as him. When Tommy had axed a lot moor questions he coom to th' question o' wages, for his waurnd a club shop ; an' th' chap's answer to this question wer just as cool as his others hed bin. " Wod wage does ti expect, like ?" Tommy axed. "Well," th' chap answered," aw'm a bit optional, like, abeawt thad, Mesthur Parker." " Wod's ti meean ?". said Tommy. "Whey, it's just o' this rooad,' said th' chap, " aw've three prices." "Three prices." said Tommy. "Aye," th' chap.went on, "aw con oather wark for thirty, thirty-two. or thirty-four shillins' a week, just as fooak likes to pay mo ; an' it's good, honest wark, mind yo." "Wel, tha'rt a quare son o' Vulcan, heaw't be!' said Tommy:; "but aw think aw con mek som,e'at on tha. . . . Come thi ways deawn th' shop, an' give us a bit o' thi thirty' bob' a week wark."
Off they went deawn th yard, an' afour long th' fitter bed getten gradely to work, an' feelin' varra fain on't, for he'd bin beawt a long while.
After bed bin agate some time, owd Tommy appeared at his bench, au' stood watchin' him a w

"Well," said Tommy, after a bit, "are ti geddin' to feelin' at hooam, like?" "Aye," said th' chap, " aw am, thank yo." "An' this is thi thirty bob system?" "Id is," th' chap answered. "0," said Tommy, "it's nowt special—look as iv tha hedn'd getten warm, quite. Aw think tha'd better let's hey!' bit e' _thirty-two !"

" Varra weel," said th' chap; an' Tommy left him. But th' next time he wer deawn th' shop he coed o' th' chap ageeon, an' as he stood watchin' him th' second time he could see there wer aboon two shil-
lin'g worth ov an improvement i' th' wark. Th' Chap hed his sleeves rowled up this time, an' he waur mekkin' 0' steel fllin's an' tackle fly abeawt i' rare fashion.
"By gum," said Tommy, "tha'rt a quare lad, mate! Time art for sure! But tine's med wonder- ful strides sin' aw raised tha two bob a week abeawt

hofe an heawr sin'. By gum, lad, tha'rt just my mon : ged agate toi thi thirty-four !" Th' chap give owd Tommy a wink as puzzled him mony a day, id had so mich meeanin' in't ; but he dud as he wer towd, an' warked away at th' rate o' thirty-four shillin' a week for mony a long year. An' a rare hard-workin', steady chap he waur, too. But he wet a droll customer as ever aw see'd i' my life."
"Aw think he waur," said Bill Stickers, "iv he wer to' droll for owd Tommy Parker; for Tommy wer a droll owd stick his-sel' when he wer th' reet side eawt, too."
"Birds'ot a feather flock together," remarked Dan o' ml Dads; "no deawt th' chap just suited owd Tommy to th' life, wi bein' a bit comical." _ _
" To'be sure," said Roger, "that wer just wod th' chap could see fro th' start."
"Let's see," said Bill Stickers, "aw've just bin thinkin' aw should know thad fitter 'at yo've bin . .
speykin' abeawt, Roger. Aw knew a deeal ov owd Tommy's men at one time. Wod wer tif chap's
"Bill Charnley, iv aw recollect red," replied Roger.

" That's the same cowt," said Bill, "just the same. He's livin' Blegburn at th' present time." " Tha never says exclaimed Roger. " Yigh," said Bill, "he is ; an' gradely weel be looks, too." " Aw'm reet deawn fain to -hear 'at he's wick yet," said Roger," tha mu n tek mo up to see him some Seterda' or other." _

"Aw will, Roger, wi' pleasure." "Is he as merry as ever he waur ?" "Aw think he welly is," replied Stickers, " he wer full o' good tales an' Jooakes th' last time aw see'd him. An' he's two-o'-thre' lads ov his own 'at's just like their fayther for bein' comical. One en em, especially, is a gradely smart lad—their Harry. He's a member o' one o' th' Football Clubs i' th'
fayther towd mo a bit 'at he'd heeard o'er one o' Harry's' larks 'when th' club wer gooin' deawn to play a match at Preston one Seterda afternoon.

Th' players-had awlus some'at or other up for a marlock when they went off, an' Parry wer welly awlus th' foormost mon iv there wer owt o' th' soo- art agate. - This particular Seterda' afternoon, when he geet to Blekburn Station, Harry bed fixed his e'e o' guard as bein' th' handiest chap to play a trick on, but he took no action till th' train hed stopped at Mill Hill, an' wer beawn to start ageeon. Then he whistled o' one o th' porters. Th' chap coom runn- in' to th' carriage window foot thing, an' Harry said to him in his smartest style, " I say, porter, will you kindly ask the guard to give my little dog a drink of water. I'm afraid he'll forget it, with hay-
ing so many -other things in the van." "Certainly," said th' porter, an' off he flew to th' 'other end o' th' train to tell th' guard. _

Neaw, yo mun understand, chaps, that Harry hed a dog, but ,id wer safe at hooam, an' nod i th guard's van, or ony other part o' th' train. But th" guard hed only ta'en charge o' th' train it Blegburn, so he waurnd quite sure o' whether there wer a dog among th' other tackle i' th' van or nod, an' he spent th' time between Mill Hill an' Cherry Tree huntin' up for th dog that waurnd theer. Well, th' train stopped at Cherry Tree; an' when id wer welly ready to start, eawt pops Harry's heead fro th' carriage window, an' he toes one o' th' Cherry Tree porters to him. "Porter, please, just ask the guard to Jet that little dog of mine, in the van, have a drink, will your' " Right," said the porter, an' he flew to th' guard. " Yo've to let thad little dog sup 'at yo hey th' van theer."

" Aw con find no dog," said th' guard. "Well, but yo hey to find id, an let id sup." "Bless the dog r said th' guard, as th' train Beet off ageeon, an' he seet to a-lookin' for th' dog. Well, of cooarse, he hed'nd fun 'id hi tb' time be reyched Pleasington ; an' he wer beginnin' to think when he reycked tbeer that th' dog had ta'en 14 hook when he waurnd lookin'. He'd partly wod mad up his mind to look no moor Rift, when he see'd a young fella as ,wer actin' as th' under station master comin' runnin' deawn fro th' other end o' th' train,

just as id were beawn to be off. When th' young fella reyched, he said; "There's a young gentleman at the other eud that's very anxious about his little dog that you have in the van. He wants you to give it a drink. It's a prise dog, he says, and"— "The d—l take his dog r yelled th' guard, "aw's never ged to. Preston to-day, iv aw've to do nowt but feed a dog 'at aw cornd find r Hoghton wer reyched e due time; an' th' same owd message wer sent. Harry popped his head eawt, an' sent a smart looking young fella deawn to th' van. "Eh, guard, just let thad dog sup 'at you hey in thee; will you ?" "Go to the deuce r" sheawted thrguard. "Who aretyou ? " axed th" young fella, "I've only 'livered mi message, as I wet. towd." "Shut thi trap ! " said th' guard. "Yo shut yores," said th' other ; an' aw believe 1 they'd ha' welly gettep to feightin' iv they'd bed time; for th' young fella, ov cooarse, knew nowt no different but what he wer th"fostrat bed bin sent to tell th' guard to let th dog sup. As for th' guard, id hed dawned on him between Pleasington an' 1 Hoghton that he e'er bein" tricked; an' when he revelled Bamber Bridge, an' a porter browt him th' same orders once moor, he wer sure on't. Iv he'd bin as sharp as some other guardshe'd ha" sin through th' fob, entirely ;. hitt he waurnd one, at could tek owt inso fast an'' though he'd begung to feel sure sure id wer o a. lark, he hedn'd sense to' see that th' porters at o• these station& wer as inno- cent as could be. They (India know 'at o th' other porters on th' way hed bin, sent wir th' same mess- age, nod they t Heawn could they? But Or guard could'nd see that an' he pitched into th'' Bamber Bridge porter wossthan be'd done at Hog-. ton an' th' porter geet 80 mad that he threatened to report him. This rued th'guard madder nor eves; an as soon as th'train reyched liteston Junction he went oth' length o' 'tie train,. carryin' on like a mad- mon, an enquiriewho hed sent th' message abenwt thad dog. Ov ceoarse, nobody said they hed. Harry werleynin' eawt th'carriage window, lookbol as cool as a cucumber, o' th' time, but when th' gourd went back, mutterin' vengeance, an' beawt th' owner o' th'dog, he leyned back th' carriage, an' laughed to, his heart% content, an' sooa dtsd o th' others i' thadicompartment. Whether th' guard heeard 'em or nod, just afoot th' train started, aw cored say; bat Harry said hs fairly looked like a thunner-cleawd at rem when they o gesh enwt together at Preston." "An' weel he might," said Roger, with s. hearty laugh, "for they'd tricked him reet." "Aye," said Cock Robin, " he'd begin to, think who id waur when he seed a lot o' jolly young fellas oin a gang, 'Birds of a feather flock together,' as yo said afoot, Dan." "He wer a slow chap wer thad guard," said Rovin' Rondle, "iv he'd bod ha' ;waited at Preston Junction Harry would happen ha' sent another porter, an: then he could ha' med. him go an" identify' Harry, as th'sayin' is." " That's just the point." said Bill Stickers," he waurrid hole sharp enough." "C!" said Roger, "id were one o' them things ''at hed'ed be be; id lest a deeal better a& id waur.' "Soo& id dud," said Bill o' ma Granny's, "me hole o' th' fun would ha' bin spoyled iv th' guard hed fun' Harry eawt." From" The Preston Guardian?'

div.head: cuernut IN THE NIGHT WATCHES.
div.p: cuernut IN THE NIGHT WATCHES.

IT WSS about one o'clock, and Mr. Klopetock's bed was In the shadow, while his sister and Ruth were seated by a little table on which burned the reading lamp. The noise which took the elder lady's attention was a faint rustling, and for a few moments the blood of the watchers seemed to run cold. Their dread passed off directly, for their reason told them that it was not likely that a second attempt would be made to rob the place, especlally as there was now a policeman sitting up with Mrs. Hall in the basement, and the law was in charge of the place for the time being. But still the rustling continued, and they sat listening for some minutes before Ruth made an effort over herself, and slightly raised toe lamp.shade so that its light fell across the great gloomy room. She shivered with fear for the moment, for there, standing beside the bed, in his long loose dressing-gown, was the figure of the old man, looking, with his ban- daged head and white face, ghastly in the extreme. He was gazing acros3 the room in a peculiarly fixed way, and as the two women watched him, he walked slowly to the large wardrobe, and stood there listen- ing, the watchers being too much overcome to speak. Then, raising his hands, he suddenly draped it open, and looked inside, muttering to himself the while, before closing the doors carof ully, and returning slowly to his bed. ." Are you in pain, dear ? " said his mister, who had summoned up courage enough to cross to his bedside; but there was no answer, for the old man was fast asleep, and breathing regularly. Miss Klopstock returned to her seat with a shiver, and shading the lamp once more, the two watchers resumed their conversation. " Whoever it was must have hidden himself there," whispered Ruth, as she glanced fearfully towards the great wardrobe, and her companion nodded assent, making an effort directly after to talk upon some in- different matter. But the recollection of what must have taken place in the room they now occupied, effectually damped all conversation, and they sat at last in perfect silence, listening to the occasional mut- terinere of the old man in his sleep. Soon after he grow agitated, and it became evident to the watchers that he was going over the struggles of the night before in his dreams, and at times his voice sounded loud and excited. Then it would sink, and the listeners hoped that ha would now sleep peacefully, when he suddenly sat up in bed, exclaiming: "Mark, Mark would you murder me?" Ruth could not contain herself as she heard these words, and a piteous cry escaped her lips—a cry that was frozen in hoiror as she stopped short, being violently clutched by Miss Klopstock. For the old man had reached from his bed and pulled open the little drawer in the table that generally bore his night-lamp, and before the two women could fully realise what was about to take place, there was a sharp click, a flash as of lightning darted across the room, followed by the report of apistol and the crash of wood. This was repeated, for the old man had fired twice at the door of the wardrobe before sinking back ex- hausted upon the bed, while the double-barrelled pistol be had taken from the drawer fell from his hand upon the floor. Directly after there were the hurried sounds of steps, the door opened, and, truncheon in hand, the constable who had been watching below entered, and on learning the cause of the alarm, undertook to sit in the room for the rest of the night. His presence, however, proved to be needless, for, exhausted by his efforts, old Klopstock lay perfectly passive, and hardly moved again before the morning of another eventful day.

div.head: CHAPTER XXVIII. UNDER THE MICROSCOPE
div.p: CHAPTER XXVIII. UNDER THE MICROSCOPE

A rare eveniful day for all concerned, especially for Mark Woolford, who was in due course brought before a magistrate to find that a terrible net of evidence was being wound around him, the various incidents con- nected with the robbery lending themselves so omi- nously against him that at time( he asked himself whether he was awake—at otlee-el ether he wag sane, almost thinking at last ft..% , A possible he might, in a fit of somnambulism; autie committed the crime wherewith he was charged. To make matters worse, it was put in evidence that he had of late lost heavily in certain Stock Exchange transactions; but so far the police had not, with all their ransacking of the house in Brunswick-square found the slightest trace ef the money. So the case was, of *aurae, adjourned. west of mental torture that wee terrible followed, for hail was refused, and Mark had to lead the life of an ordinary prisoner in the House of Detention, where, by the wise and _ eatery laws of our great etountry, a man who may prove to be perfectly innocent has to occupy a cell with the degradations of cleaning the same, and being treated in all respects as if he were &convict of the vilest clam But the longest weeks have an end, and at last came the second examination, when further evidence was erought against the prisoner, the most conclusive seing that of the constable who had, as he said, seen aim trying the door of the house, and flashed his bull's-eye upon him, when the converson already known took place. This examination dragged its slow length along, and then there was a fresh remand for the appearance of the two injured servants of the firm; and once more, feeling as if ten years had been added to his life, Mark Woolford entered the prison van, and was taken back to his cell. He had had but, little newt of his home, and much of his time had been taken up in connection with in- terviews with his solicitors Martin had, however, been and seemed terribly anxious about his fate. At last the eagerly lookedefor day arrived, and Mark lewd once more in the dock. It was eatisfaetioneven to be there, for anything was better than the- terrible suspense he had been enduring. To his Vest surprise, Ruth was in the court dressed in deep black, and seated beside his brother Martin. This was an added pangefehich he had not counted upon being called to suffer, and be believed that he turned deathly pale, for the whole place Deemed to swim round, and when the sensation of faintness passed off, he dared not look towards the closely- veiled figure, for fear of displaying some fresh emotion. Then the case went forward, dragging its slow length along, the knots of, the evidence being drawn tighter and tighter as witnesses were examined, till at last there was a faint buza of excitement, and the for- tunate occupants of seats shifted their places a little as the name of Samson Hall was called, and the pale, bandaged raan appeared, glancing round the court till his eyes rested upon the prisoner, at whom they shot vindicrtive glance before his attention was called by the official of the court, and he was duly sworn. His evidence was very short, but quite conclusive. Being sleepless and uneasy that night, consequent upon occupying a fresh bed, be had lain tossing about for some time, till, fancying be beard the click.of a lock, he had half dressed, gone to-the door, and listened, bat hearing nothing he had returned to bed. Hero, however, he could not sleep, so be once mors roan Weave a look round to see if all was safe, and went upstairs. That something was wrong he knew instantly, by seeing the counting-house door wide opal', and through this the door of the manager's room, whensstepping back, he crept downstair3 and obtained the kitchen poker. Armed with this, and being evidently a resolute. Many he refrained from giving the alarm, but wait boldly down into the vault, where he came upon someone engaged in the robbery. How did he know be was engaged in the robbery? Why, by seeing him there at such a time; but, before hemeuld defend himself, he was dashed against the wall, stunned, and, when he came to, he was fastened gain the inner safe. The prisoner at the bar was the Man. That he would swear. A severe cross.examinatnsn followed, in which be corned he did not like Mr. Wooliord, who had more than once been very hard upon him, but be wished him no harm. Hadn't done the robbers? himself? No, it wasn't likely. If be had, should be have locked •himself up in the safe, and while he was there gone and stuffed the keys behind the grate in the manager's room, and then gone and hidden the cash where no one couldn't find it? Was he sure that he was not mixed up with the robbery in any way? Well, rer'aps the gentleman as asked that Ties, tin would like to feel his head, and see what he thought of it then. Yes; the prisoner at the bar was the man who struck him down. He had a bit of a trap, thing over his face, but he could swear to him all the same. This witness stood down, and the name of Timothy Klopstock was called, when the pale, haggard face of the old manager appeared in the entry, and he was assisted into the box by a policeman. The old man drew out his handkerchief and wiped his dewy face, as he glanced round the court, his eyes resting for some time upon the prisoner, who met hie gaze without flinching. Then the old man's examination took place. He stated that he had gone to bed as usual, after

carefully going through the place according to ins regular custom. He had seen to every fastenxeg, but, ' somehow, being tired, he had not examined his bed. room. He had neither lookod under the bed, nor into a great wardmbe that stood there; and there was plenty of room in ether place for a man to hide. He then stated that he had been reading for a short time, and had fallen asleep, when he was awakened by a stifling sensation at his throat, and as he tried to rise he received a blow from a man whom he saw half kneeling upon the bed. "And now tell the magistrate who was that man." A low sigh was heard to proceed from the part ot the court where Ruth was seated, but it passed un- noticed by all, save the prisoner, who, in spite of the excitement with which he awaited the old man's next words, could not keep his gaze from where she sat. "Tell the magistrate who was that man," said the counsel, repeating his question, for old Klopstock was silent.

"I-cannot," said the old man. "You cannot!" said the counsel. "Why I have it down here—your own statement—that the prisoner, Mark Woolford, was the man." "That statement was made when my brain was suic fering from a severe injury, and I have no doubt that I believed it then." _ _ .

"And you believe it now ? " asked the counsel. "No," said the old man. "I have gone over the whole of Mark Woolford's career, and I consider it impossible that he could be guilty of such an act." "You made that statement to the police, then, when you were non compos mentis "Yes; most decidedly." "Let me see," said the counsel, turning over the leaves of his brief. "You have been on terms of great intimacy with the prisoner for peers?" "Yes." "Your sister resides with him?" "Yes, my sister resides with him." "And pray what has that got to do with it r cried sharp, angry voice. "Silence cried the usher.

"Such impertinAnt questions:" "If that woman speaks again," said the mYgistrate, sternly, "she must be removed from the court." There was a general titter, the counsel smiled. sad then the examination went on. "You have a good deal of faith in the prisoner "A great deal." "You do not believe he could be guilty of such a crime ? " "I am sure he could not be." "But the man who stood by your bed-side was exactly like him ? " "Something in build, but he was closely disguised." "That will do, Mr. Klopstock," said the counQel, who was quite satisfied. Friendship—a man's feel- ings had nothing to do with the case. His duty it was to bring the guilt home to some one, and he was doing so rapidly

, apidly. There was little more done. The counsel engaged on Mark's side by Mr. Lorme felt that it would be mere waste of time to esoss-examine, as he kne w the case must go for trial, his sole efforts being to get his client out on bail; but in the face of the evidence last given, that proved to be impossible. Mask's last look, as he left the dock, was directed at the veiled figure of Ruth, and a pang of misery greater than any he had yet borne shot through him, as he saw her leaning upon his brother, who was helping her, half fainting, from the court. This last was no more than he was bound to expeet. He had as it were worked for it, but still it pained him intensely to see Ruth so thoroughly given up to his brother. At a time like this, the love of such a woman would have supported him, and been like armour in what was to prove a desper ite tight. His sorrows truly seemed to him now almost more than he could bear. Mr. Lorme came to him and said a few hopeful words, but he made no reply, for his own danger seemed as nothing beside the pain caused by that scene. *ery moment he eeemed to be deifting hopelessly farther and farther from Ruth, and now that the reality of hie separation had come, he found that be loved her with an intensity so great that, if he were condsamed at his trial, be asked himself whether he should care to live. He was soon alone once more, with the whole of that weary examination repeating itself. The horrible thought that he fancied he bad crushed came back with tenfold strength, and he shuddered and groaned in the agony of his heart; growing at last so despair- ing and maddened by his agony, that he felt ready to curse Martin as the cause of his pain. He had loved Ruth, he thought, so tenderly and well, that, seeing, the bent of her heart, he had been ready to sacrifice himself for her sake, and to win back his brother to a better cause. But now he found that it was no tender, weak love that he possessed for Ruth, but a relentless, absorbing passion, and in the face of this he was to be shut up from the sight of men, never to see her more, save perhaps in the future as the wife of one who— Oh no, it could not be true.

°HAMM XXIX. • TRIZNDLY orrltn. B.tcx came these thoughts to Mark Woolford's mind in the darkness and silence of the night, for he had no solace now, and hope began to forsake him as the time went on. There were long weary days and interminable sleep. less nights passing in succession; and he knew dist he was fast becoming a haggard, careworn man. He had interviews with his solicitor, but they brought him no comfort, for Mr. Lorme was com- pelled td tell him that they could find no strong point on which to base a hepe of acquittal, save his previnus. probity of life. "That man's evidenee—that Hall's "—said Mr. Lorme," is so terribly damaging, that it would alone be sufficient to convict you. Then there is your own ad- mission— and it sounds so weak to tell a jury—that you went down because you fancied something was "It was the truth," saki Mark, simply. "Yes, no doubt, replied Mr. Lorme., "Then lillopetocies first statements, and then his withdrawal, considering your intimacy, all make your case worse, for it seems like an, attempt to screen you at the , expense of truth." Mark began to look upon these inteniews at last with dread, for they only deriressed his spirits as he brooded ever the unbrotherly thought he had, and asked himself whether he was to suffer for that brother's sake to the very end; while more than once he felt that if Martin would come to V= and confess that it was his crime, and offer to take his place, such &display of magnanimity would not be without its reward, for he coal have suffered for him then with- out a word. At last, one visiang day Miss Klopetock came to Pee him, and was as sympathising as her harsh voice and ways would let her be. He dared not ask her about Ruth, and she volunteered no statements; while when his brother came Ruth's notate was not men- tioned. . . . .

li-e—said- with a smile, "I could have settled the matter at once when clever Mr. Barrister was Lrying to get answers from me, but I kept it quiet." "Quiet! Kept what quiet ?" " What would have condemned you at once.' "I don't understand you," said Mark, coldly. "Do you know what you dropped in my room that night when you struck me down. Ali, Mark, it was brutal, cowardly blow." "Will you never believe that I was 0,-11 in your room —that I never struck you—that am Perfectli innocent ?" " Stuff !" exclaimed the old man, angrily. "I tell you, Mark, I forgive you, bad as it seems for roe to make terms with the man who had robbed my employers. What is the use of keeping up this fiction. We ar not in court now. There, will you own that now? he exclaimed, fumbling at his breast. " There ie that handkerchief. I found it on the floor, and tied it round my bead to stop the bleeding when I Wr's trying to get to the bell." As the old man held out a:blood-stained handker- chief, Mark snatched it from his hand, gazed at it fot a moment, and then, as the place seemed to be swim" minz round him, he opened it, and saw in the corner. M. Wool ford." curiously marked in black bait. Mark clutched at the handkerchief far a moment 01, two, for he was giddy with horror, and as be et°°° there, he thrust the handkerchief hastily in his breast. "Then my horrible thought is true,' he muttered. "May God have pity on me !" and there he stood for some time, with his eyes closed. Ile saw it all now, only too clearly, and his visitor's words of werni4 uttered months before came back with their fulif.t

force Once again he seemed to see the gentle face of the mother he had so loved, and her beuded bead as El)a busied herself marking a dozen handkerchiefs for her favourite son, laughingly saying that it was bard wo'ic to select threads from her hair that were black: instead of grey. It was true then. His thoughts were correct. •' Martin then was the culprit, and, with all the clever- ness of his deeply-laid scheme, he had left terrible proof behind. He mast haye cleverly guimd himself for his victims to have made such 6 l mistake; but, worst of all, he had beau unroarl enough to let his brother act as scapegoat for his sins. He would not believe it before, hundreds of times,9l' it was suggested to his brain, and now it seemed raa°-- dening. For he was to suffer, and he had voluntarily given over Ruth to such a despicable wretches this. he to give up--,perhaps several of the best years of Life—the love of such a woman as Ruth, and to bear when he might denounce the culprit and go free? It was more than he coal bear • Ruth must not 1)•) condemned to such a fate, and Martin must suffer fee' his crime. He would—he must denounce him, aflu He stopped short, with his hands pressed forehead, for he seemed to see before him the sof? pleading countenance of the dead,bidding him be kind and forbearing to his weaker brother, to whom be bsa promised to be protector to the end. "It is horrible," he moaned; "It is more than I call bear," and he stood there helpless and as if crushed 0 be saw his fate. Must be, the innocent, suffer for another's crime, and give up to that guilty one the love of Ruth Yes, for it was his brother whom be would save"' the brother he had sworn to protect; the living legBe? hismother had bequeathed; and, sooner thandenounce him, he felt that he would die. a it "Oh, God!" be exclaimed; "it is horrible----- too much to bear. Give me strength that I waY bea it for the sake of those I love." They were lightning - like, these thoughts darted through his heart, and not a minute had elapse° before Klopstock spoke to him again. "There,' he said, in a low whisper. " You am your friend, Mark, still. Will you deny it now "No," said Mark, looking at him with wild, desPa,s jug eyes. "I deny nothing; let them do with ice No they will.'

These last were curious interviews, for little was 3itid, and a strange coldness had sprung up between the brothers. All that Mark knew of Martin's pro- ceedings was that he said he was doing nothing but looking for the thieves, for he did not go to Hum- phreys' establishment; that was iisiponible with such a charge hanging over the chief clerk's head. At last carne the man he had hoped to see—old 'lClopetock. looking extremely wont and reduced, hut ready to shake hands with him in the most friendly .nanner. "This is kind of you," cried Mark. " Kind, els ? Well, I don't know, Mark. I'm Berry for you, and, as one who has not long to live, I name to say that I forgive you fresly." "Forgive me!' "Yes, yes But what could have induced yon to do such a thing P You must have knows that you, would be foutd out." " Klopstock," said Mark, gravely," why do you in- sult me like this! You must know better. Do you still fancy that you saw me ? " The old man gazed for a few moments in his far%, and then sadly shook his bead. "Keep to it," he said, "if it will clear you and get you off. Mark Woolford, I'd give five hundred pounds to undo my unlucky words that morning. They'll Qin- demn you. "Condemn or no,"said Marl, firmly,„ "all my deela- nations of innocence seem to be in vain.' The old man glanced at him sharply, but, said epthing. _ "You don't believe me ?" " Old Klopetock shook his head. "Then why do you come hero ? Your presence insults me." " No, no—no, no. Not to insult you, Mark. I came because I can't f2irget our old days together—our days at home and those when we have worked at:the books and produced our balance-sheets. I came to see if by any chance I might have been mistaken, for I cannot understand it, Mark. It ;sn't like you. It seems as if it were Martin, and yet it is forced upon THE me that you did it." div.p: THE RIXTON. SHOOTISG CASE.

VERDICT OF THE CORONERS JURY . The inquest as to the death of Thomas Ellaman, whose body was found with a bullet wound in the breast in the Ship Canal workings at Hollins Green, on the'27th April, was resumed on Monday, at the: Eagle and Child public-house, Rixton, by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, and a jury. The accused man, Edward William Vaughan, with whom the deceased was working just before his death, was present in charge of the police. His father and brother also occupied seats in the room. Mr. Arthur Browns, , solicitor, of Warrington, represented the prisoner Vaughan, and Saperintendent Weir conducted the case on behalf of the police. A crowd of people assembled in front ck the Eagle and Child, and the appearance of Vaughan, who came by train to `Glazebrook station from Walton, was eagerly sena- Itinised as he entered the public-house. The Coroner said that the more equitable planto the accused Vaughan would be to call all the witnesses who had appeared at• the former inquiry; and to read,over their evidence, so that Mr. Browne on behalf of the prisoner, might have an opportunity of cross-execnitring them. The witness Joseph Antall, with whom the deceased man lodged, wasthen called, and the evidence given by him at the opening of the inquiry was read over.—Asked by the Coroner Whether he recognized anybody present as the winder of the boiler engine, the witness said he could not. He'had never seent'Vaughan before the 27th April, and he did not know whether he was the man he saw with Ellaman. Frank Harris was re-called, and was cross-examined by Mr. Browne: He recognized Vaughan as the winder of the boiler engine, whom •he saw near to Ellaman's engine an hour or two before the body was found. He had known Vaughan for a long time, but had never known him to quarrel with anyone. Mr. Westall, another witness, when cross-examined, described Vaughan as" a very civil, decent young man ;" he never knew him to quarrel with anybody. Mr. T. W. Travers, surveyor, Leigh, produced a plan he had made showing the local surroundings .61c the spot where Ellaman's body was found. James Barlow, a boatowner, living at Rixton, said on Sunday, April-27th, he and James Ditchfield and Jamee Clarke were on the Rixton side of the Ship Canal, where they had gone for a walk. They went as far as the Bol- lin mouth, and walked back on the Cheshire side of the canal. They passed close to the" rocker" pump. Here they saw two men in the cutting talking together. This would be at ten minutes past twelve. He did not know either of the men. Afterwards he heard of the death of Ellaman, and he went back and saw the body, which was lying at the place where he had previously seen the •two men standing. About three or four minutes after he saw the two men he heard the sound of arpistot shot. He and his companions had then walked past the rocker pump, and they were not when they heard the pistol shot in a position to be able to see, the men in the cut- James Ditchfield, fustian cutter, living at Rixton corroborated. George Chesworth, a pump driver, said that at one o'clock on Saturday afternoon, the 26th April, he took charge of the rocker pump, and remained on duty until he was relieved by Vaughan at ten minuteipast seven on Sunday morning. When Vaughan came to the hut he showed him a revolver which he said was a six cham- bered one. put the revolver into the pocket of a jacket whidi was hanging up in the cabin. He had known forafortnight thatNaughan was in the habit of carrying a revolver.—Further examined by Superinten- dent Weir, the "witness denied that he had seen the prisoner since. He denied that he had since seen him at a new railway cutting in "Derbyshire.—Cross-examined by Mr. Browne: He was not with Vaughan the same morning shooting starlings. He did not have breakfast with him at his mother's house. He had never known Vaughan to quarrel with anybody. He was quite sure he was not With Vaughan after he relieved him at the pump. He was not at the boat-house with him. Edward Latham a youth 16 years of age, said he was employed as a labourer on the Ship Canal works. At half-past nine on Sunday morning, the 27th April, he saw the prisoner' Vaughan outside the boathouse. He had a revolver in his 'hand, and said to him, "I'll bet you a sovereign I can knock that sower out of your hat with that revolver:" He was drunk, and witness said, "Do you think I'm a dummy?" Witness then left the pri- soner, as he felt rather frightened.—Cross-examined by Mr. Browne: He heard from 'Alfred Knight that the pri- soner fired three shots into the air the same morning at the boathouse. .

George Knight;ls years of age, said he was a wagon ." fatter" on the Ship Canal. On Sunday, April the 27th, he saw Vaughan near the boathouse, and heard him ask`Lattkam whether he would let him shoot at thellower in his hat. In the afternoon he sawVaug,han follow the men who removed'Ellaman's body from the cutting. He 6V7 him near to the house where'Ellaman lodged, and when the body had been taken inside, he heard Vaughan ask a woman how far it was to Manchester. She told ' him twelve miles, and he then went off in the direction of Manchester. The witness distinctly stated that at half-past eleven he saw the witness Chesworth with the prisoner Vaughan near the boathouse. Chesworth, •re-called, was questioned as to the accuracy of his former statement, but he maintained thathe did not see Vaughan after he relieved him at the pump. Fanny Hudson, wife of George Hudson, labourer, Rixton, said that on the afternoon of the 27th April, when the body of Ellaman was removed to his former lodgings, she saw the prisoner Vaughan come up behind the hedge. He came through the gate, and she met him in frent of her house. He asked her whether he was on the right road for Manchester, and she said" Yes," and he walked off very quickly. Charles Bryant said that he took charge of the rocker pump and relieved ,Ellamon on Saturday, April 26th. The deceased relieved witness at nine o'clock on the Sun- day morning. At that time the deceased showed him a revolver and a box of cartridges. The deceased asked him what he thought of the revolver, and he replied that he did not understand such things. He saw the deceased put the revolver and cartridges on the seat in the cabin. On Monday afternoon witness searched the hut, and found the revolver and cartridges in a musical bez upon which a melodian had been placed. The jury then adjourned for lunch. After lunclaeon, the first witness called was P.C. Schofield, who said that on Sunday, April Efth, he went to the Ship Canal cutting at Rixton,and reached the rocker pump at 2.25, where he found the body of the deceased. He was not aware at that time that he bad been shot, and there were no appearances to guide hint to that conclusion. He reached the body and found 9s. 7d. in money, a watch and guard, two rings, a letter and a small compass. After the body had been removed to Arstall's house he saw a pistol wound in his breast. He then went to look for Vaughan, but was not able to dis cover him Thomas Dainteth, gunsmith, Bridge-st., Warrington, said that on the 3rd May Sergeant Barnes showed him the revolver produced which belonged to the deceased. It had never been used. P.C. Fleming produced the box belonging to the pri- soner, which he found at his lodgings in Thelwall. Ha found in the box seven ball cartridges and one empty one. He also found Ell in gold and several letters with other articles, which had been handed over to the pri- soner's father. The prisoner had seen the box that morning, and said it was his property. P.S. Barnes produced the bullet taken from the body of the deceased.

Superintendent Weir said he had now to make an application to the Coroner as to whether he would allow him to call a witness whose evidence he thought would supply a motive. He did not know whether he was in order-in calling the witness, but it would be for the Coroner to rule whether a conversation in which the deceased took part would be received. The Coroner said that Superintendent Weir had better call the witness. Mary Travis was then called. She said she was the wife of George Travis, a hamper maker. She had known the deceased for about two years, but she did not know Vaughan. She remembered going to the rocker pump to take Ellaman some hop bitters about three weeks before his death. While she was in the cabin a man named Rvcroft came, and she concealed herself and remained hidden until -Rycroft left. Superintendent Weir then asked the witness to relate A conversation which she overhead between Ellaman and Rycroft, when the Coroner said that such evidence was not permissible. It had been ruled by one of her -Majesty's judges at Chester that a Coroner might receive all the tittle tattle of a neigpourhood in order to see how a person came to his death. He (the Coroner) thought he could do this when there was no person in custody; but when they had before them a person who was charged with cauitng the man's death, he thought he was bound by the ordinary rules of evidence. Dr. logo said that since the last inquiry he had been making experiments of the effects of shots from a revolver upon clothing similar to that worn by the de- ceased at the time of his death. He had come to the conclusion that the revolver was fired at a distance of about 18 inches. This did not alter the opinion previ- ously expressed that the wound was not se'f-inflicted.— Cress-examined by Mr. Brown It is in my opinion pos- Able, but improbable, that the wound may have been inflicted whilst the deceased was examining the pistol at arm's length. Dr. Caul dwell said he did not think that the pistol wal °fired within 18 Inches of the deceased's body. He did not think the wound was self-inflicted. Superintendent Weir said that he caused search to be made for the prisoner Vatig,tran, and had descrip- tions of him circulated throughout the United Kingdom He heard nothing of him until the morning' of May 23rd, when he received a telegram from the Ross police. The same day he went to Ross and received the prisoner into cuStody from P.C. Haynes, who stated that the prisonei, had surrendered himself that morning. He brought the prisoner away on the following morning, and on the way cautioned him, and then said, "You are charged with wilfully mu rderingsone Thomas Ellaman, by shoot- ing him with a pistol and bullet, in the cutting of the Manchester Ship Canal at Rixton.about twelve noon, on Sunday, April 27th." He replied, " Wilful ! No ; It was

not wilful. It Was an accident. I did not shoot him. I had notlong Cr,, shoot him for ; he shot himself. I'll tell you how it Was. Neither of us was doing anything. I had cleaned out my boilers, and was waiting for Ellaman to get the water before I started. It was no use me pumping any water until Ellaman had got what I had pumped away. I was standing near my boilers, and saw Ellaman at the top of the slope near his pumping engine.. He called out to me and said, Come up here, and bring that thing with you.' I knew he meant my pistol. I took my pistol out of this coat (pointing to the coat he had on now), and put it into the pooket of the blne one I had on. I walked up the bottom of the cutting, and he came down the slope and met me where his body was afterwards found. I showed him •t'At, pistol, and thought the barrels were all discharged. I had been shooting rats that morning, andthought I had discharged all the barrels, but it seems there was one left. While he was examining the pistol I turned round to do something and heard him call out, 'Oh, Fred; I have shot myself.' I turned towards, him, and caught him as he was falling. I held him up as long as I could, and then let him down. He died with his head on my arm. I was frightened, and did not know what to do. I waited about, and saw his landlord come with his din- ner, and saw him find Ellaman in the cutting where I had left him. He called me to him, and told me to go and fetch someone, and I went and brought the walking ganger. I was afraid, and didn't know what to do, and I then went away." The Coroner: Did Vaughan make any statement to you as to what he did with the revolver? Superintendent Weir: He did, but that was only in reply to my question for my own satisfaction. Mr. Browne at this juncture said he did not propose to call the prisoner Vaughan. The Coroner' in summing up, said there was some satisfaction in dealing with the case, because, thanks to Superintendent Weir, it had been very ably put before them. He did not think that anything more could have been done to enable them to arrive at a conclusion. There had been a great deal of labour involved in order to put the case into ship-shape, and he thought he ought to say that Superintendent Weir had been sided by Ser- geant Barnes, the officer on the spot, who had had a great deal to do in getting up the case. In addressing the jury, the Coron3r said that in considering the posi- tion of Vaughan they were bound to recollect that there was no evidence to show that the men had any animosity towards one another. There was no suggestion of any quarrel between them. As a matter of fact, if Vaughan had taken away the life of Ellaman, there was a total absence of motive, so far as the evidence went, for the act. As to the revolvers being in the possession of the men, that seemed to be satisfactorily accounted for. Speaking of Vaughan's statement that the affair was one of pure accident, the Coroner pointed out that it was natural to believe that Ellaman would call to Vaughan and ask him to bring" that thing" with him. It was probable he would want to see it, to know whether it was like the one he intended to take to Australia. Commenting upon Vaughan's disappearance after the finding of the body, the Coroner observed that whetherhe was committed for trial or whether he was allowed to go free, he fully de-, served all the trouble he had got into. He at once assumed the demeanour of a guilty person, and at once put himself out of the way, and notwithstanding all the inquiries made for him, he evaded the police. It was for the jury to say whether the deceased shot himself acci- dentally, or whether he was accidentally or wilfully shot by Vaughan. The deliberations of the jury extended over 40 a:lb:Lutes. Upon the Coroner and others officially engaged being re- admitted, The Foreman said the jury were unanimously agreed that the death of Ellaman was caused by a pistol shot, and they were further agreed that the shot was fired by Vaughan, whether accidentally or wilfully they were unable to say. The Coroner said that was the proper verdict on the evidence adduced—and one he should have drafted him- self had he been a juror. VAUGHAN AGAIN REMANDED.

On Wednesday morning the prisoner, Edward William 'Vaughan, was brought up at the Occasional Courthouse, Warrington. before Mr. James Tinsley, and charged on remand with the wilful murder of Thomas Ellaman, at Rixton, on the 27th April. The prisoner had been brought from Padgate by the 10.15 train, in custody of P.S. Barnes. Superintendent Weir applied fora remand until the 12th inst. Mr. Arthur Browne, who repre- sented the prisoner, said he had no objection to a remand, but the day mentioned would be very inconvenient, as it was a County Court day.—The Clerk suggested that some formal evidence be offered by the police.—Super- intendent Weir stated that he received the prisoner into custody at Ross. He charged him with the offence. Prisoner made a statement to the effect that it was an accident.—Mr. Tinsley: Do you see any reason, Edward William Vaughan, why you should not be remanded?— Mr. Browne: On the prisoner's behalf, I say that I have no objection.--Superintendent Weir, to suit the conveni- ence of the defence, asked that the prisoner be remanded until Friday, 13th inst.—Mr. Tinsley thereupon granted a remand as asked.—Mr. Browne applied for bail. He said that his worship would have seen from the news- papers that the result of the Coroner's inquiry had been an open verdict. Therewas not, he thought, the shadow of a doubt in the minds of the police and himself that there could be no case of wilful murder, because the police admitted that they ,could not find any motive for the crime. That diaposed of the "wilfully and malici- ously," and it resolved itself into manslaughter or noth- ing. The prisoner surrendered to the police. His father was a very respectable man, a man of property. He (fifr. Browne) held in his hand a letter from the Vicar of Gorsley, near Newent, Gloucestershire, the writer saying that he had known the parents tor 25 years and could testify to their great respectability. As to the eon, he could hear nothing but good of him. He seemed to have been a friend of everybody and an enemy of none, and would be the last person in the world to hurt Anyone. The Vicar of St. Sohn's, Chelsea, kad written also, saying that he would do everything he could to help the family.—Mr. Tinsley : I might as w.eil tell you before you go further, that I should not grant bail without consulting Mr. Weir.—Supdrintendent Weir , lam not free to admit that there is no motive.—The Clerk: Can you tell us what the verdict of the Coroner's jury was ?—Mr. Browne: It was an .open verdict.— , Superintendent Weir: I would not feel jaistified in being: a party to vemand on bail.—The prisoner was then for- , many remanded until Friday, 13th June. He was after- , waras connefed to Walton goal, in custodyof P.C. Scho- field. #

div.head: VIE I4`,...VavIINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 7, 1890:
div.p: VIE I4`,...VavIINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 7, 1890:
WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING.

On Tuesday evening the annual meeting of the members of the Warrington Football Club was held in the Workmen's Cluli, Market-st. There was a large attendance. The chair was taken by the pre- sident :Councillor W. Pierpoint), and there were also en the platform Councillors Tinsley and Flem- ing, Messrs D. Tinnion, J. E. Warren (secretary),and T. Pemberton (treasurer.)

SECRETARY'S REPORT. The Secretary (Mr. J. E. Warren), reported that the first teem had had an unusually heavy season,4l matches having been played with the following result :-24 won, 12 lost, and 5 drawn. Total score, Warrington, 48 goals, 53 tries, 130 minors; opponents, 21 goals, 19 tries, 58 minors; majority, 25 goals, 34 tries, 72 minors. J. T. Massey headed the list of scorers with 19 tries and 1 dropped goal. P. Lawless for the first season with the first team had done remarkably well, scoring 15 tries. T. Barnes comes next with 9 tries and 2 dropped goals to his credit. Frank Turner, 7 tries; Bandies, 6 tries; J. T. Bate, 5 tries; R. Littlewood 4 tries: W. Antrobus, J. W. Evans, E. Dillon, W. Speakman, 3 each; Fair. Turner, W. Nevins, 2 each; H. Ashton, J. Boscow (full back), W. Berry, B. Eyre, W. Hastings, Jas. Holmes, J. Jolley, J. Lawless, S. Mather, W. Povey, H. Rowe, and J. T. Thomley, 1 try each. The following had kicked goals from tries or free kicks :—T. Barnes, 24; Frank Turner, 13; J. Jolley, 2; H. Webster, 2; J. Boscow, 1; Fair. Turner, 1. The" A" team had won 27 matches, lost 2, and drawn 3. Score :—For 47 goals, 87 tries, 109 minors; against, 11 goals, 14 tries, and 26 minors. Webster had obtained 18 tries and dropped 4 goals; Jolley, 5 tries, 1 dropped goal; Rowe, 4 tries, 1 dropped goal; Mather, 17 tries; Daniels, 10 tries; Thornley, 6 tries; J. Bate, Eyre, Laney, J. Lawless, A. Barnes, and Beard, had gained 5 each; Neild and Holmes 4 each; P. R. Lawless, Molyneux and T. Barnes 3 each; Heesom, Ashton, E. Dillon,F.Bate, Speakman, Howarth, and Boscow (full back) 2 each; whilst Nevins, Sampson, Warburton, Isherwood, Hast- ings, Berry, and Catterall had obtained 1 each. The goals had been placed by—Webster, 11; Isherwood, 9; J. Bate, 5:; Heesom, 6 ;T. Barnes and Jolley, 3 each; Bos- cow, 2; and Davies and Mather, 1 each. An "A " team (advertised as their " A " team) played Runcorn Recs. on Good Friday, but the match was abandoned before time played out. The score then being—Rec.'s, 2 goals, 2 tries, to 1 goal, 1 try, 3 minors. Their team was very weak, but the home team had the assistance of half-a-dozen Runcorn Ist and several "A " team. Williams and Rowe secured the tries, Heesom placing the goal. The second team had played 21 matches, won 15, drawn 1, lost 5. Score :—For 21 goals; 55; tries:; 81 minors • against 8 goals; 11 tries; 24 miners. The following had scored :—H. Rowe 9 tries.; T. Williams, 1 dropped geal and 8 tries: T. Laney, 8 tries; F. Heesom, 2 dropped goals and 4 tries; J. Berry, Buckley, and Knowles 5 tries each. Welsby, 4 tries; Oxley and Johnson 3 each. Bellis 1 dropped goal and 1 try. Russell, R. Barnes, James Bate, and H. Woodward, 2 tries each. T. Locker, 1 dropped goal. Eyre, Boyle, Catterall, Wilkin, Howarth, Sampson, and Wilkinson, 1 try each. T. Antrobus placed 4 goals; F. Hee- som 3:; A. Newton, 3; J. Knowles, 2; Oxley, 1. After the list of fixtures had been almost completed for last season, the Committee, at the earnest request of the officers of the West Lancashire Union, decided to com- pete for the Cup under the altered conditions as arranged by the League, and, in consequence, many of the League Clubs had to be met on Monday evenings under great diffictilties as regards getting good team ,„ together. Be- low is a table showing the position of each club at the end of the competition.
Nantes of Clubs. Matches. Won. Lost. Drawn. Total. Wigan Walkden l4 . Warrington . 14 ispnil Leigh Tyldesley Widnes St. Helens.. 14 - • .. •

A strong list of matches have been arranged for nest season, including Swinton, Barrow, Broughton, Leigh, St. Helens Recreation, Widnes, Moseley, Wigan, Brough- ton Rangers, Oldham, Tyldesley, Kendal Hornets, Man- chester Rangers, Coventry, Leeds Parish Church, and for the first time Llanelly, Hartlepool Rovers, Lancaster, and Rochdale St. Clements. Forty meetings of the Com- mittee had been held, the members having attended as follows :—W. Pierpoint 6, E. Gilbert 38, S. T. Thornley 38, 5. T. Bate 37, H. Ashton 35, J. E. Warren 33, G. Smitla 33,5. T. Massey 31, W. Speakman 30, W. Dillon 30, H. Rowe 30, T. Pemberton 28, T. Barnes 28,5. Holmes 24, S. T. Whittle 24, W. Antrobus 19, C. R. Adamson 18, Fair 'Turner 14. The membership of the Club is now 457, an increase of 45 on last year. TEE TREASURER'S REPORT.

The Treasurer (Mr. Thomas Pemberton) also presented his report from which it appeaxed that three benefit matches had been played during the season, resulting in the sum of £ll 17s. 9d. being handed over to the War- rington Infirmary, £23 16s. to the Welsh Colliery Explo- sion Fund, and £39 16s. 9d . to the Warrington Gymnasium Building Fund. The balance sheet showed the receipts, including a balance of £52 4s. 104 d. from the previous year, Lobe £1,03 6s. Bd., the balaace now being £153 6s. Bd. In addition to this, there was the sum of £l5 105. outstanding, whilst the club's property represented an additional £3OO. The annual sports realized a profit of £24 83. 3d.' though there was a loss on the annual ball of £3 78.31 The report was Unanimously adopted. The Chairman maid he should like to say a few words with reference to the charity matches. He thought no one could take exe,ention to the action of the Committee hi that respect. With regard to their grand contribution to the funds of the Gymnasium, he considered that there was no object worthy of more consideration than that of helping the Gymnasium forward in every possible wayi —(applause)—as it was very necessary and desirable to have such an institution. He had been requested to express to them the Gymnasium Committee's very heart- felt thanks for their kind assistance. He thought, how- ever, that what was in the interest of the Gymnasium was in the interest of the Warrington Football Club. (Applause.)

div.head: ELECTION or PRESIDENT.
div.p: ELECTION or PRESIDENT.

Councillor PIERPOINT said he wished his name to he withdrawn as a candidate for the presidency of the club If or the ensuing season. He thought that year after year it was better, in the interest of everyone concerned, and the club itself, that there should be some new blood in- fused into it. He had great pleasure in proposing as his successor the name of Councillor William Tinsley, not only because Mr. Tinsley was a personal friend of his own, but because he would make an excellent president, and had always taken a deep interest in the proceedings of the club, (Applause.) Councillor Tinsley was then unanimously elected presi- dent of the club for the ensuing year. .

Councido; TINSLEY Said he regretted very much that Mr. Pierpoint had decided to retire, as he had been such an excellent president, He, however, should try to follow in Mr. Pierpoirit's' footsteps, and do all he could for the welfare of the Warrington Football Club. (Ap-
