plause,) He was much obliged for the honour they had conferred upon him that evening. ELECTION OF CAPTAINS, COMMITTEE, &C. The following officers were re-elected without opposi- tion :—Secretary, Mr. J. E. Warren; treasurer, Mr. Pemberton; reporters, first team, Mr. G. Archer; second team, Mr. F. Howard. The votifig by ballot for the various officers was then proceeded with, the following being elected :—Captain first team, J. T. Massey; sub- captain, W. Antrobus ; captain "A " team, T. Davies; sub-captain, T. Jolley; captain second team, T. Wil- liams; auditors, Messrs. T. Wallington and W. Bibby; umpire, first team, W. Speakman; "A " team, J. lioltpes ; Committee, Messrs. C. R. Adamson, T. Barnes, J. VBate, W. Dillon, J. Evans, W. Hewitt, G. Smith, andW. Pierpoint ; trustees, Messrs. G. Smith and C. R. Adamson (re-elected).

ALTERATION IN THE Bums. A motion proposed by Mr. Rows to the effect that players should abstain from voting on the Committee when they themselves were candidates for the team was carried; as was also a motion by Mr. Tinnion that authority be given to the Committee to invest the funds of the club in first-class and safe securities.

VOTES OF THANKS. Councillor FLEMING proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Pierpoint for the services he had rendered the club during his three years' presidency. He regretted that Mr. Pierpoint had resolved not to seek re-election, as he had taken a great interest in the club, and had helped in a great measure to bring the club to its present high state of efficiency. (Applause.)—Mr. SMITH seconded the proposal which was cordially agreed to.—Mr. PIER- POINT, in reply, said that what he had done for the War- rington Football Club had been to him a labour of love. He had seen the club rise from a moderate standard to occupy one of the highest positions with regard to Rugby football in the North of England. He hoped the club's suerPoa would continue until it was regarded not only as one of the finest combinations in the North of England, but in the whole of England. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the pro- ceedings.

div.head: NEW BRIGHTON TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE NEW BRIGHTON TRAGEDY.
A STRUGGLE FOR LIFE.

The adjourned inquest on the bodies of Wm. Spicer. 14 years of age, and Henry Spicer, four years eld, who were murdered on the 25th May, was resumed at the New Brighton Police Station, on Wednesday morning, before Mr. C. W. Tibbits, deputy-coroner for West Cheshire. Felix Spicer. the father of the lads, who is in custody on the charge of having murdered them was not present, and was not legally represented. MA. Spicer, who had not completed her evidence on the last occa- sion, was in attendance during the greater part of the day, and was deeply affected several times whilst her depositions were being taken down by the deputy- coroner. When speaking of her children she wept bitterly, but it was with a firm voice she informed a juror that at the present time she had no doubt that Spicer, when struggling with her, meant to take her life. In the course of her evidence, Mrs. Spicer gave a graphic account of her desperate struggle for life with the man who is accused of the murder of the two children. In reply to the deputy-coroner, she said her real name was Mary Ann Palm. She remembered Felix Spicer coming to the refreshment rooms on the night of the 24th May. Felix asked to be let in, but she refused, and called out to him "Good night." He replied "Good night, my girl," and then went away. Whilst in bed, early the following morning, she heard a crash of glass. She looked towards the window, and saw Felix Spicer put his hand through the broken window and feel about for the key of the door. She jumped out of bed and began putting on some clothes. While she was dressing Spicer again smashed some of the windows. She at once rushed to the window to get out. He tried to prevent her, but as she was standing higher than him she managed to get through. He overbalanced and she fell also, but she did not know for certain whether he knocked her down. The next thing she remembered was that he tried to put a hankerchief over her mouth. It smelt strongly of brandy she thought. When he found that he could not get the handkerchief over her face he felt for something in his breast pocket. She saw a brown handle, and thinking it was a pistol she cried out, ." For mercy's sake, don't blow my brains out." He then pulled out of his pocket what turned out to be a knife and said, "You—wretch ;you cried Murder,' did you? You won't cry Murder' in another minute when I have done with you." They then had a desper- ate struggle, and witness most of the time was guarding her throat. She threw a skirt over her shoulders and put it round her neck, and with her right hand she held , on to the blade of the knife. The struggle seemed to last I a considerable time. She ultimately managed to knock the knife out of his hand and make her escape. He chased her up and down Victoria-rd., and she dodged him round the cabman's shelter. Mr. Bailey came to the door of his shop, and witness called out for assistance. Spicer turned round and called Mr. Bailey some names. As soon as she got the opportunity she ran into Mr. Bailey's house, he having repeatedly called to her. Mrs. Bailey met her on entering the house, and witness called out, "For God's sake follow him, in case he does something to the children." A Mr. Storey who next arrived, fol- lowed Felix..—Deputy Coroner.-When he was struggling with you, did he say anything about the children ? Mrs.Spicer: No, sir. I asked him to spare me for the children's sake. He replied, "I'll give you children, you wretch."—After some further evidence had been given, the inquest was adjourned till next Wednesday.

FOREMAN SHOT IN MISTAKE FOR A BURGLAR. At the Thames Police Court on Thursday, John Scriven, 27, boilermaker, of Millwall, was charged with shooting Stephen Parnell with a revolver. Thomas Turner, caretaker of Messrs. Bellamy's tank and boiler works, said he heard a burglar alarm go off soon after three o'clock in the morning, and he went for prisoner, and also rang for the injured man, who was head fore- man of the works. Witness helped Scriven over the gate- way, and afterwards heard the report of a pistol from the inside of the works. Witness opened the gate and saw Parnell sitting on some iron plates bleeding from the mouth. Witness saw nothing of prisoner until he re- turned with a doctor, when prisoner said "Why, Tom, I never knew Mr. Parnell was in there," and witness re- plied." No more did I." Parnell and Scriven were the best of friends. Medical evidence showed that Parnell hadreceived three bullet wounds. The bullets had not been extracted, and Parnell was in a critical state. The accused when arrested said, " I was told there were burglars in the shop. I ran up the yard and saw a man. I challenged him twice and he raised his hand. I fired, and then saw what it was." (The accused was re- manded.

div.head: , THE EXCURSIONS .I.'o HAWAILDEN.
div.p: , THE EXCURSIONS .I.'o HAWAILDEN.

MR. GLADSTONE ON THE COMMON CAUSE. On Saturday Hawarden was the scene of another de- monstration. The excursionists, who numbered in all probability between 2,000 and 3,000, came in special trains to Broughton Hall and Hawanien from Saddle- worth, Mosley, Glossip,Dukinfield,Stalybridge, Oldham, Stockport, and other plaees. The weather was unsettled and unpromising in the earlier part of the day, but towards afternoon it brightened considerably, and the change was gladly welcomed by the holiday makers. At ten o'clock Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone walked from the Rectory to the Castle, and were received with great cheering by the crowds through which they passed. It was announced that Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone would drive from the castle through the park shortly after two o'clock, and so great was the anxiety to see the distinguished couple that fully an hour l•efore the time hundreds of trippers had assembled in front of the terrace and near the coachyard gate. An attempt was made to " draw " Mr. Gladstone, and in hope that he would be induced to "say a few words," a deputation waited upon Mrs. Gladstone, and expressed the wishes of the party. Mrs. Gladstone could not give a definite promise that her husband would deliver an address, but assured the deputation that she would acquaint him with their desires. As this was not exactly satisfactory, some of the leading spirits of the excursionists determined to strengthen the inducement. Accordingly a scout was sent out in form of a small but energetic boy, who urged all the stragglers in the park to hurry to the front of the terrace, as they were to "sing Mr. Gladstone out." The assemblage was by this means considerably augumentecl, and shortly before two o'clock the crowd in waiting numbered probably a thousand. The "singing out" process then commenced. The pieces chosen ,were Auld Lang Syne " and the, hymn "All hail the power of Jesu's name." Whether it was that music had charms in this case to induce Mr. I Gladstone to "show himself" and "say a few words" is difficalt to say, but he did both. Shortly after two o'clock, in company with Mrs. Gladstone, he walked across the lawn from the Castle to the terrace wall, and was greeted with ringing cheers by the excursionists. When the demonstration,of pleasure had subsided, he said :—Ladies and gentlemen, I am afraid I am not able to offer you a speech. I must not attempt it, I cannot do that, but I bid you heartily welcome—very heartily indeed. I rejoice to think that we are united in a com- mon cause, and I think that common cause is travel- ling very steadily towards its triumph if we get an op- portunity, but they do not seem disposed to give us an opportunity. (A Voice: "Oh, you will have one.") Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone then drove through the park to the rectory in an open carriage, and were heartily cheered along the route.

div.head: COMPENSATION QUESTION.
div.p: THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.
ATTITUDE OF THE WEELEYANS.

A meeting of the Committee of Privileges of the Wes- leyan Methodist Connection was held at the Centenary Hall, Bishopsgate-st., London, the Rev. C. H. Kelly, Pre- sident of the Conference, in the chair. The meeting was specially summoned for the purpose of deciding upon the action to be taken by the Wesleyan body in reference to the proposals of the Government enabling County Councils to purchase licensed public-houses. The Committee, which is a inon-political one, was very largely attended. It was unanimously decided to offer the most strenuous resistance to the proposals contained in the Government Bill, and the Committee were autho- rized to use every legitimate means for securing the re- - jection of the obnoxious clauses. The Committee aLso considered the correspondence recently submitted to Parliament respecting Sir L. Simmond's special mission to the Vatican, relative to religious questions in the island of Malta. They were authorized to present on be- half of the Wesleyan Methodist Connection a memorial to the Crown, and petitions to Parliament, against the ratification of the measures now being passed through the Legislature of Malta, whereby the marriages of Pro- testants and Catholics in the island of Malta are to be henceforth invalid and illegal unless celebrated by Roman Catholic priests, and in accordance with the forms established by the Council of Trent.

div.head: MANCHESTER SPEAKS .OUT.
div.p: MANCHESTER SPEAKS .OUT.

--- Under the auspices of the United Kingdom Alliance, a very largely attended and enthusiastic meeting was held on Wednesday evening, in the Manchester Free-trade Hall, to protest against the proposed compensation to publicans under the Local Taxation (Custom and Excise) Duties Bill. Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., presided, and Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., and Mr. Lloyd George, M.P., were the principal speakers. A resolution was adopted declaring that the provisions of the bill for enabling county councils to purchase licences for the sale of intoxicating liquors with a view to the extinction of the licenses, were drawn on the assumption that there was a right to the continuous reaewal of such licenses, and protesting against the provisions as tending to give statutory recognition "to that monstrous assump- tion."
SIR W. HARCOURT ON COMPENSATION TO PUBLICANS.

- Sir W. Harcourt, M.P , speaking yesterday at the Council meeting of the Home Counties Division of the National Liberal Federation, said the supporters of the licensing clauses made the idle pretence that the Government proposals did not involve compensation. Nobody was deceived by that pretence. When once the principle of purchase became established it was ridiculous to pretend that magistrates would be able to exercise their discretion to put down public-houses where there were too many without compensation. In his New- port speech Lord Salisbury said he knew how compensa- tion would operate, addimg, "If you only make your compensation big enough, people will think twice before they close public-houses." That, continued Sir William, was the real truth of the whole matter. Mr. Goschen had made a mistake, and now wished he had never put the compensation posocript to his Budget Bill. The Liberal party meant to fight the matter out. The other side might do what they liked with their motley majority. The day of account was at hand. After a reference to the Tithes Bill, and the Irish Land Purchase Bill, he pointed out how little legislation there had been this session, and said there never was a Government that had more grossly or more brutally abused its power than the present one.

div.head: WARRINUTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: WARRINUTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of the Rural Sanitary Authority was held at the Workhouse, yesterday. The Rev. G. F. Roberts occupied the chair and there were also present Messrs. W. Houghton, T. Smith, R. Kilshall, A. Jolley, John Houghton,Joseph Hum- phreys, Joseph Swinton, W. Owen (surveyor), S. Sutton (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector.) Tim PROPOSED BURIAL Grump AT RIXTON.—The Clerk read the Surveyor's detailed estimate as to the proposed burial ground at Rixton. The exact Inca of the land was one acre and the total estimated cost, including £5OO for the site, was £1,210. That amount, he said, was only an approximate one and an amount should be added for contingencies.—The Clerk read some correspondence with the Local Government Hoard in regard to the matter. On the 28th May the Local Government Board wrote that they would hold an in- quiry into the matter as soon as they learned that the consent of owners of property, lessees, and occupiers. within 200 yards of the site had been obtained. Detailed plans should be prepared for production at the inquiry and trial holes should be dog to the depth of at least ten feet to asckrtain the nature of the subsoil. He read a long list of questions which the Local Government Board required answering, and the Surveyor suggested it would be best to send the site itself to London. (Laughter.)—The Clerk said the matter had been going on for 15 months, and now all those obstacles were thrown in their way.—The Chairman did not think they could take any steps in the matter, but leave it in the hat.ds of the Clerk. This course was adopted. HEALTH—The Medical Officer (Dr. Sephton) reported that during the month ending May 31st. the births in Authority's districts had been 16 males, 23 females; and deaths, four males, 11 females. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 116 per 1,000 of the population, against 179 in the corresponding month last year. The district throughout was very bhealthy and fairly free from infectious diseases. BUILDING OPERATIONS AT BURTONWOOD.—The Surveyor reported that a certificate for habitation had been issued for the house and clubhouse at Burtonwood to Mr. Mercer. Among the plans submitted for approval were 68 cottages at Collins Green, Burtonwood, for Mr. John Mercer. The report was adopted with the exception of the plans for Mr. Mercer's houses, at Burton wood, pend- ing arrangements as to sewerage. TH2 SHIP CANAL SMOKE NUISANCE.—The Inspector of nuisances reported that during the past month he had paid several visits to Latchford and booked the names of engines turning out black smoke, about which there had been complaints. Two steam navvies were at work near Latchford station and the smoke from them was at times very bad. The same might be said of three steam cranes at Cross-lane. He found that those engines were not fitted with the apparatus for consuming their nWn smoke, but he understood the nuisance c.ould be consid- erably abated if a regular qaantity of steam was kept up and the door of the fire place opened at times. The Clerk was instructed to communicate with Mr. Price, the agent of the No. six section as to the complaint. The Clerk said he thought the agent was willing to carry out aay suggestions of the Authority. IB POLLUTION OF THE MASSEY BROOK.—The Nuisance Inspector also reported that he had found Massey Brook to be badly polluted with what appeared to be tan-water. Higher up, in the direction of Lymin, he found a large quantity of solid matter, which had evidently come from the tan yards of Lvmm. There appeared to be nothing objectionable turned into the brook from Massey works. The brook appeared to be in a better state below than above the works.—The Clerk stated that the Lvenn Local Board had the matter in hand, and they would he sure to do something.—The Authority instructed the Clerk to write to the Lymm Local Board, intimating that the specter had reported upon the pollution. This was all the business.

SUDDEN DEATII OF A RAILWAY PASSENGER.

A man, whose name has not been ascertained, was taken ill at the Central Station on Sunday even- ing. Samuel Fearnside, a constable in the service of the Cheshire Lines Committee, and a porter named James Buckley, were on duty at the station at twenty minutes to nine, when their attention was directed to the deceased, who was being supported by two passengers. As it was evident he was ser- iously ill, he was carried into one of the waiting- rooms and some brandy and water offered him, lie was, however, unable to swallow it. He was placed in a cab and conveyed to the Infirmary, where he was examined by the senior house surgeon (Dr. Smith), who pronounced life to be extinct.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: INQUEST.
An inquiry into the circumstances of the death was held on Thursday morning, at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-st., before Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy. coroner.

Samuel Fearnside, a constable on the Cheshire Lines Railway, deposed that on Sunday night, at about nine o'clock, he saw the deceased sitting on a form on the down platform of the Cheshire Lines Station. That was the side for Liverpool. Deceased appeared to be very ' ill, as though in a faint. He was unconscious, and unable to move. With assistance witness took him into ' the room, and brandy and water was brought, but the Ideceased could ,not swallow it. The deceased was at once placed in a cab and taken to the Infirmary. When the doctor at that I nstitution examined him on h is arrival, life was extinct. Deceased had in his possession a third- ' class ticket from Warrington to Liverpool, of the date it:L. question. James Buckley, a Cheshire Lines porter, said that at about 840 on Sunday night, he saw two passenzers assisting the deceased, who had fallen down on the Plat- form. Ile seemed to have fainted. Witness and Fern. side took him to the Infirmary in a cab. He did not then. appear to be alive. Edward Hughes, foreman porter at the Central, gave corroborative evidence.

Inspector Spinks handecl in a copy of particulars that had been sent to various police stations, and also a photo- graph that had been taken of the deceased for the pur- poses of identification. Witness had examined the clothing of the deceased, and had found various articles. They included a knife, an old pair of spectacles with tin case, and a briar-wood pipe. A communication had been received from a lady in Liverpool inquiring about a friend who was missing, but the deceased was not the man. Deceased seemed to be of the labouring class, and was probably "on the road," as he had with him a small quantity of tea and sugar, and also some oatmeal. There was nothing at all on the body to lead to identifi- cation.

The Coroner observed that the last occasion upon which he was in Warrington, he saw the porters at the Central attending to a lady who was ill, and he must say that they gave her every care. He had no doubt that everything possible was done for the deceased man, and, under the circumstances, he did not see how they could hesitate abut cmning tp the conclusion that the deceasedt died front natural causes. .

A Juryman suggested that perhaps walking up the, steps at the Central had something to do with the sudden. illness of the deceased. A verdict was then returned to the effect that the, deceased died from natural causes, the nature of which. the evidence did not show. DESCRIPTION OF THE DECEASED.

The following is a copy of the description of the' deceased issued by the police :—" Apparently between 70 and 80 years old, 51t. 71n. long, grey hair cut short small grey beard and moustache, very thin spare built. Had on an old black worsted coat, brown tweed vest,two pairs of old grey tweed trousers, one white shirt and o:o.e. print shirt, a stripped muffler, a home made brown tweed belt with three buttons to fasten,old lace up boots,, and black hard felt "hat. Supposed belongs to Liver— pool. Had in his pockets a railway ticket, Warring,Lvea to Liverpool. Be- tides 237 Private Bills now before the House of .commons, there are sixty-nine which may be con- tidered Imperial, that is, applying to the whole of the United Kingdom, or Our foreign possessions; 11,1netY to England alone; thirty-one to Ireland a,mne ; thirty to Scotland alone ; and five to Wales al9ne. It is obvious that Parliament, as now con- .sti.tuted, is quite unable to deal satisfactorily with this mass of legislative proposals, and I therefore advorite the extension of the system of devolution, -and ii.e constitution of representative assemblies, consisting, wholly, or mainly, of the Parliamentary -representatives Of each dii:ision of the country, to Ideal with the specific and exclusive affairs of Eng- land, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, respectively rhis is a fair statement of the object aimed at; rand there is nothing about it that anybody need -fear.

MR. G. W. RAWLINS, who represents . , A Good the Newton Division of the Lan- Example cashire County Council, has set a ..g°odexample to other County Councillors by coming before his constituents and giving an account of Ills stewardship. Summer is not a good time -for meetings of this kind, but Mr. RAWLINS ex- Plains that he has been waiting until a financial ~ atatement was issued of the working of the past ' -3'er. The result may be pronounced satisfactory, or, although in connection with the good work 'one, there has been a slight increase in rates, that , rease is due to the failure of the Chancellor of , he Exchequer to carry the proposed van and wheel I! , which was to be banded over to the County 'uncils, rather than to any extravagance or mis- .'"nagement on the part of the County Council " !..self. This defect in the Imperial contribution ~ being remedied, and there is reason to believe , Pat it will have the effect of bringing about a re- !' notion of rates. The total expenditure amounts z ,' £424,000, and of this sum no less than £160,000 1: on account of the police. Mr. RAWLINS thinks 1 ' ' e sum far too large, but what he justly '"Plains of is that the Councillors as a body no control over this heavy expenditure. 4 jo in t Committee, composed of magistrates ..'d councillors, has charge of the police, and the : lof it is, that such a Committee is not respon- ,%lB to the ratepayers who provide the money. 'eh a system is bad on the face of it, and cannot, to be hoped, last long. It is a piece of :.„°l7ism of the worst type, and was retained in the ruity Council measure despite the protests of „wle Liberals in the House of Commons. Another 14(1 feature of the Act which was referred to, the provision for the election of Aldermen. That, .', ought to be abolished. Town Councils would ' ' be all the healthier and strorger if they were dof the Aldermanic element. It is not that Al- '? "en would not, as a rule, make good represents- of the ratepayers. It is because they cease as derrnen to be responsible to the ratepayers that "Y deterioriate ; they lapse into the practice of Presenting themselves rather than anybody else. 40ther point touched was the proposal to confer kitelf.Poil County Councils the power, under certain urnstances, to buy out publicans. So far Iv ,fr. Its.wmrs saw, there was no County Council -hich liked this idea of purchasing licenses. Why it may be asked, should the work be thrust -,... 'n them, whether they like it or not? The , 'N'ernment have no mandate from the people, and ,' 'Y have no demand from County Councils, to - With the licensing question in this piece-meal, hazard, and ridiculous fashion ; and they ought :.' be compelled to withdraw this portion of their .. .• • • Mr. RAWLINS was cordially thanked for his .: .tructive address. Perhaps we shall hear some- , , ,g soon from other County Councillors who '6-8 hitherto made no sign ?

In the June number of the West/6n- Review," "Home Rule all round" is the title of important contribution by Mr. John LEND, 3.f The article is the substance of a paper, which, recently read at the National Liberal Club, el3d would'he well if it could be sent broadcast throilga out the kingdom. His suggestions are :1- the (I) ,That the members for each division or kingdom shall constitute an Assembly of RePres?fig tativea Council, or House of Parliarnent'fordesh with the specific and exclusive affairs of that ronn try. Of Without committing ourselves to the. these suggestions, we may remark that there leis; question as to the desirability of the. main P,int namely, that there should be a separate Perlis/3;40v 'foreach nation, and one Imperial Parliament' ,the discussion and transaction of r nen.. The word Parliament has a high ,7our, with it,, and it is rather startling to sore° ,to, begin talking of four Parliaments and e. Imperial Parliament. They instantly and hoUgn lessly. rush to the conclusion that this would illeact disintegration and separation, while the real fan - is that it would tend unquestionably to the coos ,solidation of the Empire. A Parliament is an -01 a embly for the transaction of national business. an i , t 7 'f in the course of time it be found that there 1.4 more busigess to do than can be efficientlY trai.r ultr 'meted, what can be more reasonable than In- ;plying the machinery in order that the work rall 'be properly done? This is effected on scale by the powers and authorities are delegated to local bodies, such as 175, Boards, Town Councils, and, more roe° 0 r tre .1_ 'County Councils. Their functions are, it ,for the most part administrative,, but considerabia latitude is allowed them in the, way of making bY,,tr,. laws. What is now neededis. that we should 3;1 the great gap that exists, between the 00111 Councils and the Imperial Parliament. This,. ;I 'it seems to us, can only be done by fourNetiel3_, Parliaments. How absurd' to occupy the atteu,„ tion of members of Parliament with a number :: ' local bills, such as the, Ship Canal Bill,. and t e Warrington Improvement Bill, when theY es not even time to deal with Imperial uleastiZ of the highest moment!; At the present, time I parliamentary machine may be said to, be blockea' The by accumulating orders for work to be done. Government have control of the machine,,ena the most that they hope to accomplish vert into law their Irish Purchase 131';'' the Tithes Bill, and the Compensation Bill. pier:. are scores of measures which require earrYin. lo• through before some of the reforms can be. acomplished upon which the people have set their t is to con harts, but there is no chance in the Present generation of their becoming law unless we eau !3% ur machinery equal to:the work to be done. It Is, mitter of course now to say that a separate Parlli.r; melt will be granted to Ireland. They are the last to stir, but when they do stn. we lo not doubt that they will press forward and get he work accomplished in a thoroughly practical way. In concluding his article, Mr. LES° saYs:—,. div.p: "MAINLY PERSONAL."
BY "TOUCH AND Go."

There are some readers, I dare say, who missed the usual column of "Touch and Go ' last week. Man proposes, but the east wind disposes; it laid me on my back; and lying on one's back may do for thinking, but it is not favourable for writing.

It came about in this wise. There was a Whit- suntide trip to Scarborough, Filey, and Whitby. That was a temptation to a gad-about who had not seen that part of the north-east Oast; and when to this was added the fact that two tramping chums of old standing were "going that way," the temptation was irresistible. I went, and saw, but the east wind conquered.

Emerson says the laws of disease are as beautiful as the laws of health. He is right, no doubt, viewing the matter from an impersonal standpoint; but when observations of the subject are strictly personal the element of beauty doesn't seem to come in. That, at any rate, was my impression when bronchitis took possession of me, and breath- ing under difficulties became the order of the day and night.

It must be a horrible thing to die, as so many die, litually struggling for breath, and all the time feeling that one is getting the worst of the struggle. To the old and aged, death comes as a sort of re- lief. The King of Terrors has no terrors for them, for he steals upon them insensibly. They cease to live, just as a clock ceases to tick when it has run down. It is different with those who are struck down in the prime of life. Nature will assert her- self; she will struggle to hold her own; and the struggle is painful.

It is told of one of the tyrant kings of olden time that he had a cell so constfucted that the iron walls contracted a little every day; and the fate of the unhappy prisoner who was placed with- in that cell was to be crushed finally—and to know that he would be crushed—by the walls closing in upon him. Imagine--but nobody can imagine— the horror of the approaching end!

It must be pretty much the same when the end comes through an acute attack of bronchitis. The contraction in this case is in the air tubes. It is gradual, but it is certain; and there is the ever- present consciousness that, as air passage after atr passage closes, Life and Death are at hand-grip with each other, and that Death will conquer.

There is, of course, bronchitis and bronchitis. You may have a "touch and go "of it, which is merely a reminder that there is such a thing as a breathing apparatus, and that it is just possible it may get out of order. Or it may seize you as if it meant to strangle you; your pipes giving out ir- regular notes with irritating regularity ; while you draw in air with a feeling that some heavy, al- though invisible, monster must be sitting on your chest.

And it all comes, as a rule, of east wind. Why oh why, are there such things as east winds, fleas,' and—" Intercepting, Depots ?" Charles Kingsley used to have a good word for the east wind. He called it the "wind of God ;" but I cannot imagine why; for an east wind punished him, and, if I mis- take not, it was an east wind that killed him.

"It, was a very foolish thing for you to go to Scarborough," says Everybody, on seeing the result; and, as what Everybody says must be true, I say the same. It is so assuring to be wise after the event. But perhaps it is as well to state that there had been no intimation by post or telegraph that the weather,from being like a little oven below, would change the day after my arrival, a special blast being sent on from some outlandish place between Siberia and the North Pole.

Still, I saw Scarborough—and felt it. It has its merits, but its merits are not in its sea breezes. Nor are they to be found in the narrow streets, stuffy houses, and peddling shops of the old part of the town,which are altogether too much in evidence, when strangers wander, as we did, down the main thoroughfare and on to the harbour.

We saw the worst first, and got it over. Scar- borough has really some fine features—the Castle, the Spa, the Grand Hotel, the Park, and Oliver's Mount. Then there is the new.part on the North Bay—quite a little watering place of its own. There will be a gay time this summer when Prince Edward opens the new promenade and pier, as he has promised to do. Yes, Scarborough is a grand place; new and old, it is a compound of Dignity and Dirt.

We walked on to Filey—eight miles away—to see the place, and more particularly Filey Brig—a great natural breakwater ranning straight into the sea. It was interesting to walk on this pier of the Old Dame's making, and watch" the league-long breakers" dash themselves into spray as they thundered against its adamantine sides. But—eh those "buts "—it was an east wind that was blow- ing.

There was another old dame at Filey besides Dame Nature; and we had an odd adventure with her. She occupied "a cottage by the sea," which was gay with white-wash, and sweet with wall- flowers. She was recommended to us by a bene- volent " Bobby " as a woman who would make us comfortable. Could she accommodate us for the night ; and could we have something to eat, at once? "Oh, yes, but she had nothing in the house besides some tea, and the cakes she was baking." Well, that would do, at a pinch. So we washed and waited, and napped, and grew more hungry. In an hour there was a rattle of pots. "All! those cakes are baked, and she is coming." Bat she didn't come; and another half-hour passed, and then there was an invasion of the kitchen with the following colloquy— Old Dame: Aw'm weshin' up, yo see. Visitor: Yes; we thought you were getting tea ready? Can we have it now? Old Dame: Aw told yo aw'd only a bit 'o tea, an' nothing to eat. Visitor (aghast) : Do you mean to say we can't have tea, after all ? Old Dame: Aw told you ; aw've neither milk nor butter—only some tea i'th' house.

A prospect of dry cakes, and tea without milk, after waiting an hour and a half ! "Oh, what a fall was there, my countrymen." In five minutes we had settled with the old dame, and were on our way to the Ship Inn. An hour later, we had shown ourselves what the landlord would call good trenchermen, and were at peace with all mankind.

How we went to Whitby, which we found very picturesque, but colder even than Scarborough, must remain in the ink-bottle for the present ; for I am wheezing and coughing again, and the doctor says I have no business to write a line.

RESIGNATION OF TIIE REV. C. F. ARED. It is stated that the Rev. C. F. Aked, pastor of the Park-rd. (St. Helens) and Earlestown Baptist Churches, has accepted the call to the pastorate of the Pembroke Church, Liverpool. It is expected that he will commence his duties at that place of worship on the Ist September next. SUMMER FASHIONS. now showing at J. &W. Durres's, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. THE LANCASHIRE HUSSARS _ .

The Lancashire Hussars completed their week's training at Southport, on Saturday last, and a plea- sant week was spent by the men. The weather was fine, and nothing occurred to mar the proceedings. The annual review of the Hussars took place on Friday at Birkdale, in the presence of a large and fashionable assembly. The troops went through their evolutions with much spirit, and the regiment appeared to be splendidly trained. Colonel Liddel was the inspecting officer, and the regiment was put through various movements by Colonel the Earl of Lathom, Colonel Earle, Major Lord Gerard, and other officers. After the inspection the officers entertained a distinguished company to luncheon at the Victoria Hotel. The annual non-commis- sioned officers' dinner also took place on Friday night at the Bold Arms Hotel. Regimental-Ser- geant-Major Eastham occupied the chair, the vice- chair being filled by Bandmaster Batley, and among the non-commissioned officers present were Quarter- master Howard (Newton-le-Willows), Quartermaster Hamilton (B Troop), Veterinary-Surgeon Dixon.

THE SHIP CANAL: WHEN IT WILL I3E 'COMPLETED. At an inquiry held at Liverpool, on Thursday, with reference to the position of the powder magazines in the Mersey, Mr. Leader Williams, engineer to the Ship Canal Company. stated his belief that the canal would be completed by the contract time—i.e., January 1, 1892. It was intended to open the sec- tion from Eastliam to the river IVeaver in six months time. TRANIMLING TRUNKS.—Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge- st., Warrington.

denominations there had been a million more spent in liquor than in the previous year or in years gone by. If the whole of the religious oanisation of England failed to put a stop to this infernal monster, drink, which was the ruin of the working-classes, what could Government do by buying public-houses. They merely heaped money upon one who had already got plenty. He suggested that the Government should bring in a Bill for doing away with the licenses where an infringement of the law had taken place. (Applause.) By doing so they would destroy gradually the great evil of intemperance and by the accumulation of the taxation on the liquor traffic would be able to make use of the surplus money to pay off the tremendous and astounding national debt of £800,000,000. (Applause.) Mr. C. P. Fielding supported the resolution, and described the compensation clauses as nothing else but legislation for the rich at the expense of the poor, and they said, as Liberals and Conservatives, that legislation for the classes at the expense of the masses was the relic of a barbarous age. Compensation ought to be paid not to the publican and the brewer, but to the hundreds and thousands who had been ruined by the accursed trade. (Applause). Mr. Bryan, of Waterloo-road, here asked whether the Government intended to compensate the publicans out of the public funds, or whether they intended to tax beer and spirits for the purpose— Mr. Fielding replied that the compensation would be given out of the public funds. The Government in- tended to increase the tax on spirits 6d. per gallon and that added to the already increased tax of 3d. per barrel or beer would go into the public funds and out of that fund compensation would be paid. (Applause). Mr. Bryan was not satisfied with the answer, and he further asked whether they considered it absolutely wrong that any beer or spirits should be sold in this country.

Mr. Fielding said he had opinions of his own and other gentlemen had their opinions, but he was not going to insult the audience by turning the meeting into a pro- hibition meeting. (Applause). Mr. Bryan said he did not consider all publicans were vampires. He knew several in the town who were hon- orable men and who discountenance drunkenness. (Applause). He was not a publican himself nor con- nected with one,but he looked upon publicans as trades- men quite as much as the butcher, baker or tailor, and if they lost their living through Government action, they ought to be compensated. Mr. E. W. Humphreys said supposing for the sake of argument that the sum of half a million per annum was , allocated to the County Councils for the purpose of pur- chasing licenses, and supposing they did not exercise their option, what became of the half a million. Did it go back to the ratepayers or did it go into the public funds for the general expenses. Mr. Fielding said unfortunately the money did not go into the public funds. The money was invested in Government stock, and could not be used for any other Purpose. The Chairman said the money could only be got by increasing the drinking of tho people, and yet according to the Government it was a temperance measure. (Ap- plause. The resolution was carried, only Mr. Bryan voting against. The Rev.J. Holden moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Fairish for his services in the chair, and that he be respect- fully requested to forward copies of the foregoing resolu- tion to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the First Lord of the Treasury, the President of the Local Government Board, and Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. He remarked that enough had been said to convince any candid Englishmen, or any man that was open to conviction that the Govern- ment proposals were not in the interests of the people of this country, nor in the interests of religion or temper- ance that such a Bill should be passed by the House of Parliament. (Applause.) He was glad that the pcople of Runcorn had given an emphatic " No "to the Bill. Mr. J. J. Howitt seconded the motion, and remarked that if the Government proposals were adopted, they would do more harm to the temperance cause than any- thing that had taken place for many years. (Hear, hear.) It was a question for the ratepayers. They were told by one of the greatest financiers this country had ever produced, that it would take 200,000,000 millions of money and 700 years to pay off these licenses. Was the country prepared to pay so much and wait so long before they swept the drink traffic away? He did not think they were. (Applause.) The Rev. J. Simpson supported the resolution, and protested against the Bill because it was unjust and immoral. It was unjust because it sought to compen- sate the very men who had fattened on the trade, and it was immoral because it countenanced a trade that had done so much to demoralise the country, and to ruin our homes and to make men demons. (Applause.) The motion was carried by acclamation, and the meet- ing terminated.

The election- of ;even members to supply the vacancies on the above Board, which took place on Tuesday, created little interest. There were two polling booths, one in the Daresbury Board School, and the other in Moore Infant School, both of which were opened from twelvo noon till eight p.m. Twelve persons had been nominated for the seven vacancies, namely, Mr. Alfred Broome, Preston-&- th'-Ifill, farmer; Mr. Thomas Smith-Burgess, Walton Superior, estate agent and farmer; Mr Sohn Cooper, Walton Superior, corn merchant and provision dealer; Mr. William Richard Earn, Preston Brook, tanner; Mr. Henry 'Hayes. Daresbury, farmer; Mr. John Highfield, Moore, retired farmer; Mr. Charles William Phillips, Daresbury, licensed victualler; Mr. George Rogers, Newton Bank, merchant; Mr. Peter Tickle, Preston-o'-th'-llill, farmer; Mr. Thomas John West, Keckwick, farmer; the Rev. Thomas Whitley, Daresbury. clerk in holy orders; and Mr. Henry Whitlow, Hatton, farmer. Messrs. Phillip Darbyshire, Newton-by-Daresbury, and Robert Hewitt, Hatton, had also been nominated but they retired from the contest. The Rev. Thos. Whitley /chairman), and Messrs. T. S. Burgess. P. Darbyshire, R. Hewitt, W. Jackson, P. Percival, and P. Tickle were members of the old Board. Mr. Henry Linaker was 'the returning officer. Mr. William R. Earp, in a circular issued to the electors, pointed out that he had withdiawn his candidature in favour of Mr. Alfred Broome. but as the with- drawal had not been sent in the form required it could not be accepted by the Returning Officer. His name, therefore, appeared among the list of candi- dates. He would, however, still withdraw in favour of Mr. Broome. The result of the poll was as follows :—Burgess, 500: Tickle, 341; Whitley, 314; Cooper, 240; Rodger, 227; Phillips, 191; Broome, 129; Highfield, 91; Weir, 71; Hayes, 65; Whitlow, 64; Earp, O. The first seven were duly elected. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Knowles, vice- chairman, presided, and there were also present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Mesers. Aaron, Turner, T. Lewis, J. Whitlow, J. Baguley, J. Stokes, HeWitt, W. Whit- low, Bretherton' Knowles, Parr, Horton, Priestner, Weir, Taylor, J. W. Baguley ; H Linaker (clerk),and H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk). THE BATING OF MACHINERY BILL —A letter was read from Mr. H. Tollemache, M.P., stating that he would present to the House of Commons the petition of the Guardians against the Rating of Machinery Bill. THREATENED APPEAL AGAINST ASSESSMENT. The Assessment Committee reported to the Board that Messrs. W. R. Earpe and Co. had given notice of their intention to appeal against the assessment of their chemical works at Runcorn, and the Committee asked for the authority of the Board to resist the appeal,and that Mr. A. Linaker be instructed to appear at the special sessions at Runcorn on behalf of the Gomrnittee.—Mr. Aaron moved that the request of the Committeebe complied with. He remarked that there were small public houses at Runcorn, which were assessed as highly as these works.—Mr. Whitlow seconded the proposal, and remarked that Mr. Earpe had first agreed to take the decision of a valuer,and then repudiated it, because his valuation was a few pounds higher than that of the Runcorn overseers.—lt was stated that the valuation of the premises referred to had been reduced from £BO gross to £74 gross.—Mr.- Aaron's motion was agreed to. TEE Pools FARMERS.—It was reported that some of the townships of the union were in arrears with their calls, and Mr. Aaron and Mr. Taylor protested against this sort of thing being allowed, as both Weston and Runcorn had paid up.—Mr. W. Whitlow said he observed that the defaulting townships were those in which farmers predominated. It was very hard to whistle without a top lip—(laughter)—and it was very hard for farmers to pay money when they hadn't got it. It seemed to be all paying and no receiving for farmers just now, and he asked them to be a little lenient. It was all well enough for Mr. Aaron to speak in the way he had done, for he turned his capital over fourteen or fifteen times in the year at 10 per cent., but the farmer only turned his over once. (Laughter.) The subject then dropped. There was no other business of public import- ance before the meeting.

div.head: RUNCORN REPUDIATES THE PUBLICANS'
div.p: RUNCORN REPUDIATES THE PUBLICANS'

ENDOWMENT BILL. On Monday evening, a public meeting was held in Runcorn Public Hall, for the purpose of protest- ing against the Compensation Clauses of the Local Taxation Bill. The body of the hall was crowded and a considerable number of persons occupied the gallery. Mr. W. Fairish, J.P., of Chester, occupied the chair, and he was supported on the platform by the Revs. H. Burson (Wesleyan), Dr. Gastaldi (Catholic), J. Holden(Established Church), W. Kendrew(Wesleyan), John Simpson (Congregational), and G. Thompson (Me- thodist Free Church) ;Messrs. S. C. Beckett, 'l'. Handley, J. J.Howitt, E. W. Humphreys, F. J. Norman A. R. Norman, John Simpson, T. Simister, and C. P. Fielding, of the United Kingdom Alliance, Liverpool. The Rev. H. Burson read a letter from the Rev. C. Finch (Primitive Methodist), who apologised for his inability to be present. In reply to the resolution passed by the Nonconformist Sunday School teachers, on Whit Monday, Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P., said: "I trust you will continue your good efforts without flagging until the fate of this iniquitous proposal of the Government is finally decided. The whole temperance movement is going through the greatest crisis of its history and we must all prove worthy of our great cause." (Applause.) The Chairman opened the proceedings with a brief speech, in which he stated that all sections of the tem- perance cauSe were agreed in rejecting the proposals of the Government. .

The Rev. G. Thompson proposed "That this meeting, representing various shades of political opinions, hails with satisfaction the effort on the part of the Government to restrict the evils of the liquor traffic by lessening the number of public-houses, but strongly disapproves of the proposed compensation clauses as contained in the Local Taxation Bill, inas- much as such legislation would create a vested interest in annual licenses, and thus render more difficult the work of temperance reformation." In dealing with how these clauses would affect the temperance move- ment, Mr. Thompson said they could get some idea from the fact that the drinking interest applauded the pro- posals. When the devil praised the church, they thought the church was in a very bad state—(laughter)—and when the drinking interest applauded a bill that pro- fessed to make for temperance, they were afraid that the temperance part of the affair was in a bad way. (Hear, hear.) It was all to their interest to perpetuate the drinking system, and were they likely to favour a mea- sure that was likely to diminish the traffic? No section of the temperance party favoured the proposals, except a very small set of the Church of England Temperance Society. (Hear, hear.) As to the clauses, he asked, why give the County Council power to buy public-houses when the magistrates had power to shut up without buy- ing, on the sole ground that they were not required ? (Applause.) These clauses were altogether unnecessary for diminishing the number of public-houses, and they could only do it in the smallest degree, and at the greatest possible cost. (Hear, hear.) But they were sufficient to establish the principle of compensation, and it behoved them to lift up their united protest against the Bill. (Applause.) The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi said it was a great pleasure to him to address them on a platform surrounded by friends of all denominations. (Applause.) He was not there on a political nor a religious question but upon a social question which ought to be dear to everyone of them. He willingly and conscientiously seconded the resolution. Be contended that the Government by making a pro- posal to buy public-houses would not lessen the great evil of intemperance, and if it did not succeed in that it was only a bugbear. it was only throwing dust in the eyes of the people. He read in the newspapers recently that with all the efforts made by the temperance societies and by all the good pastors and ministers of every religious

div.head: NEW BAPTIST CHAPEL FOR WIDNES.
div.p: NEW BAPTIST CHAPEL FOR WIDNES.

The ceremony of laying the memorial stones of a new Baptist Chapel took place in Deacon-road, Widnes, on Thursday afternoon. Twenty years have elapsed since, with the kind co-operation of the Rev. H. Stowell Brown, of Liverpool, the mem- bers of the Baptist denomination in Widnes formed themselves into a church, and their career, as an organi- sation, has certainly been a chequered one. The first service was held in the old Public Hall in September, 1871, when Mr. Brown was the preacher for the day, and here they continued to worship for several years. • Then a room in the Temperance Hotel was engaged, and even- tually a chapel in Cromwell-st., which had belonged to the Congregational body, was purchased, and the religi. ous work was carried on with varying success. Through the development of chemical works in the vicinity, and the fact that the chapel became hidden in a back street, it became impressed upon the members that to continue the work with any hope of success a new chapel must be obtained in another part of the town. The Rev. R. Yeatman, who is now abroad, laboured most assiduously for several years to attain this end, and by means of bazaar, &c., the sum of £3OO was raised. In 1888 the chapel was disposed of for a further sum of £3OO, and the whole sum was invested until a suitable site could be obtained. In the meantime the members worshipped in the Baths Assembly Room, and in the officer's room at the Drill Hall, and by this means have succeeded in keeping the organisation effec- tive. The new chapel is to be built on a site in Deacon- road, purchased for a sum of £l7B, and the construction of the sacred edifice, the contract for which has been placed in the hands of Messrs. Sayee and Randle, will cost a further sum of £l,lOO, Towards this there is £B3O in hand. The design has been furnished by Mr. Richard Owen, architect, Westminster Chambers, Liverpool, and shows a building in Geometrical Gothic style. The chapel will be 47 feet long by 31 feet wide, with sitting accommodation for 250 people. At the rear is a school- room 46 feet by 17 feet, the two ends of which will form transepts to the chapel. Arrangements will be made to divide this room into three separate parts with a series of rolling shutters, each room having a separate en- trance. All the woodwork of the interior is to be of varnished pitch pine. The entire structure will be built with red Ruabon Terra Cotta bricks, finished with local stone. The memorial service was conducted by the Rev. D. P. McPherson, 8.D., of Myrtle-at., Liverpool, and amongst those present were the Rev. S. W. Bowser, 8.A., (Birkenhead) ; Rev. R. Lewis, (Liverpool) ; Rev. C. F. Aired, (St. Helens) ; and Rev. J. Calvert, Rev. D. Davies, Rev. R. G. Hughes, Rev. T. Law, and Rev. G. S. Meek, (all of Widnes) ; Messrs. E. 'Carey, R. H. Davis, R. Owens, W. Clark, J. Cripps, J.P. (Waterloo), T. B. Wealthy, Ed ward Mounsey (Liverpool), and John Knight. The Rev. Robert Lewis delivered an address on the principles of the Baptist faith, and afterwards Mr. E. Carey laid the first memorial stone, remarking that he did it in the memory and on behalf of his mother, who was so deeply interested in everything connected with the Baptist denomination in Widnes. The second, third, and fourth stones were laid by Messrs. J. Cripps, E. Mounsey, and R. 11. Davies. Each of the gentlemen were presented with a silver trowel, with ivory handle, and bearing a suitable inscription in commemoration, of the event. Subsequently a good company sat down to tea provided in the new schoolroom, which is partly finished.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BuARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BuARD.
The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi presided, and there were also present Messrs. S. Taylor and J. H. Salkeld, with G. Moss (clerk).
ALTERATIONS AT MILL BROW.

The Committee reported that, accompanied by Mr. F. Wiswall, engineer to the Ship Canal Company, and Mr. Barker, the town's surveyor, they had inspected the alterations made by the company near Mill Brow School. It was found that the old canal wall had been removed, and a new wall of a much more substantial kind built in its place, and Mr. Wiswall said the founda- tion of the new wall was built on the rock, and was sufficiently strong for building the wall of a school upon at any future time if required. As the company did not intend to carry the wall any higher than the slope of the land, the members thought it desir- able to carry it higher as a fence to the limit of the Board's land, strong enough„to build upon or to act as a playground, thus making provision for any extension of the school that might be necessary in the future, and re- covering land which would otherwise be lost. Mr. Wis- wall mentioned that the company were about to run up a fence wall on the top of the one alluded to, and probably the company would be willing to carry it up in the stronger way, if the School Booed would contribute its share of the cost. ,As this appeared a feasible suggestion, having the merit of economy, the members accepted Mr. Wiswall's offer, and requested him to make an estimate of the cost.—The minutes were approved.

div.head: INCREASE OF SALARIES.
div.p: INCREASE OF SALARIES.

The Committee recommended that an assistant mis- tress (an ex P.T.) be advertised for, for Greenway-road girls school in place of two pupil teachers ; salary £45 per annum. It was further recommended that visitor Bowyer's salary be increased from £lOO to £lO5 per annum, and that visitor Howard's salary be increased from £75 to £BO per annum. Accounts for sundries amounting to £B2 14s. lid. were passed for payment.— The minutes were passed.
STATISTICS.
The following returns were presented for May : Certified Government accommodation, 3,287; total num-

ber on the rolls, 3,377; total average attendance, 2812.5:; percentage of attondances,B3„ During the month of May eight parents have been proceeded against for contravention of the bye-laws ; 46 parents have appeared before tile School Attendance Committee ; 427 warning notices have been served for irregular attendance. School fees were granted to five parents for 13 children.

div.head: RuNcoUN MAN DROWNED .AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: A RuNcoUN MAN DROWNED .AT EARLESTOWN.

Yesterday-morning, about half-past eleven' James Catten, 18 years of age, of Runcorri, employed on the flat Sarah, belonging to Mr. R. Abell, of Runcorn, was drowned in the Sankey Canal, at Earlestown. The flat was proceeding from St. Helens to Runcorn, and the deceased was steering. There was a stiff breeze blowing, and when nearing the Newton Common Locks he was pushing with his back against the steering bar, when hit foot slipped on the wet deck, and overbalancing him- self, he fell into the canal. Some time elapsed before his body could be recovered, and it was then too late to re- store animation. _ _ .
~........................—. IRON BEDSTEADS 84 BEDDING.—Garland, 51, Bridge-at., Warrington. DEATH OF A WIDNES WORKS MANAGER.

Our readers will regret to hear of the death of Mr. A. E. Smith, of Ditton, which took place at his brother's residence, Derby, on Friday last week. Over twelve months ago Mr. Smith had to relinquish his occupation in consequence of an attack of pleurisy, and since that time he had been under the care of able doctors at Derby, but although several operations were performed upon him, he succumbed to the disease as stated. He was 42 years of age and leaves a widow and several children to mourn his loss. For twenty years Mr. Lewis had been connected with the Chemical Works of Messrs. Hutchin- son and Co., for the last eight or nine years in the capa- city of manager, and the workmen regarded him with feelings of the highest regard **cause of his kind and just disposition. He was a most genial and good natured naan, ever ready to extend his sympathy and help, and his untimely death will be universally regretted. The funeral took placeat Derby on Monday and amongst his friends and former workmen who travelled to that town to pay the last token of respect to the deceased gentleman were Messrs. J. T. Allen, A. G. Kyle, W. Treacy, Adam Hoghton, and R. Lewis. Mr. Hadley, the proprietor of the works also attended the funeral. SUMMER FASHIONS, now showing at J. & W. Dorms Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. MR. T. C. EDWARDS-MOSS, M.P., AND COMPENSATION. Mr. H. B. Shore, secretary to the Widnes Division Liberal Association, has received the following letter from Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P, for the division : " Otterspool, Liverpool, 12th May, 1890.—Dear sir,—l beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter enclosing copy of a resolution passed at a meeting held in Widnes Liberal Club on the 19th instant, condemning certain pro- posals contained in the Local Taxation (Customs and Excise) Bill now before Parliament. I must express my regret that the Widnes Liberals in conjunction with the majority of their party, have thought it right to offer their earnest opposition to the earnest endeavour of the Government to do something for the causeof temperance, and, as far as their proposals go, to deal equitably with the temperance question. I enclose some extracts on the subject from the speeches of Liberal leaders, and I venture with all respect b submit them for the con- sideration of the members of your club. They afford a proof that the so-called compensation of publicans is a principle which was by no means unrecognised by the Liberal party ef a few years ago. Stern party opposition instead of the hearty support, which, from the enclosed extracts, we might have been led to expect from the Liberal leaders, is hardly, I fear, likely to encourage the Government to increase their exertions or extendT their proposals for the settlement of the temperance question. This I for one cannot but regret.-1 remain, yours faith- fully, T. C. EDWARDS-MOSS." SUMMER Fisaroiss, now sbowing at J. & W. DUTTON'S, Sankey-it., Warrington - Advt. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. In the absence bf the chairman and vice-chairman, Mr. Heywood was elected to preside. There were also present—Messrs. Aaron, Turner, T. Lewis, J. Whitlow, J. Baguley, J. Stokes, Hewitt, W. Whitlow, Bretherton, Knowles, Parr, Hor- ton, Priestner, Weir ; H. Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), J. Farring- ton (sanitary inspector).—The Pollution ofaßrook.—Mr. Farrington reported as to the pollution of Warford, or Keckvvick brook, by liquids from a tannery at Preston Brook, and he produced two samples of the water taken from the brook at two points. Mr. Farrington added that the analyst had been supplied with samples, but his report had not yet been received. In the course of some discussion it was stated that along some parts of the brook there was no other water for cattle to drink, and Mr. W. Whitlow remarked that his cattle would not drink the water on any account, and had to be removed to another part of the farm where there was purer water to drink. It was decided that the inspector should be requested to take further samples to be forwarded to the analyst. —Medical Officer's Report—Dr. Adams reported a case of three children suffering from measles at Appleton. The children were now, however, con- valescent. As there had been typhoid fever on the same premises last year he suggested that the water supply be analysed. A case of scarlet fever occurred at Sandy- lane, Weston Point, and a further case at Netherton.— This was the principal business. GARDEN Too.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington Eariestown.

div.head: AN ILLMATCHED PAIR AT RUNCORN.
div.p: AN ILLMATCHED PAIR AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. G. L. Davies and Dr. Steele, John Henry Bowman was ct arged with using threats to his wife Eva Bowman. The complainant said she had lived apart from her hus- band fcr four and a half years, and she maintained her- self and one girl. She had never received one farthing from him since she left him. On Whit-Monday he called at her mother's house and wanted her (witness) to sign a paper to let him be married. Shetold him she should do no such thing, andhe kicked up a row and threatened to" put a knife through her." She told him he was too lazy to maintain one wife, and he accused her of living " tally " with a man in Liverpool. She produced a letter from her mistress to disprove his words. She left the defendant because he attempted to murder her, and she was afraid he would do her some harm. The defendant said four years ago his wife left him in charge of two children, one of which was at the breast at the time, and he maintained them. He afterwards became ill, and Dr. McDougall sent him to the Workhouse hospital, and while he was there his mother-in-law fetched the eldest child out. During the whole of that time he had only seen his wife twice. On Whit-Monday he asked her to take both children, so that they would not be separated, and allow him to pay so much a week towards their sup- port, and as soon as he spoke she " started scandalising him shameful." He "had had a drop of drink and started scandalising back again, but no threats came out of his mouth."—The Bench bound the defendant over to keep the peace for six months, in his own recog- nizance of £lO.

div.head: -- PRESENTATION TO MR. SUPERINTENDENT
div.p: -- PRESENTATION TO MR. SUPERINTENDENT
JOHNSTONE, OF WIDNES.

A gathering was held in Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday evening, for the purpose of saying farewell to Mr. Superintendent Johnstone, on his retirement from the force, and also to present him with a token of the respect and esteeni with which he was held in the neighbourhood. In the absence of Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., who was unable to be present, Mr.. R. Lewis took the chair, and in the course of an appropriate speech, he dilated upon Mr. Johnstone's good qualitice and alluded to the friendly feeling that existed between the police awl the public during the time Mr. Johnstone had had control. The town would suffer a great loss through his early retirement, which, all regretted, was caused through failing health. He rejoiced, however, that Mr. Johnstone left a worthy successor—Mr.Noblett. The persons who had undertakPn the canvass had met with great success, and he had great pleasure in handing to Mr. Johnstone a purse containing £B4 3s. 6d. (Ap- plause.) Speeches were delivered by -Mr. C. H. Lewin (magistrates' clerk), Mr. J. W. Knowles, Dr. Hutchinson and S'n^.Printendent Noblett, all of whom spoke in high terms Ld' praise of Mr. Johnstone's personal character, and of his public work. In acknowledging tLe gift, Mr. Johnstone asked what he had done to deserve that testis monial, and all that had been said of him. He had tried to act honestly, and he believed every man under him had done so too. Alluding to his successor, Mr. Johnstone said they would find Superintendent Noblett a decent fellow and a good officer. A vote of thanks to the Chair- man concluded the proceedings. The members of the county force who have served under Mr. Johnstone in Widnes and elsewhere, have also presented that gentle- men with a purse of gold.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MISS' BPEAKNIAN, OF RUNCORN.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MISS' BPEAKNIAN, OF RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Parish Church, on Tuesday, Miss Ada Mary Speakman, eldest daughter of Mr. Philip Speakman, C.C., of the Mount, Higher Runcorn, was married to Mr. Victor Douetil, of Cheynelea, Surbi- ton. The high positiod occupied by Mr. Speakman in the community, who have placed him at one time or other in every public position it is in their power to bestow, invested the event with more than the customary interest and importance in social circles. Although the wedding was fixed for half- past eleven, persons anxious to witness the ceremony began to occupy the church at ten o'clock, and by half- past ten, when ordinary morning service commenced, a large company assembled, and it is doubtful if the ser- vice was ever listened to by so numerous a congregation since it was instituted by thd Vicar. By eleven o'clock the sacred edifice was well filled, and outside hundreds lined the pathway to the church, and large numbers assembled in the street. From numerous build- ings in the town flags floated in the breeze and streamers were stretched across High-st., and Devon- shire Square, and many• of Mr. Speakman's numer- ous tenants made quiet a show of bunting. Of course, the greater portion of the cong,regatien was composed of the fair sex, and their curiosity was kept fully alive by the constant arrival of the wedding guests. At length a buzz of excitement announced the approach of the bridal party, and Mr. Johnson played an inspirit- ing tune on the organ as the bride entered the sacred edifice, leaning upon the arm of her father. She was attired in a charming dress of white brocaded satin, and depending from the spray of orange blossoms which wreathed her brow, was a beautiful flowing white veil, the gift of her sister. In immediate attendance upon her were four bridesmaids, Miss Bertha Speakma.n (sister), Miss Elam (London), Miss Howe and Miss E. Howe (Durham), who each wore white and yellow silk Empire dresses, fastened at the throat with gold and pearl brooches, the gift of the bridegroom. Their heads were adorned with yellow feather hats, and in their hands they carried bouquets of marguerite daisies. The bridal party were met in the chancel by the bridegroom, who was attended by his brother, Mr. C. N. Douetil, who acted as best man, and the other groomsmen were Mr. T. W. Speakman and Mr.?. E. Speakman (brothers of the bride) and Mr. S. Roberts (Surbiton). The bridal party having arrayed themselves before the communion, the following guests occupied the choir stalls, and their bright and handsome toilets made up an effective picture :—Mrs. Speakman (mother of the bride), Mrs. Preston, Colonel Tomlinson, M.P., and Mrs. Tomlinson, (Preston); Mr. Duncan Graham, C.C., Mr. W. Simpson, (Wigan) ; Mr. W. Rogers, (Wigan) ; Mr. J. A. Davies, (Cressington) ; Misses King, (Northampton) ; Mr. and Mrs. Clarison, (Liverpool) ; Mr. J. Norman, Mr. and Mrs. Marwood, Mr. and Mrs. Watts, (Winnington) ; Mr. Arthur Barlow and Miss Barlow, of Farnworth ; Rev. G. H. Seeley, Miss Preston, Mr. I. Speakman, Mr. Eaton Speakman, Mr. Charlie Speakman. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. Dr. Preston, M.A., vicar of Holy Trinity Church, who was assisted by the Rev. A. J. Jameson, curate ; and at its conclusion, the wedding party retired into the'vestry, and the usual formula gone through. When they emerged, Mr. Johnson played the Wedding March on the organ, and the bells rang forth a merry peal. As the happy pair left the church a number of young girls strewed flowers in their path, and rice was showered upon them from a score of hands. The wedding party and guests were conveyed from and to the Mount in ten carriages drawn by pairs of handsome horses supplied by, Messrs. Yarwood Bros. Lunch was provided for the guests at Mr. Speakman's residence, and in the catirs ,af the afternoon Mr. and Mrs. Douetil departed by train to Devonshire, where the honeymoon will be spent. In the evening a ball was held at The Mount, and on Wednesday a picnic on the Dee was arranged, The following is a complete list of the presents : Mr, and Mrs,. On Thursday evening, Mr. Speakman entertained to dinner at The Mount, the office staff and the captains in his employ numbering in all about 35 persons. Mr. and Mrs. Speakman, Miss Bertha Speakman, and Mr. T. W. Speakman were present. After the repast. the toast of the Queen was proposed and honoured in the customary style, and theri Mr. Speakman, addressing those present as fellow workmen, said he was pleased to see them there on the occasion of that happy event in his family. This was the first break in his family, and he could only trust that throughout the lives of Mr. and Mrs. Douetil, happiness might reign as it had done in the begin- ning. (Applause.) He had great pleasure in asking them to mink to the health of Mr. and Mrs. Douetil, and long life to them. (Applause.) The toast was cordially honoured.—MS. W. Carroll proposed the health of Mr. and Mrs. Speakman and family in a few well chosen words and the toast was given with musical honours. Mr. Speakman and Mr. T. Speakman responded. The toast of" the Staff" was then given. by Mr. Speakman, who coupled with it the name of Mr Carroll, who responded. Mr. Tom Speakman proposed the toast of" The captains and in,n, and the com- modore captain, Mr. Henry Lewis, responded. The toast list concluded with the "servants of The Mount" to which Mr. Backer, the gardener replied. Afterwards the company viewed the colle,:tion of beautiful presents, which were displayed in the drawing, room, and spent the remainder of the evening in the gardens.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday, Mr. James Dobson presided and there were present Messrs. Meadowcroft, Wiswall, Imison F. A. Lithe (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor),

div.head: RIAL-TH OF THE_ TOWN_ '.
div.p: RIAL-TH OF THE_ TOWN_ '.

The Medical Officer of Health (Dr. McDougall) re- ported that during May there were 26 deaths registered of which 4 were inquest cases and of the remainder 5 were due to bronchitis, 3 to phthisis, 2 to convulsions, 2 to heart disease, 4 to inflammation of the lungs, 2to mesenteric disease, and one each to malignant disease of the lungs, premature births,apoplexv, and inflammation of the lining membrane of the brain. The 26 deaths showed an average death rate of 17.3 per 1000 per annum and, exclusive of the inquest cases, of 14.6.—1 n answer to Mr. Meadowcroft, the Medical Officer said there were some cases of infectious disoa-se in the town, but were no deaths. There was nothing of an epidemic character.

A discussion took place as to the desirability of placing the plans on view in the reading Room oithe Free Library or in the entrance to the Hall, but no decision was arrived at.

NI GHTSOIL REMOVAL. On the recommendation of the Nightsoil Removal Com- mittee it was resolved that the stables at the Royal Hotel be taken for twelve months with the option of a renewal, at a rental after the rate of £2O per annum free of all rates and taxes; and that the boat. The Board went into Committee to consider the tenders for the Ellesmere-st. sewer, and on resuming the tender of Messrs. M. W. Walmsley and Co., was accepted.
