There were also present the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester. Rev. C. W. Wooll, Rev. DeanFineg,an, Messrs. J. Leatherbarrow, J. Mercer, J. Whalley, C. B. Johnson.. J. Marsh, G. E. Chadwick, W. Lowe, E. Birchall, J. Burchill, J. Ellison, W. Middlehurst, .1. Ranson, E. Syder, J. Buckley, G. Davies, W. Tyrer, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 479 inmates of the house this week, 484 last week and 498 in the corresponding week last year; 80 vagrants had been relieved during the week, against 57 41 tll5 corresponding week last year. LITERATI:MR.—At a meeting of the Visiting Committee on the 2nd June, it was recommended that the chaplain be instructed to incur an expenditure not exceeding £l5 for books for the use of the inmates ; and that the Clerk order one of the London daily papers.—The Clerk intimated that the matter had arisen through an appli- cation received from the Rev, Mr. Norrie, the workhouse chaplain, who for some years pig had had to depend on gifts from friends, Ise., in order to provide literature for the inmates.—The Chairman said he was sure every Guardian would sympathise with the recommendation. , —The recommendation was unanimously adopted. AN OFFICER'S GUARANTEE.—The On* repOrted the receipt of a guarrantee bond for £l5O from the Ocean and General Guarrantee Co., Limited, on behalf of Joseph Tracey, relieving officer. PAEPERISM.—Mr. J. J. Henley, Government Inspector, wrote on the 29th May enclosing 20 copies of his annual statement of pauperism, and expenditure of the various unions in Lancashire. He suggested that they should be 'handed over to any Guardians interested in the subject. —The copies of the return were formally laid on the , table and several members took a copy each. This was all the business.

div.head: DESPERATE FIGFET WITH NEGRO CONVICTS.
div.p: DESPERATE FIGFET WITH NEGRO CONVICTS.

Advices from New York say that two powerful negro convicts, both undergoing long terms of imprisonment at Trenton State Prison, State of New Jersey, have made a desperate effort to regain their liberty. The two des- perate characters pounced on and overpowered their keeper on Wednesday night, and got clean away before the gagged custodian could raise an alarm. On the escape becoming known, however, two mounted police- men went of in pursuit, and overtook them on Friday on the high road. When ordered to halt and surrender themselves, one coolly turned round and shot the officer dead with a revolver. The other officer immediately presented his rifle at the murderer, and avenged the death of his comrade by shooting him dead on the spot. The other convict meanwhile jumped on to the dead officer's horse and galloped away. A posse of mounted officers at once went into pursuit, and a latter telegram announces that the second convict has been recaptured.

div.head: SUSPECTED DYNAMITER AT – RAW ARDEN. AMUSING STORY. – --
div.p: A SUSPECTED DYNAMITER AT - RAW ARDEN. AMUSING STORY. - --

A cprrespondent relates that something of a disquiet- ing character happened at Hawarden Village on Whit- Tuesday. A gentleman of respectable appearance called at an official establishment, presided over by a lady, and asked permission to leave a Gladstone bag there. • He had come, he said, with the excursion from Bristol, and the bag would be a great tie upon him unless she would take charge of it. This was a small favour, and a gracious permission was accorded. But, with surprise, the lady observed that it took much exertion to raise it from the ground to the counter. "What is it ?" she asked. "I hope it's none of that dynamite," said she. "No, ma'am," rejoined he, "it's money; and please take care of it." And with a smile, which the lady thought sarcastic, he bowed himself out, and was lost among the crowd of West of England Liberals in Hawarden-st. "Here's a pretty how d'ye do" thought the fair proprietress, as she hurriedly took counsel with another of the sex. It was heavy, was the bag, and it did'rit sound like money when (with their united strength) it was lifted up and gently (for fear of an explosion) placed down again. So it was taken outside and put among the coals. But, on more mature thoughts it was considered that should some hidden clockwork inside "set it off" the side of the house would certainly be blown in, and set free the roof to follow the law of gravitation. So, with much labour and more alarm, it was removed to the summer-house at the further end of the garden, in which enclosure none belonginz, to th 3 house ventured until evening, when the bag was re- claimed and taken away. It is plea.sing to be able to state that the contents of the bag were not dynamite, and that it was good and lawful coin of the realm, received from those of her Majesty's lieges who came by the Gladstone excursion trains from Bristol that morning.

div.head: THIS MAN WAS FRIGHTENED.
div.p: THIS MAN WAS FRIGHTENED.

And on reading the facts it will appear that he had reason to be. The man referred to was Edward Perrin, a guard on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway. In September, 1837, he met with an accident which gave a temporary shock to his system. Not long afterwards he began to feel a pain in the chest and have difficulty in breAthing, and threw up a great deal of mucus (phlegm). He at once concluded he had some serious ailment of the lungs, and sought medical advice. The doctor said it was so, and added that there was no cure for it, and that he could do no more than give him something to ease the pain and the cough. Then the doctor gave Mr. Perrin a certificate, stating that he was suffering from " Catarrah Plithisis," which is the pro- fessional term for that dreadful malady, Consumption. Further symptoms soon appeared which seemed to con- firm this alarming opinion. The poor fellow experienced great pain in eating, and a tightness across the chest which felt, he said, "as if some strong man was grip- ping him around the body under the arms." The rest of Mr. Perrin's narrative is best related in his own words. He says : "I soon commenced to have a brackish taste in the mouth, as if I had been sucking copper. Then came cold chills and sweats in turn, the cough got hollow, and I raised more than I had done. These terrible symptoms so scared me that I went and consulted a doctor. He examined me carefully, and certified as follows :

------- "In the case of Guard Perrin. This man is evidently frightened. He is suffering from Phthisis and Dyspepsia. Cod liver oil and iron are indicated." "This fully bore out what the other doctor had said, so I now looked upon myself as done for. I took every- thing I could hear tell of. I have drank gallons of cod liver oil and sherry, and have had many quarts of camphorated oil rubbed on my chest, until my wife was sick of rubbing. I was also poulticed continually, but in spite of all this terrific dosing and medicating I got gradually worse. In a half-a-dozen words my condition was this : I believed myself to be fast going to the grave with consumption; my friends said so, the doctors said so, and it looked like it if anything ever did. It is understood that consumption is sure death, and I made up my mind for that awful end. I had been off my work from 1887 to 1838. I was ashamed to be away so much, as I was obliged to draw funds from the Club all the time to help support my family. "While I was thus doing nothing but waiting to die, crawling about feebly like a man who has virtually done with this world, I happened one day to meet one of the Traffic Inspectors of our line. He was shocked at my looks, but said, "Perrin, I don't know as anything will help you, but if anything will, it is Mother Seigel's Cura- tive Syrup." I remember that this idea amused me, miserably broken and ill as I was. Help me? Could it cure consumption? Not likely. Impossible! Still it could not make me worse, and so I got a bottle and be- gan to take it. I could scarcely credit my own feelings, but as sure as truth is truth, before I had used up that bottle of medicine, I found relief. Now comes what you may find it hard to believe—l took but two more:bottles and went back to work, and have been sound and healthy ever since. I told the doctor about it, and although he saw I was well, he seemed displeased. "You say Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup cured you ?" he said. " Non- sense. It is only a quack medicine; it is nothing but stuff and rubbish." Well, all right, I said to myself, it may be stuff and rubbish, but it has made a sound man of me after that very doctor had me booked for the graveyard, and said no earthly power could keep me out of it. That was enough for me, and will be enough for thousands of others in this country. "I am exposed to all sorts of weather, but have never had a return of the bad breathing, chest pains, nor any of the other symptoms that nearly frightened me out of my senses. I eat and enjoy my food as well as any man in England. Now what was the secret of this getting well? If I really had consumption it was nothing short of a miracle,but I never had consumption at all. The doctors were all wrong in calling it that. What I actually suffered from was indigestion and dyspepsia., which causes the same symptoms that mark true consumption; hence lots of people who are supposed to have lung com- plaint might be as easily cured as I was if they would let cod liver oil alone and take Mother Seigers Curative Syrup." Mr. Perrin's address is—No. 36, Gorton Brook-st., Gorton Brook, Manchester, and he will reply to any letters written to him concerning his case.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
WIFE ASSAULT.

At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, a foreman bricksetter named John Murphy, was summoned for having assaulted his wife, on the 30th ult. On Saturday night she asked him for some money and he struck her on the mouth. Defendant, who promised not to offend again, was ordered to be hound over to keep the peace for six months, or go to prison for a week in default.

CHARGE OF STEALING DI7CIC.S. At the Warrington Occasional Court on Thursday morning, before Mr. Ziba Armitage, three young men named George Fogg, George James Hankinson, and Edward Bate, were charged with stealing two ducks, the property of Mr. J. Perrin, of Croft, and valued at es., on the Ist inst. Evidence in support of the charge having been given, the defendants were remanded until the 18th June. 'Bail was accepted. A FIGHT FOR A Swit.EatiMAßT. On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, two young women, named Mary Jane Conway and Mary Coffey, were charged with having committed a breach of the peace. A police constable found them fighting in Buttermarket-st. It transpired that they had quarrelled about a young man, and, to settle the dispute, had de- cided to fight it out. They had since become friends. The Bench discharged the defendants on payment of ,costs.

- - A KNOWING Don. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, John ?della., Who arts as the custodian of the fields at Arpley. was summoned under the Dogs" order for having allowed a dog to be at large unmuzzled. It appeared that the dog had bitten a little boy, named Warburton, and the police were informed of the matter. Consequently pro- ,ceedings were taken. Defendant stated that the dog bad since been destroyed. It was a very quiet dog in the streets,'but when at Arpley it knew its bminess and would go after anyone directly.—The Chief Con- stable: Especially if they shouted " Mickey Mealy ?" Defendant: The moment they shonted that he would be on them. I would sooner, if I could have afforded it, 'have paid £5 than destroy the dog.—A fine of Is. and costs, 3s. 6d., was imposed.

div.head: DRIVING A CART OVER A HOSE-FIFE.
div.p: DRIVING A CART OVER A HOSE-FIFE.

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, a man named John Hickey was summoned for haring damaged a hose-pipe belonging to the Corporation, an the 24th ult. Evidence was given to the effeetthat on the date in question, when a fire was raging in Buttermarket-st.. defendant, who was in charge of a fish cart, drove it over the hose pipe. Very little damage was done, but Superintendent Turner said that had the pipe been broken the result might have been serious. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said that the defendant had ren- dered considerable assistance at the fire, and the defend- ant himself said that he went over the pipe with his cart accidentally, as he was excited. Under th e cir- cumstances, he was only ordered to pay the cost of the summons, and 6d. as damages. ROIMING AN ACTOMATIC MACHINE. Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a lad named Thomas Robinson.(l4), pleaded guilty to hav- ing stolen ten packets of sweetmeats from an automatic machine on the Central Station platform. He obtained the packets tqr putting lead cheques into the machine in- stead of pennies. It was stated that no fewer than 82 bogus coins were found in one machine, and the Chief Constable said that this kind of fraud was very exten- sively carried on at Warrington. The Chairman (Alder- man Harrison) described the offence as a deliberate and systematic fraud. A manager of the company said that Warrington was the worst station he had heard of for -this offence. Manchester and Liverpool stations were nothing as compared to Warrington.—A fine of 40s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment, was imposed. Two BEOTTIERS CHATIGED WITH STEALING LEAD. On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, two men named Thomas Leatherbarrow, factory hand, Prince-st., and Robert Leatherbarrow, tanner, Whittle-st., were brought up in custody on a charge of havingstolen 60Ihs. of lead from the premises of William Twiss, builder, 114, Wilderspool-rd. The prisoner Thomas pleaded guilty.— Mr. Arthur Browne represented the other prisoner, and pleaded not guilty.—The lead was placed in prosecutor's yard on Thursday evening. The following evening the prisoner Thomas Leatherbarrow was found concealed behind a pair of bellows in the yard. When found he was sitting on two ingots of lead. Asked what brought him there, he said he was "looking for a rat." It was afterwards found that some lead had been sold by Thomas Leatherbarrow to Richard Clifton, a marine store dealer, and it was contended by the prosecution that Robert Leatherbarrow was acting in collusion with his brother. Prisoners were apprehended and charged by P.C. Alonaahan. Thomas replied (pointing to his brother) "Ho was not with me at all. I took it myself, end sold it to Clifton for 11,-. 6d." Robert said "I never went into the yard. I know nothing about it,"—The
Bench gave Robert Leatherberrow the benefit of the doubt, and dlschargvd him. Thomas Leatherbarrow they committed to prison for two months, with hard labour. '
A MARINE STORE DEALER FINED.,

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court,a marine store dealer named Richard Clifton, was sum- moned for having purchased a less quantity of lead than he was by law authorised to do. Mr. J. L. Whittle (town-clerk) said that the proceedings arose out of a case that was before the magistrates a few days ago, when a man named Leatherbarrow was convicted of stealing a quantity of lead. At the trial the defendant Clifton was called as a witness, and admitted having purchased the lead. Evidence was given by Constable Monoghan to the effect that last Sunday morning he went to the defendant's houie in Admiral-st., and asked for the lead that defendant had purchased. Defendant denied hav- ing bought any, but on witness making a search he found some of the lead produced. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence, and said that the restrictions were puzzling, and defendant was under the impres- sion that the quantity he bought, over 561b5, was suffi- cient. He would .undertake in the future to be very careful in such matters. The Bench said that they could not see their way to inflict anything less than the full penalty of £5, as there were other summonses against the defendant. They imposed a. fine of that amount, and thereupon the Town Clerk withdrew the other sum- ' mouses.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), Alderman Harrison, and Alderman Sutton. DRUNKESSESS.—The following persons were deal with for this offence :—Michael O'Neil, in Church-st., on Saturday night, fined ss. and costs; Edward Mannion, in Irlam-st., on Saturday night, fined ss. and costs; Martin Ward, in Tanner's-lane, on the 24th May, fined ss. and costs; John Kelley, in Sankey-st., fined 53. and costs; Mary Mannion, in Old-road, Latchford, fined ss. , and costs; Hannah Cook, in Wilderspool-road, on the 28th ult., fined 10s. and costs. A DESERTER.—Richard Wright. a deserter from the Royal Engineers, stationed at Aldershot, was remanded to await escort. BREACH OF THE PEACE. James Wainwright and William Connor were summoned for having committed abreach of the peace, by fighting in Butttermarket-st. on the 27th May.—After evidence had been given, Connor was bound over in one surety of £lO to be of good behaviour for six months. Wainwright was ordered to pay costs. MISCELLANEOUS.—James Leonard, Wm. Rourke, and William Dunbobbin, boys, were each fined 2s. 6d. for throwing stones in Howley-field. on the 23rd May.—Jas. Lanady, Thomas Lanady, Patrick Murray, and Thomas Dalton, boys, were each summoned for having played football in Winwick-st., on the 25th May.—ii fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed in each case.—For having allowed the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire on the 25th May, Wm. Gorst, Heath-side, was ordered to pay a fine of is. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett and W. Owen. DRUNKEN-SESS.—Luke Cunningham, for having been drunk and incapable in Mersey-st., on Monday evening, was cautioned and discharged. &Hoot CASES.—A number of persons were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fines were inflicted. Mr. George Riley proved the cases. FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison and Chandley. THEFT FROM A PUBLICHOTJSE.—CharIes Johnson (18), a tinsmith, pleaded guilty to having stolen a blue pilot coat, of the value of 205., from the kitchen of the Hop Pole publichouse. The coat was the property of Mr. Harry Dale. It was stated that prisoner had been occasionally employed as a waiter at the Hop Pole, and he admitted taking the coat. The Bench imposed a fine of 10s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment in default. HUSBAND AND WIFE.—John Clare, summoned for hav- ing assaulted his wife, was bound over to keep the peace, in his own recognisance.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WRDNESDAY.—Before Captain Withington, Mr. James Marson, and Mr. W. Tinsley. A Nig= SCENE.—Samuel Terry and Charles Higgin- son were charged with having. on the 17th May, com- mitted a breach of the peace in Warburton-St. A police- constable stated that he saw the men, who had had some drink, fighting in the street ; one had only his trousers on, and the other his shirt.—Captain Withing- ton : He had been in bed, and got up to fight. —Defend- ants were bound over to keep the peace. OBSTRUCTING THE HIGHWAY.—Gilbert Brundrett was fined is. and costs for having, on the 25th May, at Rix- ton, obstructed the highway by allowing a horse and cart to stand there for an unreasonable time. A SLEEPY DRlVER.—William Hankinson was fined is. and costs for having, on the 23rd May, at Rixton, been asleep whilst in charge of a cart. ASSAULTING A WlFE.—William Gilbert was charged with having assaulted his wife, Elizabeth, at Poulton, on the 12th May. The two quarrelled about what they should give their son for supper, and the complainant alleged that her husband struck her across the face. Defendant denied this, and said his wife was of intem- perate habits, and had broken the house up whilst he had been away working.—A fine of ss. and costs was

imposed. - Don AT LARGE.—Samuel Atherton, boatman, was or- dered to pay costs for hating, on the 21st May, at Pen- keth, allowed his dog to be at large.—Joseph Lindley, for a similar offence, was dealt with in a like manner. A:CARELESS DRIVER. —For riding on a cart without reins, at Cuerdley, on the 10th May, John Knight was fined Is. and costs.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

.....,..s.„— MONDAY.—Before Mr. G. L. Davies and Dr. Steele. DRUNIENNESS.—For this offence, Mary Riley, Thomas . Bates, Thomas Rawlinson, and Robert Moore, were each ; fined 2s. 6d. and costs; John Berks, George Taylor, and 1 Lucy Taylor, were each fined ss. and costs.—John Moss 1 was charged with being drunk in the Aston Arms, Sutton, and was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. William Orme, and George Pye, young men, pleaded guilty to being drunk in the Lord Rodney Inn, and they were each fined 10s. and costs. A. FATHER AND HIS SONS.—Stephen Lowe was sum- moned to show cause why he should not pay £.5 4s. arrears due under a magistrate's order for the mainten- ance of his sons, George and James Lowe, who are under detention at Stockport Industrial School at a charge of 4s. per week.—The defendant admitted the debt, and pleaded that he had been ill and unable to keep up with his payments.—P.C. Ratcliffe sainhe defendant earned 30s. per week at the Old Quay, and he had only one son 16 years of age.—The Bench ordered him to pay 6s. per week towards the arrears,and 45. per week under the order. A GROCER AND HIS DOGS.—Walter Collier, grocer, Church-st. was summoned for keeping a dog without a license. P., S. Gosling said the defendant had three dogs, and only two licenses. The defendant said he had a St. Bernard dog from Mr. Bibby on trial for a fortnight, on the understanding that if it turned out a good yard dog, he should pay for it. He took out a license for the dog when he found it suited.—Case dismissed. DoG AT LARGE.---John Filkin was fined 6cL, and costs for allowing his dog to be at large. A SLEEPY CARTER.—eamuel Roberts was fined 10s .and costs for being asleep whilst in charge of a lurry and three horses. CEIIMNIRS ON FIRE.--Jabez Horrocks and James Sellers were summoned for allowing the chimney of their res- pective dwellings to be on fire, and a fine of 6d. and costs, Be. 6d., was imposed in each case. lINZUST SCALPS —John Wm. Glynn, a fish dealer, was charged with having a pair of scales in his possession for use for trade, which were unjust. Snperintendent Large ' said the defendant's wife was hawking fish on a cart, and he examined the scales and found they were nine drachms out of balance against the purchaser, which was a great deal too much.—The defendant, !die said he did not know the scales were incorrect, was fined ss. and costs, Bs. 6.1. A DISHONEST SERTANT.—Annie Fernihough, a domestic servant, was charged with having, on the 27th May, stolen Is. 6.1., three brooches, and other articles, the property of her master, Joseph McQuinn, shoemaker, High-st.—She was remanded for a week.

CHIMNEY ON FIRE .—Alfred Whalley, Walmesley-st ,was fined is. and costs for allowing the chimney of his dwell- ing to be on fire. A POLISH .QUARREL.—Hannah Passick, 20, Barn-street, was summoned for assaulting Zouser Rucoky,on the 20th ult. While gathering cinders at Hughes' chemical works, a quarrel arose between the parties, and Passick struck Rucoky, causing a wound on the hand. The evidence had to be repeated by an interpreter.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed. CARD FLAYlNG.—Richard Forbv, Michael McQuirke, Thomas Jones, and Richard Keating, of Ditton, were summoned for playing cards on some waste land near Ditton Station, on the 25th ult.—The defendants denied that any money passed, and the Bench dismissed them with a caution, but ordered them to pay costs.

GRAPPENHALL Sr. WINIFRED'S v. WARRINGTON AMATEDRS.—This match took place on the ground of the former, on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by 44 runs. The home team batting first could make no stand against the bowling of Pownall and Hackney, the former taking three wickets for six runs, and the latter five wickets for 15 runs. Score :—Grap- penhall, 25 ; Amateurs, 69. WARRINGTON v. LIVERPOOL.—This match, played at Aigburth on Saturday in dull and cold weather, resulted in a tie. Liverpool won the toss, and commenced bat- ting with D. Q. Steel and H. B. Parr to the deliveries of Jolley and Adam. In the latter's first over Mr. Steel was well caught by Mr. S. M. Crosfield (1 for 4). Mr. Brancker came next, and runs came freely from Jolley, but Captain Adam could not be got away. With the total at 14 Mr Parr was badly missed in the slips. At 29 Mr. Brancker gave a chance in the long field, but with the total at 36 Captain Adam bowled Mr. Parr. Four runs later Mr. Bra ncker was well caught by Clarke, and Mr. Wright retiring without scoring, 4 wickets were down for 48. Messrs. W. O'Dwyer and T. M. Patterson carried the score to 110 before the former was run out for 7. the result of nearly an hour's play. Pat- terson was next out for an invaluable 59, the result of some very hard hitting. He was, however, badly missed when he had made 40. From this point the game was very slow, and ultimately Liverpool ended their innings at 4.40. At 4.55 Warrington began batting, but made a poor start, Mr. S. M. Crosfield unfortunately being run out, with the score at 15. Mr. Smith was also run out after scoring 17 in very little time, by three 4's, one 2 and three singles (2 for 41). Mr. J. J. Crostield was the next to go, being splendidly caught in the slips by Mr. Hornby, who had to jump to reach the ball. Mr. Gros- field's 18 was the result of good cricket, and did not in- clude a boundary hit. Messrs. Clarke and Lawton added 27 rims before the latter was given out lbw ;4 for 70. Mr. Jolley joined Clarke, and both scoring freely, the Liver- pool captain put White (pro.) on at the railway end at 85. The first ball was very short, and Jolley hit it hard to leg for 5, and the next over from the same bowler Jolley got him away to leg for 4, bringing up 100 at six o'clock. Nine runs later Clarke retired, after scoring 32 in good style, marred only by one chance. While at the wicket he hit four 4's; 5 for 109. Mr. Voisey was next out at 128, and one run later Jolley retired for 36, made up of one 5, four 4's, two 3's, three 2's, and three singles —7 for 129. Captain Adam retired at 140, and Mr. Reynolds being caught in the slips first ball, 9 wickets were down for 140. Messrs. Podmore and Armstrong were together. The former placed Mr. Steel for 2, and then drove him hard along the ground, and was attempt- ing a second run for this stroke when he fell, and so lost his wicket. Pull score : LIVERPOOL. THE EXAMTNER, SATURDAY, JUNE 7, 1890.

WIDNES v. GARSTON.—Considerable interest centred in, the meeting oi the Widnes and Garston elevens at Widnes on Saturday, from the fact that on the previous Saturday, the Garstonians had scored an easy victory. This week, however, slightly changed, Widnes were first to bat, and they kept the wicket nearly all afternoon. scoring 113 by fine cricket. The principal contributor was Mr. H. B. Thorpe, who batted in splendid form, and was not out for 46. Watson 11, D. Jones 11, and Colquitt, J. A. Briggs and Ashall nine each, also deserve a good word of praise. The Garston bowlers were all severely punished. Moss Jackson having the best record with six wick Ats for 46. Time only allowed three of the visitors to bat, but they ran up 24 for the loss of one wicket, and when time was called Rabbitt and Morrow were well fixed, and to all appearance would have scored heavily. The Widnes second team suffeied a disappoint- ment at Garston, the second eleven there refusing to play because James Briggs was in the Widnes team. This was rather too much for the patience of the visitisg, team, as Briggs is not a professional now, but simply a groundsman.

SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GOOD TEMPLARS.

--- Tne quarterly session of South-west Lancashire District Lodge of Good Templars was held on Saturday, in the Wesleyan Chapel, Huyton Quarry. The lodge was called to order at three o'clock by Bro. Morris Jones, D.C.T., when a large number of representatives were present front Liverpool. War- rington, Southport, St. Helens, Earlestown, Bootle, Ashton-in-Makerfleld, Golborne, Waterloo, and else- where. The roll of officers was called,and responded to, after which the D. L. degree was conferred upon several candidates. The report of the D.C.T., Bro. M. Jones, dealt comprehensively with the various phases of district work, entering largely into questions of detail and matters essential to the welfare of the order. Bro. R. D. Peterson, D. Sec.' reported an addition of two new , lodges during the quarter. The returns from all the lodges showed an upward tendency, and pointed to a large increase of membership at the close of the official year. Bro. It. W. Eirlrus, D. Treas., reported the finances to be in a very healthy condition, with a balance in hand. The report of Bro. Arthur Newell, D.S.J.T., was of a most encouraging description and referred to the fact that the South-West Lancashire Juvenile District was now the largest in England. The report of the executive having:been adopted, the resolutions from lodges were taken, after which the nomination and election of a suc- cessor to the late Bro. Pickersgill, D. E. Supt., was pro- ceeded with, and eight candidates having being pro- p.sed, Bro. George Lamb, P.D. Ch., was elected. Bro. Arthur Newell having resigned the position of D.S.J.T. owing to failing health, the recommendation of his suc- cessor, Bro. F. W. Hall, came up from District Juveniles Council, and, after discussion, was confirmed. An in- vitation for next session of D.L. to be held at South- port, was received, and being accepted, the date fixed upon was Saturday, the 23rd of August.— Bro. .J. B. Collings, honorary grand secretary, proposed, and Bro. R. W. Kirkus, D. Treas., seconded, a vote of sympathy and condolence with the widow and family of the late Bro. J. Pickersgill, and a similar token ot regret was, on the motion of Bro. J. A. Lee, D. Chap., seconded by Bro. G. R. Allison, also ordered to be conveyed to Bro. M. Bebbington, in the loss he has sustained in the death of his wife.—Other matters having been disposed of, the D.L. closed in due form.—After tea, open-air and , indoor meetings were held, and addresses delivered by , Brea. Pastor J. Bennett Anderson, Morris Jones, D.C.T., , J. A. Lee, D. Chap., George Lamb, D.E.S., and others, and resolutions condemnatory of the Government linens- Fag proposals were unanknously adopted.

But withoulMmpensation. (Applause.) Was it not a fact, proved by overwhelming evidence, that the liquor trader of the kingdom was producing in the community much misery, poverty, and crime and premature death? He believed that the evidence was overwhelming that the traffic was also in a large measure responsible for the lunatic asylums, poorhouses, and the prisons. He should not like that evening the cry to be raised that compensation would be enact of justice to the publicans, because the interests of the individual publican were a very small item. Most public-houses were tied, and belonged to wealthy brewers, and therefore compensa- tion in 99 cases out of every 100 would go to compensate wealthy brewers, who had already been compensated enough, and not individuals. (Applause.) The Chair- man, in conclusion, said he earnestly hoped whatever might be the views held by any friends in that room, the proceedings would be characterized by order and kindliness of spirit. (Applause.)

THE RESOLUTION OF PROTEST. Mr. W. 11. BUTLER proposed—" That this meeting pro- tests against the proposals of the Government in the Local Taxation, Customs, and Excise Bill, relating to licences." The first argument he brought against the I proposal was, that instead of the liquor trade :being treated on its merits, it was being made a mere question of finance. If the Liquor Bill was of such importance, let it be thrashed out in a fair and manly spirit. It was not a party question, but one that concerned them as citizens of the commonwealth. Mr. Goschen was evi- dently graduating for the office of the Lord High Execu- tioner of the present Government, and he would bring about its dissolution if he forced the Bill upon the country. (Hear, hear.) If the Bill was passed, what kind of public-houses would be bought out? The poer, miserable houses of the publican who can hardly make ends meet, while the large establishments,lit by the elec- tric light, would be continued. (Applause.) The money would be spent in buying up the little houses that were no good.. The country had, he thought, decided upon the question, and if the battle had to be fought, let it be fought on the larger and fuller issue. (Applause.) Mr. Twxss seconded the motion. Referring to the old Church-street fair, he said the beer taps at that time used to run all night. (A Voice : "Very good ale, then," and laughter.) There was no difference recognised then between night and morning, and had such a Bill as the present been introduced at that time, it would have afforded evidence of good faith. But there was too much light for that now, and the time had gone by for persons to wink at the existing condition of things. Sir Wilfrid Lawson was still alive. (Applause and laughter.) His work was not yet done, and if this question could be left over till the country could have its say, there would be a large majority in the House of Commons on the other side. The speaker then referred to the compensa- tion paid to slave-owners, during which he was fre- quently interrupted. Mr. JOHN GANDY supported the motion. He was thoroughly in earnest upon this question: It was a gre.t shame that the efforts of those who wished well to their country should be retarded by a clause to compensate those who were the greatest degraders and demoralizers of the country. (Cries of "Shame" and applause.) There was no gainsaying the fact. It was an undeniable fact that drink was the great curse of the country, and the sooner they were freed from its thraldom the better it would be for all of them. (Hear, hear, applause, and a Voice : " Are you a teetotaller?") Poor ragged children came to his shop, children he was sorry to see, and their condition was owing to the drink trade.

A Voles: Are you a teetotaller ? Mr. GANDY : I have been a teetotaller for seven years. (Applause.) Continuing, Mr. Gandy said that he hoped the Government would be compelled to withdraw the clauses. There was scarcely a publican in the town who was not sUbject to three months' notice—(cheers)—in- deed, he had been informed that they were liable to be discharged at a moment's notice. The compensation, therefore, did not apply to them, but would go to those who had already grown rich beyond the dreams of avarice. He entered his emphatic protest against the proposals. (Applause.) Mr. W. DIOGLE intimated that he had an amendment to propose, to test the views of the meeting. The CHAIRMAN said the meeting had been called by the Warrington Temperance Federation. (Cheers.) Therefore it was a meeting of the friends of temperance. They should be perfectly within their right if they declined to admit any amendment. (Cries of" No, no; It is a general public meeting.") Ihther than appear to give the slightest show of unfairness, he was perfectly willing to allow Mr. Diggle a hearing. Mr. Droome, who said he did so in favour of temper- ance, then proposed as an amendment "That, in the opinion of this meeting, the Government Bill dealing with the Licensing Question is an honest, straightfor- ward, measure, tending to promote the true interests of temperance progress." The Bill had been introduced for the purpose of reducing the number of public-houses,and the money to enable that to be done would be obtained from those who consumed the drink. Therefore they were I assisting the temperance cause and temperance people. Teetotallers were not asked to contribute a single penny of compensation. The Government proposed to Put a tax upon a certain liquor' and those who consumed it paid the money required for purposes of compensation. If they wished the number of public-houses to be reduced, here was a plan by which it could be accomplished. (A Voice: "Bosh.") Bosh or not, the remark was quite true. That was his view of the matter, and he contended that the Bill had a tendency to assist the temperance Cane. Mr. SAMUEL BARLOW seconded the amendment. He thought that after.the intemperate speeches which had been given in favour of the original resolution, the re- marks made by Mr. Diggle must commend themselves to the approbation of the audience. (Hear, hear). A pub- lican was as much entitled to compensation as Mr. Gandy—who had a large business—or anyone else: and he contended that his fellow-townsmen would not sub- mit to see a poor publican injured. (Laughter and in- terruption). The publican should not be deprived of his living. He was entitled to compensation, and there was no law in the land that would deprive him of it. If the next election was fought on this point Englishmen would, he was sure, come to the rescue, and thus override in- temperate teetotallers, who would find their level. (Laughter and applause.) The amendment and the original resolution were then put to the meeting, and the Chairman declared the latter to have been carried by a large majority. (Applause.) ANOTHER RESOLUTION.

Mr. T. BIRCHALL, mOved, "That the chairman be re- quested to forward a copy of the first resolution to Lord Salisbury, Mr. Goschen, Mr. Ritchie, and Sir Gilbert Greenall. ' (A voice : " Three cheers for• Gilbert,") (laughter, and hooting.) That, Mr. Birchall continued, was not a question of teetotallism at all, but a question whether licenses should become a vested interest to be purchased, or Should continue to be granted from year to year. In making the proposition they had done the Government had gone against the ruling of one of the high law courts, which had decided that the justices had a perfect right to refuse a license, and that a license was only granted from year to year. The grant of a license was a great privilege which very few obtained, and it raised immensely the value of certain houses, and he contended that the power which gave this license could take it away. If a license were given for the public con- venience, and afterwards it was found that the public convenience did not require the license, it was a matter of plain commonsense. that it. could be taken away again by the authority that eaveit. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He believed that if compensation were given very few would get any share of it besides the rich brewers ; such men as Sir A. B. Walker, Sir Gilbert Greenall, the Guiness's, Allsopp's, and people of that sort. (Hear, hear, an applause.) Mr. HEmtv THORNTON, speaking from the audience, said he should like this question answered : Was. the ' license granted to the man or the house? (Voices: "To , the man.") Well, if that were the case it was clear that I a man who had a license granted to him for twelve months was independent of the house, and could stick to the license and set up shop elsewhere. But that was not so, and it had never been attempted. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. Thomas BAINES, also speaking from the audience, contended that the license was granted ti the man who, so long as he held the license, would be entitled to the compensation. Mr. Baines explained that at present he was a teetotaller, though he did net know how long he might remain one. (Laughter.) The Rev. JorrN GIINNBLL seconded Mr. Birchall's pro- posal. He remarked that the actual wording of the act, about which there had been some little dispute,was this: "It (the license) shall be in force for one year from the date of its being granted." That, he thought, so far as an Act of Parliament could settle a matter, had for ever settled that particular question. (Applause.) It was for one year, and one year only, the permission to sell was granted. (Hear, hear:) He seconded the resolution for several reasons. The proposed Bill would create a new vested interest of a most formidable character, which had no basis in law, and no support in the decisions of the judges, and would be detrimental to society at large in years to come. There was no property in the license. (" Oh !") It was simply a permission to sell intoxicat- ing drinks under two or three very stringent conditions. The first condition appointed a time, and the Act of Parliament clearly showed that time to be one year. Thera was no such thing in point of law as a renewal of a license. (Hear, hear.) The word had no legal status The license when granted each year was a new license, not a renewal. (Applause.) The other condition was as to character. If a man holding a license committed a breach of the law, the license was taken from him, and he found extreme difficulty in obtaining another in any town. So that there was really no property in a license, and he held that you could not compensate when there ' was no property involved. (Applause.) Another reason for supporting the motion was that by the passage of that clause the action of any Licensing Board would be most seriously fettered. A further reason was that it would throw back the tensperance reformation by half a cen- tury. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) The Rev. E. Moone supported tile proposal. He said the burden of proof rested upon those who asserted that the refusal of a license entitled a publican to compensa- tion, but, although he had been listening with consider- able interest to the remarks on the other side, he had yet to learn that there:was any legal ground, or any just or moral claim,on the part of the publicans to compensation. (Hear, hear.) They had come to the conclusion as a nation that they must have fewer public-houses.

If that were so Ile failed to see where the claim for compensation catne_9l* He felt sure the Bill would not become law. It was ow/ an electioneering trick on the part of the Government ; bid for the support of "the trade "at the next election. (Loud applause.) (Haar, hear, and loud apPlatl'•—• ving Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS seconded the motion, obser of that be was very greatly obliged to the publicans to Warrington for coming to that meeting and helPing od make it such a magnificent success. (Laughter CO applause.) As treasurer of the Warrington Tenilae."—ds Federation, he should be most happy, as their friel:l the publicans had had such a fair and impartial heatrhal:i that evening, to receive one half of the expenses °f hear, meeting from the funds of the publicans.- (Rear' ,and laughter.) div.head: COMPENSATION QUESTION.
div.p: THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.

OPPOSITION MEETING AT WARRINGTON. On Tuesday evening, a meeting called at the in- stance of the Warrington Temperance Federation, was held in the Cairo-st.-Co-operative Hall, with the object of protesting against the Compensation clauses of the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill.

There was a large attendance. In the unavoidable absence of the Rev. J. J. Langham, the chair was oc- cupied by the Rev. John Yonge, and amongst those present were the Revs. F. K. Freeston, J. Davies, F. R. Roberts, J. Gunnell, E. Moore, E. H. Jackson. Messrs. T. Birch all, R. Garnett, J.P., W. Twiss, J. Gandy, S. P. Stringer, W. H. Butler, W. Davidson, J. Harrison, T. Dale, W. Gleave, J. Evans, J. Owen, T. Hawthorne, G. S. Allan, W. Beswick, and Richard Storey. Several members of the Licensed Victual- _ _ . . _

lers' Association also attended. LETTERS FROM ABSENTEES. At the commencement of the proceedings, the Trea- surer, Mr. William Roberts, explained that Mr. Lang- ham, one of the coroners for London, had met with a serious accident. Mr. Langham was the father of their esteemed friend the Rev. J. J. Langham, vicar of Pad- gate, and in consequence of the accident he had been summoned to London. In consequence of Mr. Lang- ham's absence, it fell to his lot to propose that their friend the Rev. John Yonge take the chair. (Applause.) The Rev. Joni.; YONGE having done so, called upon Mr. Roberts to read letters of apology for non-attendance. Mr. ROBERTS then read the following letter from Mr. John Walker:—" 5, Grappenhall-road, Latchford, June 3, 1890. Dear Mr. Langham,—Were it not for an illness which has confined me to the house for a week, I should certainly be with you this evening to join in the strong protest which will, I trust, be made against the Compen- sation Bill. The highest courts of the land have decided that there is no such thing as a vested interest in a license. The license is a privilege which lasts for twelve months, and it is altogether unreasonable and inequitable to propose that privileged people should be compensated. The Government are trying to force the Bill upon an un- willing Parliament, and an unwilling people. They are doing it, they say, in the interests of temperance. This is to add insult to injury, for there is not a tempeiance society in the country worthy of the name that has not already protested against this mischievous Bill. I trust you will have a good meeting, and help to drive the Government, as they were driven two years ago, from a false and dangerous position. If one meeting be not sufficient, we must have another and another." Councillor Henry Roberts wrote :—" Rose Cottage, Latchford, June 3rd, 1890. Rev, and dear sir,—l am extremely sorry at being prevented from attending to- night's meeting. I should have been glad to have had lan opportunity of protesting against the barefaced attempt of the Chancellor of the Exchequer to create a legal title to, and to provide the means for payment of, a compensation to publicans, which the highest tribunal as yet appealed to has declared in effect to be hitherto non-existent. Compensation, forsooth ! Yes, there is need for it—the man whose property has been depreciated by the opening of a drinkshop close to his home deserves it, the long-suffering ratepayer who is annually mulcted to keep up a system of police, workhouses, goals and lunatic asylums, because of this abominable system : the widows and children of hundreds of thousands of our countrymen whose early deaths have resulted from the habit of intemperance—all these and many more have a far prior claim to compensation than have the religious millionaire • brewers, whose licenses are only held by obedient nominees. Surely the brewing monopoly has squeezed enough out of our people without seeking, Shy- lock like, for another pound of flesh.'" Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P. wrote: "Oak Mount, HeAy, Warrington, 3rd June, Dear Mr. Roberts,—l am obliged for your P. C. to hand this morning. It would have given me pleasure to be present at your meeting to-night; but itias so inconvenient to haveto return home to Helsby twicd'in the day, and to walk home a distance lof more than a mile at 10.30 to 11 at night. This I would do, however, if I did not know that Fon are well supported in this crusade against the Goverrnment Pub- licans' Endowment Bill. lam fully with you in senti- ment, as I do not see the• justice of compensating the brewer or publican for a fictitious value given to his premises by the granting of a license which is only annual, and which the magistrates have a perfect right to refuse to renew, without compensation. Mr. Caine's speech seems to me unanswerable. I should be disposed to deal as leniently as possible with the publican,and give him ample time to look about him before taking his license away, if he had conducted his house in a respect- able manner. But I see no reason for this leniency in cases where the house has been badly managed. With kind regards, yours faithfully, E. J. Guest. THE CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH. The Cnsonateri, who was received with applause, said that the compensation question wal one that had two sides, and if both sides should find expression in one way or other, he hoped such expression would be in perfect friendliness, perfect good temper, and perfect good order. His experience of Warrington meetings led him to believe that such would certainly be the case, and he trusted that they would be able to reason out the matter in all brotherliness and neighbourliness of feeling. That was a meeting which had been called by the Warrington Tem- perance Federation, who were interested in the advance- ment of temperance throughout the country. It was not surprising that the friends of temperance should be some- what astonished and alarmed at the proposals of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, who proposed, by means of the Local Taxation, Customs, and Excise Bill, to devote £440,000 a year, derived from the customs and excise duties, for the purpose of extinguishing public-house licenses in the kingdom. The intention was to hand over £350,000 of this sum to England and Wales,to the County Councils,who would have power to buy up superfluous houses. Perhaps upon the question of superfluous public- houses some of them might have an idea that the num- ber of such was very large. Such being the case, they I might be disposed to say that the amount of money was ridiculously inadequate., It was alleged by the Govern- ment that they were doing this in the%interests of tem- perance ; that their aim was gradually to reduce the number of public-houses in the kingdom. Well, he hardly supposed that there was anyone in that room who would object to the reduction of public-houses, but there were, he hoped, a majority of them who would say that it should be done by the means in existence—by the power that the justices already had vested in them to refuse new licenses, and, when they saw it desirable, to curtail the number of licensesalready in existence. (Ap- plause.) Sometimes they heard used the phrase "renewal of licenses." He supposed that was incorrect. A public- house license lived for a year, and then died, and if the publican was to go on again the next year, he had not to obtain a renewal ef the old license, but anew license altogether. He believed it had been decided over and over again by the highest courts that a license this year did not give a claim for a license next year. In other words, that a publican had no vested interest be- yond the twelve months for which his license ran. (A Voice : "He should have.") When his license expired, he had no legal claim against anyone 10 respect of it. The Government proposed to over-ride all the decisions that had been given by the highest legal authorities, and to create for the first time a vested interest. It was an attempt to carry by a side-wind a principle that public opinion declared against two years ago. He could not help saying that in his opinion the Government was ill- advised in re-opening the question. It seemed to him that there were ample reasons why they should protest against compensation being given to publicans. A liquor license conferred a monopoly upon the man who possessed it. He believed that political economists were agreed that monopolists could have very little, or no, claim to c3mpensation, because the monopoly they were enjoying was equivalent to anything in the shape of compensation. Compensation to a liquor seller would be a very one-sided ,and a very unjust thing. Was it not the case that when a license was obtained the property surrounding the house deteriorated in its value, and yet no one compensated the hcuseholders for the infliction of the license? Then again, compensation had never yet ban recognised by the law of the country. In some parts of the country the Sunday traffic in the sale of drink had been stopped, by which one-seventh of the trade of the license holders had been taken from them; but they had not been com- pensated. The hours of sale had frequently beenreduced.

div.head: MARKETS COMMITTEE.
div.p: MARKETS COMMITTEE.
. The miputes of this Committee, which reported a total of receipts of £133 12s. 10d., were adopted on the motion of Councillor HUTCHINSON seconded by Councillor TAYLOR.
RIVERS' COMMITTEE.

To this Committee the Borough Surveyor reported that the Upper Mersey Commissioners had obtained clauses in the Widnes Brine Company's scheme which compel the Company to alter the bridge proposed to be put over the river at Fiddler's Ferry, to a width of 450 feet between the piers (which piers will be placed outside the tide- way); with a height of 75 feet above high-water spring tides. In the Widnes Brine Company's original scheme, it was proposed to construct a bridge only 200 feet be- tween the piers which would have caused one of the piers to be in the tideway. Alderman Dome, inproposing the confirmation of the minutes, said that the Committee had had to consider as to how far the river would be damaged if the Widnes Brine Company were allowed to carry a bridge over it at Fiddler's Ferry. The bridge the company proposed would have had one pier in the tideway, and would have inter- fered with the navigation up to Warrington. The Mersey Commissioners, having only a small fund at their dispo- sal, appealed against this in conjunction with the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board and the River Conservancers, with the result that the company were required to provide for a bridge 450 feet span, without any pier being placed in the tideway. That was a clause in the Bill, but the Bill had been thrown out. He should like the Council to feel, however, that the Upper Mersey Com- missioners, although they contributed only a small amount to the funds, were careful to look after their in- terests. Had the Bill been passed, it would have been greatly to the interest of Warrington to have the clause put in. Councillor HEATON seconded the proposition, which was carried. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. THE WATER WORKS PURCHASE. . .

_ The minutes of the General Purposes Committee re- commended that, on the advise of counsel and the par- liamentary agents, the township of Poulton be withdrawn from the proposed extension of the Borough, and that notice thereof be given to Messrs. Hutchings ; and that the Town Clerk be authorised to insert clauses in the Bill on behalf of the Cheshire County Council, providing for the adjustment of financial relations between the county and the Borough by. the Local Government Board. The minutes also contained the terms of purchase as finally arranged with the directors of the Water Works Com- pany, and recommended that the Town Clerk be in- structed to make a final offer of such terms to the company. The terms, which were fully detailed in the last issue of" The Examiner," state that the considera- tion for the purchase shall be a sum equivalent to 30 years' purchase of the maximum statutory annual divi- dends upon the present paid up capital of the company. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman BURGESS seconded, the adoption of theminutes. Councillor FLEMING drew attention to clause 8 in the terms of purchase, which read :—"The Corporation shall pay to the company at or before the date of transfer a sum of 13,000, to be placed at the disposal of the direc- tors, and applied by them in, payment of the costs, charges, and expenses incurred by the company, of, and incident to the Corporation Bill, the negotiations, the transfer of the undertaking, and the winding up of the affairs of the company, and also in compensations and gratuities to the company's officers and servants." That seemed to him to be a very large sum. He had under- stood that about £1,500 would be the maximum charges incurred in winding up the company. If that was the case, he would like to know how the other £1,500 would be spent. Alderman HARRISON: He would be a very cunning member of this Council who could explain it. (Laugh- ter.) Councillor FLEMING : Well, if I cannot get any infor- mation on the point, I beg to move that instead of 3,000 being paid to the Water Works Company, we pay them only £2,000. Councillor JAMES FAIRCLOUGH seconded the amend- ment. _ . _
The MAYOR: You can only move that that particular clause be left out. Councillor FLEMING : I Will move that the clause be left out.

The MAYOR said he thought Councillor Fleming would get a satisfactory explanation later on. Councillor Morals said that no explanation had been given of the withdrawal of the township of Poulton from the Bill. He did not know what explanation there was to be made, or what action they were prepared to take with respect to the other portions of the town that might not wish to be within the line of the boundary. He did not see upon what grounds they could ask works like theirs to be brought within the borough boundary when they excluded other portions of the district simply because they happened to have opposed. He regretted very much now that they did not put themselves in a position to oppose the Bill before the Lords. It was not too late to oppose it llefore the Commons, but he did not wish to take any action unless forced to it. If they ex- cluded one portion from the Bill, he did not see why they should not exclude another. Alderman BURGESS explained that the exclusion or striking out of the Padgate portion of the Bill had taken place in consequence of the representations of the Parlia- mentary agent and the counsel who drew up the Bill. They were of opinion that Poulton being outside the limits of the Parliamentary borough could not be included in the Improvement Bill, for no Committee would listen to it for a moment. The Committee had no other reason. They would have been glad to have retaiaed it if they had not been advised that it would never have been passed by a Committee of the House. Councillor MUIR: Is the Council supposed by this action to confirm the whole Bill? The MAYOR: Yes. Those were the very best terms the Sub-Committee had been able to make, and if they were not adopted the whole thing must fall through. Councillor FLEMING : But if the shareholders of the Water Works Company decide otherwise? The MAYOR: A meeting of the shareholders has been called for the purpose of considering these very terms. Councillor FLEMING.: How about the £3,000.

The MAYOR It is to cover the Parliamentary costs, and the costs of winding up. Alderman HARRISON said that, as a member of the Sub-Committee who waited on the directors of the Water Works Company, he might perhaps give a little explana- tion of what was done. At a meeting held on the morn- ing they met the directors a motion was moved that the Sub-Committee should offer as an ultimatum the sum of £2,000. That was to cover the expenses of winding up, Parliamentary costs, and all other incidental expenses. An amendment was moved and carried giving the Sub- Committee power to go to the extent of £3,000. They went to the company, and did everything they could to limit the amount to £2,000. Three or four interviews took place between the Sub-Committee and the directors that morning, and ultimately, when it was found that they could really do nothing better, the sub-Committee offered £3,000. The directors wanted £3,500, but the Sub-Committee would not go beyond £3,000, because ' they had not been empowered to do so. Councillor Fleming had asked what the sum of £3,000 was for? He (Alderman Harrison) could net tell him, neither could the deputation. He could not explain it, and the directors would not do so, because they did not consider themselves bound to. They said that the £3,000 would not more than cover their expenses incidental to the winding-up and transfer of the concern to the Corporation. Whilst he was of opinion that the acquisition of the Water Works by the Corporation would ultimately be to the great advantage of the town, he was far from believing that the ratepayers would reap any immediate advant- age. He did not think they would. ("No.") He thought they would have to put their hands into their pockets by paying something out of the rates ; but that the undertaking would in the end be of advantage to them he had little doubt.

Councillor FLEMING said that, after Alderman Harrison's explanation, he would withdraw his amend- ment. He should be very sorry to see the Bill wrecked for the sake of a thousand pounds. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR, in submitting the minutes, remarked that any gentleman who was personally interested in the Water Works Company ought not to vote in the matter, and Alderman Davies, and Councillors Tinsley, Shaw Green, and Hepherd then left their seats. The resolution was put, and carried unanimously, and the Council then rose.
