WARRINGTON RAGGED SCHOOL.

Sir,—Kindly allow me, on behalf of the Warrington Ragged Sunday School Committee, to thank all those benevolent friends who have assisted us with their liberal gifts in money, food, clothing, &c.; also the "Cheshire Lines Amateur Dramatic Society" for their kindness in trying to help us by performing the play of "Macbeth," which was rendered in an efficient manner, but owing to its beins, "Passion Week," and there being several other attractions in the town, it proved a great loss of time, trouble, and money. Therefore, we make a special appeal for help to our r:ch people, in order to enable us to carry on this goorl, arduous work, in training, the pom children to be sober, honest, and industrious, and in helping them in the best way we can. There is a decided improvement in cleanliness, behaviour, and dress, so that our labours are not in vain. We are trying to clear a debt off the school of over £2O. Anyone desirous of seeing the school will be cordially received on Sundays at 2.30 p.m. and 6.30 in the evening, when a service is held for children and their parents who do not attend any place of worship. Short addresses are given by friends, and singing and reciting by the children. Subscriptions thankfully received by JAMES SKELLAND, Superintendent, 60, Bewsey-rd. RICHARD DALE, Parker-st..
JAMES RIGBEY, Foundry-st. Messrs. OSBORNE and OWEN, Eustace-st.

THE GOVERNMENT LICENSING PROPOSALS. Sir,—Although present on Tuesday evening at the Temperance Federation meeting on the ...question of compensation to publicans for withdrawal of licenses, I could not see my way clear to vote for either the reso- lution or the amendment, for I think that the only way to get a satisfactory conclusion is to place the matter before the country in a constitutional manner. The Rev. F. K. Freeston lifted the subject from the teetotal and publicans'grooves, into which it had drifted, and placed it in its constitutional sphere. Most of the speakers must have thought that they were speaking to a crowd of infants. Very little or no notice was taken of the question of custom, equity, and the moral aspects of the case, but a great deal too much was said of the legal view of the subject. Whether my opinions are worth anythin., or not, I feel I must be straight- forward and say 'that I believe that the question will never be properly or fairly settled unless some method is adopted of compensating those persons whose licenses may be withdrawn. There was great doubt expressed at the meeting as to whether licenses were renewed, or whether new licenses were granted. The decision of Mr. Justice Field, however, settles this point and leaves no doubt about it. His decision was expressed in these words "In every case, in every year there is a new license granted. The legislature recognises no vested right at all in any holder of a license." I do not support the amendment, believing that the Bill now before Parliament would be no use to either the temperance party or the publicans. It does not lay down any line or method by which compensation is to be awarded. It simply gives County Councils power to go to the licensed victuallers and say that they wanted to buy out their licenses for the public good. Under these circumstances publicans might ask what they liked, a proceeding which would be very unfair and unconstitu- tional. There should be precise lines laid down by which compensation should be awarded, and if a Bill was brought forward laying down precise lines of compensa- tion on moderate terms, I think it would, in the interests of the public good, be expedient to pass it. The licensed victuallers interest is the work of centuries,and whatever be done they should be dealt with fairly and honourably,but at the same time I think there should be a proper limit as to time and amount of com- pensation, together with a certain degree of compulsion where deemed necessary. The licenses should be bought out upon some fair valuation, and not under a measures which sets up a principle of compensation with- out laying down any definite rule or method what- ever. The question is an important one and involves serious issues, and I contend that no measure'dealing with so large a question should have been brought forward until it lu..d been submitted to, and approved of, by the con- stituencies. The amendment further expresses the opinion that the present proposals of the Government would promote the cause of temperance. How can the cause of temperance be promoted by taking off the licenses of small beerhouses and giving a greater mono- poly than exists at present to those in more favourable circumstances? This would not, to my mind, cause any decrease whatever in drunkenness. The promoters of the meeting cannot fairly congratu- late themselves at the result of the voting, which cer- tainly did not give them a rnajority of more than 50. Hoping that this question will be honourably and fairly settled in accordance with the principles of custom and equity.—l am, yours truly,

div.head: 10, Ellen-street, Bewsey-road. Warrington, June 4th, 1890.
div.p: 10, Ellen-street, Bewsey-road. Warrington, June 4th, 1890.
THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me space to ask you and your readers a question on what appears to me an im- portant matter? The question is, what reason or com- mon-sense is there in giving a man, or combination of men, a sum of money to buy that which neither he, nor they, nor anyone else want, and have no earthly use for, and is no earthly good, but cn the contrary is a positive evil? Common-sense would dictate that, if it is an evil, suppress it without ceremony or compunction, paying nothing for what is not only worthless but mischievous. But common-sense is a quality that our law-makers and administrators utterly ignore, or they would never think of devoting the surplus, or part of the shrplus income from taxation, to the purchase of rotten licenses, granted for one year to unsuitable and badly conducted houses. Let these licenses lapse if they are not wanted. If the grocer's shop is not wanted, or the baker, or tailor, or any other tradesman. is not wanted,he must shut up and go where he can, and no one thinks of purchasing his good-will ; simply because.it is worthless. Why then should the drinkseller be singled out for special favour? for of all men he deserves the least. His case is one of continual worry to the legislature, to the magistracy, the police, and the community in gen- eral; his trade has to be safeguarded by special laws and looked after to prevent a breach of those laws by an army of police ; and his customers, very, very, many of them, have to be attended by a host of officials in the shape of poorlaw Guardians, relieving officers, police- men, gaolers, warden, madhouse keepers, &c., &c. And now when he gets too bad to go any further he must be bought up with the public money and made happy for life! How very kind, philanthropic, disinterested . Five thousand pounds invested would insure an in- come, a very modest one, of 15s. a week to each of the Balaclava survivors, but Mr. Stanhope save the money cannot be spared—" It is impossible !" Were a clause inserted in the public-house Compensation Bill to give each of these poor fellows that amount not a word would besaid against it. There would be neither adverse vote nor criticism, but it seems thatthe useless drink-manager is preferred before the worn-out soldier. The one has risked his life a hundred times in the defence of his country on a pittance that would not permit him to save £l.O in ten years. The other stands behind his bar re- ceiving* other men's earnings, conferring no benefit upon the community but rather the reverse, and whose house when shut up benefits the neighbourhood far more than when it is open. This compensation clause is a stroke of Tory policy, a sop thrown to the drink interest. Even should it fail there is the desire shown by the Tory party to benefit their friends who must take the will for the deed, and be satis- fied with the attempt, even should it fail. The endeavour to cram us with the idea that this compensation clause is in the interest of temperance is sheer rot and hum- bug. Why all the jubilation among the drink-sellers if it is in the interest of temperance ? Temperance and drink are as fax asunder as the poles. The publicans have besti drinking Mr. Goschen's health, so they say, and write to i Sir Wilfred Lawson to boast of it—all n " the interest of temperance." The publican's interest is the interex of a class who fatten upon the improvident, and whost busi- ness conduces to poverty and crime. The interests of temperance is the interest of ;the community at large, tendin,e: to increase our national and persond wealth, aud to augment the sum of human happinesr by direct-

ing the wage earnings of the people into legitimate and wealth producing channels, and by bringing comfort to homes previously made comfortless and miserable through drink. The drink traffic is a monopoly now, hanging like a millstone on the nation's neck. Pass thisclause and it will become heavier and more firmly riveted than ever. Spurn it. then, and let all right-minded people unmistak- ably declare that such an infamous clause shall not be added to the statute book.—l am, sir, yours respect- fully, Sankey Bridges, June 2nd, 1890.
[ADVERTISEMENT.] TIIE CHURCH OF ROME.
CYMRO.

Sir,—l have felt disappointed that none of your Protes- tant cprrespondents have stated a little more clearly some of the leading doctrines and practices of the Church of Rome. We could scarcely expect Mr. Williamson to do so. It is the policy of the Church of Rome in a Protestant country like England to keep them as much as possible in the back-ground. In a country where the Church of Rome has no power, Protestants appear to lose sight to a great extent of what she really is. I will name a few points which I think are worthy of notice. No Bible is allowed in English but the " Douay Bible" with the Apocrypha, wed no one is permitted to read or possess that without the written authority of the Bishop. The Church is the sole interpreter of the bible. The bible derives its whole authority from the Church. The Church makes tradition equal to Scripture. The Church of Rome claims to be the only true Church upon the earth. Thomas Aquinas says, "The Pope, by divine right Lath spiritual and temporal power as supreme king of the world, so that he can impose taxes on all Christians and destroy towns and castles for the preservation of Christianity." . . . . . .

The Church of Rome claims to be infallible. All other societies arrogating to themselves the name of church, guided by the spirit of darkness, are sunk in the most pernicious error, both doctrinal and moral. Seven sacraments were instituted by Jesus Christ and necessary for salvation. All children, whether of Jews, heretics, pagans, or any other, who die unbaptised, (in the Church of Rome) are excluded from heaven.

The Council of Trent says whosoever shall deny that in the sacrament of the Eucharist "there are truly and substantially contained the body and blood of Jesus Christ together with his soul and divinity, and consequ- ently Christ entire, but shall affirm that he is present only in a sign and figure, or by his power, let him be accursed." "If anyo.te shall say that this holy sacra- ment should not b 3 adored," "nor held up publicly to the people to adore it, or that its worshippers are idola- ters, let him be accursed." Auricular confession: Few Protestants understand the horrors involved in this practice. Priestly absoluticn : The priest, not God, is the judge and grants the absolution. Works of superorogatiott, or good works done beyond what God requires.

Purgatory: Prayers for the dead. Celibacy of the clergy. Prayers to the Virgin and all the saints. The services of the church are all conducted in Latin. The granting of indulgences, that is liberty, for a cer-
tam n term, to 'Commit sin without having to pay the

penalty. Mariolatry : In 1840 the Pope granted an indulgence for 100 days to everyone who should recite a prayer to the Virgin Mary to this effect" 0 immaculate Queen of heaven and of angels. I adore you. It is you who have delivered me from hell ; it is you from whom I look for all my salvation." In 1849 the Pope says" Let us have recourse to the most holy and immaculate Virgin Mary, who, being the mother of God, and our mother, and the mother of mercy, finds what she seeks and cannot be frustrated." One principle on which the Church of Rome acts is, "No faith with heretics." Antother is, " The end sancti- fies the means." Anyone wishing to know more fully what the Church of Rome is, should make himself acquainted with the history of the Jesuits and the Inquisition. It is interesting in connection with these matters to notice what is going on just now in Malta.—Yours faith- fully, 28th May.
JULIUS.

div.head: EDWIN WRIGHT.
div.p: EDWIN WRIGHT.
A CANDID CRITICISM.

Sir,—May I crave your indulgence for a few lines in the "Examiner," on a question which closely touches the honour of the town ? By way of introduction, I may say that Warrington has the distinguished honour of being my birth-place. Though resident for the last 35 years in the midland metropolis, I often pay a visit to it, to wander over ground Iso often trod in my early youth, and also to spend a few pleasant hours in the com- pany of very dear friends of mine who still reside within its borders. My interest in its welfare and fair fame is still further enhanced by the fact that I chose thepartner of my life from amongst its many pretty lasses, and any- thing that tends to degrade the softer sex,or bring dis- credit upon its inhabitants generally, I view with pain and sorrow.

My visit was timed to be at Whitsuntide, not perhaps a very favourable time to estimate or gauge the social habits of its people. The inhabitants of the town ever since I can remember have always had an unenviable notoriety for their drinking habits ; still I was fain to , believe that during a period of 35 years some change had , come over them ; that they had caught the spirit of ; improvement which has marked so long a period of time; , that the many social agencies which have been established ' in other parts of the country with such decided success had succeeded in reaching Warrington, thus checking the giant evil that stalks through the streets with unabashed effrontery. But I am sorry to say I saw no change in their habits, at any rate no change for the better. There were the same scenes in the street—of men, and women too, reeling from one side of the street to the other, with the evident intention of trying to keep in the middle, the same lounging and congregating of bemuddled tipplers in the public thoroughfares, block- ing the way of the more respectable portion of the inhabitants, and the language that was indulged in by these groups was of the vilest and foulest kind, polluting the very air they breathed. One of my friends in War- rington has several times given me a rub of the rough element in Birmingham, and I do not deny the " soft impeachment" that there is a rough element in "the best governed town in the world," but I saw more drunkenness from Monday to Saturday, heard the vilest language, from both sexes alike, and witnessed more disorder in the public streets of Warrington than I have seen in Birmingham the whole of this year, though Bir- mingham is:more than ten times the size of Warrington. One particular case that attracted my attention, and of which I was an eyewitness, I feel I must mention. As I was crossing over from Church-st. to Fennel-st., I saw a female in a beastly state of intoxication being helped home by her husband, whit was little better than his wife. As I approached nearer, I heard her giving vent to the foulest and most obscene language I ever heard in my life,in a voiceof stentorian tones which could be easily heard across the street. I did not learn upon whom this vile abuse was being heaped, as I could not single out anyone in the crowd to whom she paid special attention in her obscene expressions. This scene began at the corner of Dial-st., was carried on along Fennel-st., up Church-st. as far as Orchard-st., when she disappeared from view. On her way every now and then she relapsed into a quieter mood, and then, with a sudden jerk, she would release herself from the grasp of her husband and return to the charge with renewed violence and with ntore forcible language—if that could he possible. The scene lasted for about 15 to 20 minutes. What struck me mostly, and what I was most astonished at, was that during part of the time, an officer of the law, a preserver of the public peace, stood within sight and earshot calmly surveying the proceedings, without so much as lifting his finger to suppress it. How is this,l Mr. Editor? Why was she not "run in " ? Is it because the police are powerless to act, or because the scene I have attempted to describe is of too frequent occurrence for interference? Surely this kind of thing can be put down if the powers that be are alive to the responsibili- ties that belong to the office they fill. What are the magistrates doing to remove the disgrace that attaches to the town? Is the Watch Committee, who have the control of the police, asleep that they do not grapple with it? Or is it due to the incompetency of these bodies that such a state of things exist? If so, I should strongly recommend the mere sober and orderly portion of the community to take the matter into their own hands and potition the Lord Chancellor to appoint a new batch of magistrates; and also to select a class of men on the governing body of the town who are more in sym- pathy with law and order, and have the weal and good government of the town at heart. Now, ,gir, I do not write in the interest of any Teetotal or Temperance Society. lam not a teetotaler. lam not a railer against the publicans. I have not yet joined that oody of visionaries who would suppress public- houses by coercion. I claim, however, to be a lover of lass and order and public decency, and would mete out punishment with a strong hand on all people who out- age and offend the taste of decent and respectable citizens. Trusting that you may see your way to insert these few lines in your paper, and hoping that some improvement may take place in the direction I have indicated, before I next visit Warrington,—l am, ON OLD WARRINGTONIAN.

THE VICARAGE OF Sr. MARY'S LOWTON.—The Rev. William Berridge, of Upholland Grammar School, near Wigan, will shortly take up the position which is at present held by the Rev. W. A. Nicklin, as curate-in- charge. Mr. Nicklin is expected to proceed to South- port.

div.head: SHIP CANAL "GRABBER"
div.p: SHIP CANAL "GRABBER"

One of the most interesting pieces of mechanism used on the Ship Canal is the " grabber," an illus- tration of which we give this week. A glance at the illustration will show that the machine is worked somewhat on the principle of a moveable crane. The grabs which in the illustration are open ready to descend, force their powerful claws or teeth into the clayey soil, and, closing, bring away with .them a consideFable quantity of material, which is swung round in the same way as is the soil in the bucket of a steam navvy, until it reaches a position over a train of wagons. The mechanism then causes the grab to open again, and the material drops into the wagon. This operation is repeated over and over again with surprising rapidity, and during a day's working a large amount of soil is dealt with. These machines can be used for a variety of purposes, such as dredging docks, harbours, and rivers, and for gold dredging; excavating for new docks, canals, and railway cuttings; cutting trenches for pipe laying ; lifting grain, coal, coke, land, blasted rock, &c. ; pile driving, or as an ordin- ary portable engine. There are three different types of the bucket or grab, to suit the various classes of materials to be dealt with, and these tools are made with capacities of three hundredweight to three tons.

div.head: FATALITY ON THE SHIP CANAL WORKS.
div.p: FATALITY ON THE SHIP CANAL WORKS.

On Wednesday morning a man named James Rich- mond. aged 28, residing at Rush Green, and who works on the Ship Canal, went to speak to another man named Joseph Teat, who was engaged close to an American navvy at Statham, and while so doing some wagons were seen by Teat coming along the ballast line. Rich- mond's attention was at once called to the danger, but before he could get out of the way he was caught between the buffers:of the moving wagon and the stationary one near which he was standing. He received terrible injuries, but was able to ask his companion to lift him up. This was done, and a locomotive was at once pro- cured and the injured man taken to the hospital at Thel- wall. Teat went with him, and during the journey Richmond was quite conscious. The resident surgeon on seeing the nature of the injuries at once sent for the man's wife, to whom he had been married about a year, but before she arrived the injured man expired.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL (VARIOUS POWERS, &c.) BILL
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL (VARIOUS POWERS, &c.) BILL

On Thursday it was formally reported that in the case of this Bill there had been a non-compliance with the House of Lords standing orders, inasmuch as a petition for an additional provision was not received at the usual period. The matter was referred to the Standing Orders Committee for their consideration whether or not this non-compliance can be excused. The promoters seek to add to the preamble of the bill a statement that arrange- ments have been made with the Cheshire County Coun- cil, the Daresbury Highway Board, and the London and Northwestern Railway Company, which render it desir- able to abandon the construction of the Ackers-lane Bridge, that a new road should be constructed in Bud- worth, and that in Flixton a new footbridge should be constructed to carry Parsonage-rd. over the Manchester and Liverpool Railway of the Cheshire Lines Committee. The clausesfurther provide for the diversion of a portion of the road between Warrington and Manchester, near Irlam, and for other road alterations at Runcorn, Walton, Latchford, and other places, while at Runcorn power is sought to make, if necessary, a new cut in connection with the Bridgewater Canal, and to deepen the big pool at Halton.

div.head: SCHOOLBOY DROWNED AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: A SCHOOLBOY DROWNED AT WARRINGTON.

A fatal accident eccurred on Thursday afternoon, to a boy named Herbert Unsworth, who was eleven years of age, and resided with his parents at 165, Liverpool-road. The lad left home shortly before nine in the morning, ostensibly for the purpose of attending the People's College, but meeting with some companions he was induced to play truant. The boys spent the morning playing by the canal side at Sankey, and were on their way home, when, near the turnbridge opposite Mill-lane,tinsworth slipped and fell into the canal. Before assistance could be procured, he sank and was drowned.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.

The public meeting to protest against the Com- pensation clauses of the Local Taxation Act was carried out with success on Monday evening. The gentlemen on the platform repres flted all shades of political opinion, and held different tenets of religious belief, and no one would have the hardi- hood to allege that it was a party gathering in any sense of the word. If there were others in the audience who objected to the resolution of protest there was only one who had the courage to hold up his hand against it, and the Chairman had an easy task in declaring it carried. l Dr. Gastaldi enlivened the latter part of the pro- ceedings by exhibiting what he aptly termed relics of barbarism. In his peregrinations he had picked up beneath a bed pillow, a bottle of whisky, the solace of an old woman, a .shilleleigh, which had been wielded by a "loving husband," and a poker which had also been used with effect when the head of the household had been under the influence of the " rosy wine." As the learned Doctor remarked, there was no need to go to Africa for barbarians, when drink made us so many at home. The great event in the social world of Runcorn during the past week has been the marriage of Miss Speakman, the daughter of the County Council representative of Runcorn South, to Mr. Douetil, of Surbiton. It is many years since so stylish a wedding was solemnised in the ancient Parish Church, and the sacred edifice was well filled with a gathering of all shades of local society anxious to see the interesting ceremony performed. The "happy pair" were greeted with the usual shower of rice from numerous well wishers, but the most graceful tribute to the bride was the strewing of her path with charming flowers, by a number of young girls, and one can only hope that this pleas- ing act may truly symbolise the progress through life of Mr. and Mrs. Douetil.

The annual report of Mr. Fletcher, chief inspector under the Alkali, &c., Works Regulation Act, 1881, contains information which will be hailed with delight by the people of Widnes. No town has suffered more by the nuisance arising from the deposit of alkali waste in the neighbourhood. In addition to the deposits being of a most unsightly character, they emit a most offensive and disagree- able smell, through the sulphur contained in the compound. Dir. Fletcher states that most of the leading manufacturers in Widnes have adopted the Chanc4 process for the recovery of sulphur from this objectionable material, and it is stated that the quantity of waste thus treated in Widnes at the present time is about 1,000 tons. Mr. Fletcher expresses the belief that there will in future be a great abatement of the nuisance now existing and I it is sincerely desired that his belief will prove well founded.

At a meeting of the Primrose League at Prod- sham, a few weeks ago, Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., made a reference to Mr. Slater Lewis, the County Councillor for the district, which that gentleman states is a reflection on his character. Failing to ob- tain any satisfaction by correspondence, Mr. Lewis promises to make Mr. Reynold's speech the subject of a meeting he intends to hold at Frodsham, and he invites Mr. Reynolds to be present on the plat- form for the purpose of I" settling accounts." Al- though this has rather a sanguinary ring about it, we suppose it means nothing more deadly than "words, words, words," and if Mr. Reynolds would only accept the challenge, the wordy warfare would be worth walking a few miles to listen to.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 7, IS9O

div.head: LATE MR. BEAMONT.
div.p: THE LATE MR. BEAMONT.
A HANDSOME MEMORIAL.

It will be rseTneiii-lTe.;;lti-at Mr. Robert Davies, soon after Mr. Beamont's death, expressed his inten- tion of erecting a brass to his memory. The com- mission was given to Messrs. Thomason and Son, of Manchester, with instructions that the brass should be a work ot art as well as a memorial, and it has ever since been in hand, only one man being able to labour upon it. A place was, by the permission of Lord Lilford and the Rector, found for it in the Atherton Chapel in Warrington Parish Church, and the brass was fixed there on Wednesday last in anticipation of the anniversary of Mr. Beamont's death, which took place yesterday. It is of large size and is fixed upon a black marble tablet, which adds much to the effect. The inscription, which is given below, is in red and black ecclesiastical letters, surrounded by a broad border containing a fruiting vine on blue enamel. At each corner appear the emblems of the four Evangelists, the eagle of St. John, the ox of St. Luke, the lion of St. Mark, and the angel of St. Matthew. The two Latin lines of the inscription are taken from the rhythm of Barnard de Morlaix, English Monk of Cluny (12th century). This is the rhythm from part of which the hymn," Jerusalem the golden," and ()the/ well- known hymns, are adapted. The two lines referred to have been translated :

div.head: ••_Then glory yet unheard of
div.p: ••_Then glory yet unheard of

Sliall shed abroad its ray, Resolving all cenigmas, An endless Sabbath day." The inscription runs as follows :—" In pious Memory of William Bcamont of Orford Hall: born on the 12th September 1797, and baptised in this Church : died on the 6th June 1889, and buried at Padgate Church: first Mayor of Warrington: Chair- man during many years of the Museum and Library Committee : some time Vice President of the Cheet- barn Society: a Governor of the Warrington Gram- mar School: distinguished for his Antiquarian re- searches and writings: a lover of classical learning: always forward in good works : and an honour to the legal prpfession : this brass is here placed by Robert Davies and Vere Beamont Davies. Tune nova gloria pectora sobria clarificabit, Solvet enigrnata, veraque Sabbata continuabit. November, 1889."
THE PROPOSED EXTENSION OF THE WARRINGTON INFIRMARY.

On Monday evening the Town Ball, Park, and Baths Committee received deputations from the Infirmary Board of Management and the Working- men's Committee on the subject of the allotment of a portion of park land required for the exrension of the Infirmary. The Board of Management was represented by Alderman Davies, Dr. Richmond, Dr. White, Major Litton, and Mr. T. Birchall, and the Workingmen's Committee by Messrs. John Roberts, Burton, J. Potter, Croskill, H. Eyes, Big- ginson, Taylor, and T. Roberts, (secretary). Mr. W. Owen presented plans of the proposed extension.— Alderman Davies, in stating the case for the Infir- mary, said that the public had come nobly forward with funds to enable the work to be accomplished, and in face of that fact the Committee would surely not stand in the way of the extension of such an admirable institution.—Dr. Rich- mond, in urging the acceptance of the plans, said the committee would only be doing justice to themselves by affording erery opportunity for the extension of the In- firmary.—Mr. John Roberts remarked that if it became a question of a vote, three-fourths of the ratepayers would agree with the proposals of the deputations.—Alderman Davies, in answer to some members of the Committee, promised that no mortuaries should be erected on the Park lands that might be granted.—Councillor Bolton observed that they were rather short of space in the Park. Instead of giving any away they wanted some.—Major Litton asked why the Committee did not utilize the land on which a large quantity of lumber and hothouses which contained vines and produced grapes, which went— 'where? Well, he supposed that was known only to members of the Council. (Laughter.) As to the mortuaries, &c., being an eyesore, they could not be a greater eyesore than the Corporation stables, adjoining the Town Hall.— Alderman Chandlev was most favourably disposed to- wards the application, and thought it should be granted. Mr. Birchall and other speakers also supported the pro- posals.—The deputations were then asked to retire while the Committee discussed the matter.—On being read- mitted, it was intimated that the Committee had agreed to recommend the Council to grant a plot of land according to a plan amended by the Committee. The members of the deputations expressed themselves satisfied with the amended plans, and withdrew. The proposals of the Committee do not differ materially from the plans sub- mitted by the deputations. The extension will not interfere with any of the present walks in the park. A meeting of the Working-men's Committee was after- wards held. The efforts cf Alderman Davies were warmly eulogized. Progress was reported with respect to the collection for the extensions. Messrs. Mason (Mr. Thomas Hutchinson) and Thornton (Messrs. Robin- son and Skinner) were elected members of the General Committee.
It will be seen from our report that the subject of the Infirmary extension was referred to at the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesda.y evening.
LYMM.

BILLIARD HANDICAP.—The result of the billard handi- cap, which has for some weeks been in progress at the Lymm Liberal Club, is as follows :-Ist, Thomas Worrall ; 2nd, J. Knowles; 3rd, Thomas Knowles. ALLEGED THEFT.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Wed- nesday, before Mr. G. B. Dewhurst (in the chair) and Dr. Brabazon. James Abraham Smith, a travelling showman, was charged with stealing a jug and glass, the property of John Scattergood, of the Green Dragon, Heatley, of the value of Bd, on Tuesday, put the case was dismissed.

PROPERTY SALE.—OU Tuesday night a sale of property was conducted by Mr. James Percival, at the Plough Hotel, Lymm. Brook Farm, Croft, in the occupation of Mr. William Kelsall, realised £1,475. For Heatley Cottage, Rush Green, Lymm, the sum of £BBO was given; and for two houses at Lymm, with gardens, producing a yearly rental of £36, the sum of £755 was offered and accepted. Four Ship Canal shares, on which £6 had been paid up, were also sold, and realised £5 ss. each. _ .

THE VOLUNTEERS.—The H (Lymm) Company of the 3rd V.B.C.R. arrived at Lymm, after their week's en- campment at Tatton Park, on Sunday afternoon. It is stated that at the official inspection, which took place on Friday, the Lymm representatives acquitted themselves very creditably. Colonel Marshall was in command, and the Lymm officers present were Captain T. A. Jones and Lieutenants Cookson and Groves. Captain Jones. was called upon to put the regiment through a variety of movements, and a company was told off and drilled by Lieutenant Groves. A careful scrutiny was made of the camp, and the men's accoutre- ments. Colonel Brownlow, in complimenting the men on their efficiency, said he should be glad to be able to make a favourable report of the battalion. In the course of the day Lieutenant Groves, of Lymm, was examined for a certificate by a Board of Examiners, consisting of Major and Adjutant Deering and Captains Telfar and Grove.

div.head: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.

A meeting of this body was held on Thursday even- ing, at the offices at Lymm, Mr. Cameron presiding. There were also present Messrs. Brazendale, Dutton, Rogers, Thomason, Swallow, Harrison, Forster, Gibbon, Ridgway (law clerk) and Mullard (clerk). MISCELLANEOUS. —A circular was read from the Asso- ciation of Local Boards asking the Lymm Board to join the Association, but no decision was come to in the matter.—The usual reports of the surveyor and gas manager were read and adopted. . . .

THE WILLOW BEETLE.—The sewage farm report stated that the former enemy, the Willow Beetle, made its appearance in the early part of last month but the numbers were small as compared with previous years, and little or no damage had been sustained. The willows were at present looking healthy THE CONDITION OF MASSEY BROOK.—A short disdussion took place in regard to an alleged pollution of Massey brook, and it was decided that the Law Clerk write to the parties at whose works it was thought the pollution originated. THE SHIP CANAL AND RATES.—A letter was read from the Ship Canal Co. stating that certain land upon which an assessment had been made was in the hands of the contractor and the Company had no beneficial occupa- tion, and were therefore not liable to be rated.—The I Chairman said he thought the rate was not insisted upon last year, and the Clerk stated that he thought the Com- pany were entitled to have it remitted on the ground that they had no beneficial occupation.—Mr. Brazendale thought the Company ought to make some recompense for the damage they did to the roads by heavy traffic.— The Clerk said if there was extraordinary damage they could make a claim for extraordinary repairs.—After a little further discussion it was resolved to communicate with the Company in regard to the traffic. ALLEGED OBSTRUCTIONS.—A discussion took place with regard to alleged obstructions near the Cross by the erec- tion of booths and stalls, and it was stated that in certain cases proceedings had beei taken against offenders but the cause of complaint was not put a stop to. The Board considered as to what further action should be taken, and finally the matter was left in the hands of the Law Clerk.
This was the principal business. -..-.

WIIISTON POOR HATB.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Mr. E. Range, assistant overseer for Whis• ton, applied for magisterial sanction to a new poor rate of is. in the pound for the township of Whiston. The rate was estimated to produce £94.6 15s. 3d. and the arrears en the old rate were a 15s. The Bench signed the rate book.

div.head: ATTEMPTING TO SET A WIFE ON FIRE.
div.p: ATTEMPTING TO SET A WIFE ON FIRE.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a man named Robert Daniels, a mechanic, was brought up in vustody on a charge of having, on the day before, committed an aggravated assault on his wife, by attempting to set fire to her. He was also charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and two children. He pleaded guilty. Constable Jones (29) said that early on the afternoon of the previous day, he was in Church-st., when he re- ceived a complaint as to the misconduct of the pri- soner, who lives at .32, School-brow. Looking through the window of the house, he saw prisoner going to the fire-place with a bundle of papers in his hands. When questioned by witness he said he was only burning some papers. The floor was covered with burnt paper, as well as the fire-grate. Witness had received a complaint that prisoner was trying to set both his wife and the house on fire--A Mrs. Molyneaux, a neighbour, said that when prisoner burnt the paper his wife was sat near the fire. She was ill, and was unable to stir from that poAtion. Witness removed her to another chair. Prisoner was not drunk, but had had something to drink. Witness thought that if she had not been there, prisoner's wife would have been burned, because she could not move herself.—Constable Bruen said that a child came to the Polite Station and said prisoner was trying to set his wife an fire. The wife appeared to be very ill. Witness thought it was not safe for prisoner to be left in the house, and locked him up. —Mr.Garnett said that the house was in a filthy con- dition, and as there was no proper food in the house, and the wife was ill, he had her taken to the Work- house.—The magistrates thought the case a bad one, and sent Daniels to prison for a month, with hard labour.
THE FIELD CLUB IN LONDON. (FROM A CORRESPONDRNT.). .

Last week the Warrington Field Club carried out a long cherished idea of a visit to London as one of its summer excursions. Through the good offices of the chairman, convenient arrangements having been made with the railway company; and no one (notwithstanding the untimely hour at which the start was made) having succeeded in missing the train, the result was that shortly after ten o'clock on Saturday morning some ten good and true members of the club stood on the steps of the Natural History Museum, in the Cromwell-road. The architecture and decoration of the splendid building received some meed of admiration, but architecture and decoration are not included in the programme of the Field Club, and this (as the reader will see) was strictly a business trip. On entering, the first attention was given to the cases of hybrid, and intermediate forms,—of speci- fic variation under natural and domesticated con- ditions,—of albinisim and melanism, which stand prominently in the hall as illustrations of the working of those mysterious and complex forces of nature which govern the variation of organic forms. It is a striking and suggestive circumstance that whilst the whole strength of the Museum is con- stantly employed on the distinction and definition of the various forms of life, opportunity is taken in the vestibule to impress upon the visitor that from Nature's point of view there are no such hard and fast lines, but that anything may change and everything has close relations with something else. Whilst the members were enjoying this first dis- play of the very records and charters of evolution- ary theory, the party was met by the distinguished naturalist, Professor Flower, F.R.S., Director of the Museum, to whose kindness and personal attention the club is indebted for a great part of the interest of the visit. tinder his genial guidance, a tour was then made of what is called the Introductory Collec- tion, which surrounds the hall, and serves admirably its function of forming a vestibule to the study of animal and vegetable morphology. Hence, for we cannot possibly go into details, it is but a step into the British Coilectien, where the chief interest was in Lord Walsingliam's cabinet of Lepidoptera, with their larvae. The attraction of this case was so great that it was made a point of rendezvous during the day. Then came what to most visitors is the greatest treat in the Museum, and which on this occasion was declared to be worth "all the money," an inspection of the series of natural groups of British Birds. The great value of this series, apart from the skill shown in the mani- pulation, lies in the fact that the accessories are not a generalized representation of the usual habitat of the species, but are in each case the actual sur- roundings of the particular specimen,either brought bodily away, or reproduced with the greatest fidelity. Later in the day, Professor Flower took us into the Taxidermist's Room, and Dr. Giinther, the learned Keeper of the Zoological Department, described with true collector's fervour, how he him- self had taken the Tit's nest containing ten young ones, then under preparation, and we learned some- what of the care with which any interference with, or addition to the actual conditions is sought to be avoided. Here also we were shown the newest rarity, a gigantic specimen of Black Coral, for which a separate case was being made. After a careful inspection '_of the bird-groups the party divided. One section made its way to the Insect Room, where, through the kindly intervention of Mr. Waterhouse, whose nappy lot it is to spend Ids days 'in the study of unlimited new beetles, they were treated to a glimpse, really extensive but of course comparatively very slight, of some of the contents of innumerable cabinets of resplendent Papilionid, gigantic Lamellicorns, and we know not what else. Others were introduced by Mr. Boulen,ger, who has charge of the Reptiles, Amphibians, and so forth, to the "spirit department," a building behind the museum where all the specimens preserved in inflammable fluid are carefully isolated from the rest of the establishment. The graesome sights they saw -we will not detail. Meanwhile the geologists, acting up to their idea of how ttp spend a happy day. had whiled away the afternoon in the company of the ' Mammoth, the Archaeopteryx, and the multitudes of other extinct animals which fill the acre or more of galleries composing the Geological Department The re-united party were piloted by Dr. Flower himself into the perietralia of the Bird-room, where are stored the 300,000 specimens of birds upon which is based the great catalogue, which is in course of publication by Mr. R. Bowdler Sharpe, the assistant keeper in charge of the department. We cannot describe even every point of special interest —the delightful series of specimens forming the "Introduction to the study of Mineralogy," the Botanical Gallery, the—but there, suffice it to say that the interest of the place and the kindness we received were such that closing time was approach- ing when tired eyes and weary feet drove us to seek the refreshment of green grass and fresh air in the Park. Next day the party assembled, being provided with tickets by the courtesy of the Secretary of the Zoological Society, in the Society's Gardens. In the study of the unrivalled collection of living animals which there dwell, apparently in perfect health, and manifesting that supreme content which the unfailing regularity of the dinner-bell is said to produce in even the most savage natures,_ several hours were profitably and pleasantly spent. Theuce to Kew, where the botanical section were expected to reap as large a harvest of instruction as that which their colleagues had already gathered at the Zoo. But botanists were few amongst us, and human strength must fail, and we fear that the de- light of strolling on the grass and taking it all in " at the pores," like Joey Ladle,finally overcame the scientific attractions of the Herbaceous Ground and Museum No. 3. We did the sights of course, and then the sail down the river which was the last item on the programme was felt to be an appro- priate and soothing conclusion to a most delightful day. "And io home." The trip throughout was a great success. The only regret felt was on behalf of those misguided members who had etsyed at home.

div.head: HEAT AT NEW YORE.
div.p: THE HEAT AT NEW YORE.
Twelve deaths were caused in New York, on Thurs- day, by the extreme heat.
FATAL CAB RACING.
Two cabs, racing for the same farein West London, on Thursday night, collided, and were smashed. One of the drivers has since died from the injuries received.
THE WEIDEMANN WALPOLE CASE.

The case of Weidemann v. Walpole was ciDwn for hearing, before Mr. Justice Matthew and a special jury, in the Queen's Bench, yesterday. Just before the court rose for luncheon the Solicitor. General, who appeared for Mr. Walpole, said he understood the iplaintiff desired to make an application to his Lordship.—Mr. Jubtice Matthew: Is not the lady represented by counsel? Miss Weidemann said she had been informed that her cotnsel had retired from the case.—The Solicitor-General: I have a letter from the plaintiff's solicitors, in which they said that Mr. Cook, Q.C., having decided to retire from I the case, and both junior counsel having adopted the same course, they had no alternative but to do so too. They had informed the plaintiff of this.—Mr. Justice ' Matthew : Does the plaintiff wish to have an adjourn- rent to instruct counsel ?—Miss Weidemann : Yes, for a fortnight.—The Solicitor-General : Ido not object toan adjournment, but I cannot agree to a fortnight.—Mr. Justice Matthew said the case would stand over for a week, and would then be taken whether plaintiff had counsel not not.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at a quarter-past four. MISCELLANEOUS.—SeveraI private bills were advanced a stage. Lord Say e and Sele was added to the Select Committee on Metropolitan Hospitals. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS.—Mr. RAIKES, replying to Mr. Leng, said the British delegates to the International Telegraph Con- ference at Paris would gladly help to secure any reduc- tion of signalling fees to shipowners that foreign Govern- ments could adopt.—Sir JAMES FERGUSSON, replying to Sir T. Osmonde, said he could not make a statement respecting purchase of French rights in Newfoundland.— Mr. GOSCHEN, replying on behalf of Mr. Smith, to Mr. Borthwick, said the Government had seriously considered Mr. Trevelyan's motion, favouring earlier closing of the House in summer, and the First Lord would submit proposals in a few days. (Cheers.) THE TITHES BlLL.—With rezard to the Tithes Bill, the Speaker announced that six instructions to Commit- tee, which had already been declared out of order, had been succeeded by three other instructions also out of order. He had, therefore, no option but to leave the chair. (Ministerial cheers.)—The House then went into Committee of Supply. THE NEW Cons.—The adjourned debate was resumed on the vote for public Education to England and Wales. Mr. PICTON spoke in favour of the Kindergarten system, and, referring to the new code, he said it embraced three improvemements, namely, the greater simpli- city in the allotment of the grant, less variation in the annual grant, and the abolition as far as possible of the noxious system of payment by results, and the great boon to teachere, liberty of classification.— Mr. S. SMITH was glad that manual instruction had been put into the new code, and also that the vice-president of the Council had expressed himself in favour of Con- tinuation schools,at which he suggested attendance should be compulsory.—Sir J. LUBBOCK spoke in favour ot making education more interesting, and keeping children longer at school.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS
ELECTION.

The time for receiving nominations for the vacancy caused on the Board of Guardians by the death of the late Mr. John Greening closed on Thursday evening. The following gentlemen have been nominated as candidates :—Mr. Wm. Roberts, shoe manufacturer, 29, Arpley-st., proposed by Mr. Jos. Podmore, of 37, Allen-st. ; Mr. William Diggle, gentleman, nominated by Mr. Samuel Davies, of 15 and 17, Wellington-st. ; and Mr. William Eddowes, licensed victualler, 8, Bewsev-st., nominated by Mr. J. McCollom, 47, Bewsey-st. For the township of Haydock, in which there is also a vacancy, Mr. John Turton, a member of the Haydock Local Board, and Mr. Thomas Harrison, licensed victualler, have been nominated. There will, consequently, unless some of the candidates retire, be a contest in both town- ships. The voting papers will be distributed next Thursday, collected on Friday, and the votes counted on Saturday.

div.head: BOLD-ST. WESLEYAN SUNDIY SCHOOL,
div.p: BOLD-ST. WESLEYAN SUNDIY SCHOOL,
WARRINGTON.

Anniversary sermons in connection with this school were preached on Sunday, by the Rev. John Stevinson, of Alderley Edge, Manchester. There were good congregations. After the sermon in the morning the choir rendered the anthem "What are these arrayed in whiter' (Stainer). In the after- noon a sacred cantata, entitled "A day with our Lord" (by T. M. Pattison), was given by the choir and school children. The Rev. E. H. Jackson con- ducted the service, in the course of which solos, duets, Sze.. were contributed by the following:— Messrs. Fanshaw and Richardson, and Misses Gun- ton, Fanshaw, and Rawling. The singing of the children, who had been trained by the conductor of ' the choir (Mr. Fanshaw) was most praiseworthy. In the evening the Rev. J. Stevinson again occupied the pulpit. Miss Fanshaw sang the solo "Upon that cross of Jesus," and prior to the collection the choir contributed the anthem "I waited for the Lord" (Mendelssohn), the soloists being Misses Gunton and Fanshaw. Mr. Harrison was at the organ. The col- lections for the day realized a total of £55, an increase of £lO upon last year's amount. At the conclusion of the evening service the preacher paid a high compliment to the teachers and scholars of the school. He had, he said, seen many Sunday schools, but had never met with better .conducted scholars than those at Bold-st.

div.head: LECTURE BY MR. STEVINSON.
div.p: LECTURE BY MR. STEVINSON.

On Monday evening, the Rev. J. Stevinson lectured in Bold-st. Wesleyan Sunday School, on" Modern Italy, and the men who made it." The Mayor (Alderman R. W. Francomb), presided over a good attendance. The pro- ceeds of the lecture were in aid of the Sunday school. The LECTURER referred at length to the life and charac- ter of Guiseppe Mazzini, and the successful and noble efforts made by him to secure his country's freedom. Whatever England might say of Mazzini in Italy his name was loved. There they reverenced die man who, when foes were many and friends few, fought fearlessly for his country's freedom. Every character ought to be studied in relation to the times and the prevailing modes of thought. Mazzini was undoubtedly a declared Republican. They as Englishmen were justly proud of the r Queen, who had won the affections of her subjects. If, however, the hand of tyranny were raised against the m to take away their rightful heritage, there was not on e of them who would not resist. Atthe close of the 18th century two kinds of government prevailed--despotism and republicanism. There was little or no unity of pur- pose. That was the state of Italy when Austria first appeared upon the scene. By cunning intrigue and art- ful diplomacy, she succeeded in making her presence felt throughout Italy, and tried to destroy the spirit of liberty and freedom. At length the timecame for Italy to shake herself from that oppression and tyranny, if over- thrown in the attempt. She had drunk the cup of humiliation to its loathsome dregs. Such was Italy in the youth of Mazzini. He it was who ploughed the earth and sowed the seed, but it was left to others to gather the harvest. He was imbued with the love of his country, and though possessed of personal ambition, he was indifferent to applause. Mazzini believed in Divine Providence, in Jesus Christ as the Redeemer of man, but protested against the intolerance of the Papal court. 'ltaly, for the Italians" was his motto. Mr. Stevinson also referred to Count Cavour, Garibaldi and Victor Emmanuel, but said that the man who gave the Italians their watchword was Guiseppe Mazzini. Garibaldi's victories, Cavour's successful statesmanship, and Victor Emmanuel's ascent to the throne of united Italy all paled before Mazzini's triumphs. the lecture was thoroughly enjoyed. At the conclusion the Rev. E. H.Jackson pro- posed a vote of thanks to Mr. Stevinson and a similar compliment was also eccorded to the Mayor for presiding, on the motion of the Rev. J. STEVINSON seconded by the Rev. J. Guioamt.
